entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: I notice how little the narrator says he knows, but how much he's willing to say, about Myriel. Just gossip and rumors. Which allows him to say possibly contradictory things at once: Myriel was maybe a playboy, but nobody’s sure, maybe got serious because of the horrors of the French Revolution, maybe had a Road-to-Damascus-style conversion experience. Hard to say how you end up with what Myriel is going to turn out to be.... In fact, at this moment, we know more for sure about his sister: Mlle. Baptistine is almost too holy to be human (but not “venerable” without children, I guess?? 🤷‍♀️– to Hugo’s credit, he seems skeptical about this too). No questions about her past like there are about his.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: Imagine what monseigneur Henri Puget and his dinner companions from 29 July 1714 would think of monseigneur Bienvenu!! 🫣Remember how, we couldn't know anything for sure about Myriel in chapter 1? Now, we have his exact budget, *in his handwriting.* He gives to mostly religious orgs, especially those focused on education and charity, and to the poor, sick, and prisoners. The one critique we get of him in this chapter is from someone who opposes the church as an institution, and who clearly doesn’t have (doesn’t want) all the information about monseigneur Bienvenu.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: A Hard Bishopric for a Good Bishop
entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: The Bishop’s sarcasm about riding the donkey is one of my favorite moments of his! The Church’s love of status and conspicuous wealth gets no free passes from this guy. The ways he describes the difefrent communities helping each other out here are wonderfully targeted to ease poverty and sufefring in the specific contexts where they happen. What would he encourage people in our world to do, I wonder?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: The first half of this chapter continues the kinds of anecdotes that we saw in the first 3 chapters, concluding with a remark on how strangely the Bishop saw things, which, Hugo remarks cuttingly, he may have gotten from the gospels. In the second half of the chapter, we confront crime, punishment, and the death penalty. Hugo was passionately opposed to the death penalty, which was carried out exclusively by guillotine in France from the Revolution until it was abolished in 1981, in public until the 1930s. Horror at the guillotine shows up in a lot of Hugo’s works, and attributing it to the Bishop, who will be the foundation stone of everything else in this book, is signifciant. It’s also worth noting how close he got to that horror in accompanying the condemned man in this chapter, continuing to encourage him until the moment the blade fell. Other characters will engage in politics, and Hugo himself did so when it came to the death penalty, but the Bishop focuses on alleviating individual sufefring, in every situation, including that one.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Que monseigneur Bienvenu faisait durer trop longtemps ses soutanes
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Monseigneur Bienvenu made his Cassocks last too long
entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: A couple of details about the Bishop’s day-to-day life that strike me today (beyond the personal vow of poverty and the work to provide for the poor, which aren’t new): He gardens, and also refers to his reading and study as metaphorical “gardening.” He will be the first in a series of gardeners in this book… 🌹🌷🪻 As out-of-the-ordinary as Hugo makes him, he *does* do the ordinary work of a bishop – just makes it very much his own. Did you catch how Hugo wrote himself in around the edge of the story here?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. Par qui il faisait garder sa maison
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: Who guarded his House for him
entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: For those of you who know the story and have been eager to see Jean Valjean, I’m afraid you’re still waiting, but you got a few teasers today! 👀 “The beautiful is as useful as the useful. More perhaps.” – I’m not as much about pithy quotes as I once was, but I do like this one. 🌹🌷🪻 Another book I read with students is Albert Camus, La Peste (The Plague), and the Bishop’s doctor metaphor here makes me think of the (wonderful) conclusion of that book – I think the Bishop and Rieux would get along. (And Camus inherited Hugo’s opposition to the death penalty as well, which does not seem coincidental.) Lastly, this is another chapter, like chapter 3, where much of what we see is specific to the time and place Hugo is describing. What would the Bishop’s home be like today?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: The thing that’s (sort of) new about the Bishop today concerns FEAR. He utterly refuses fear, particularly if it keeps him from his work, or creates prejudice. And it’s self-fulfilling: the fearsome mountain bandits respect him. We don’t know how Cravatte came to be what he is, but the Bishop’s stubborn rejection of fear and his consistent concern for people who matter to no one else seem to be what earns the bandits’ respect. We also, once again, have a convenient gap in the narrator’s knowledge. What did he do with those valuable stolen goods? Did the guy who doesn’t go in much for Church wealth and always gives everything he can to the poor give them to the Church or to the poor? 🤷‍♀️
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: There will be quite a few chapters like this along the way, and I’m going to leave it to each individual reader how much you’d like to learn about the many references like the ones the senator makes here. Google is your friend for these sections!! Broadly, though, the senator’s philosophy is pretty understandable: he’s a materialist, believes only in the physical world, no soul, divinity, or afterlife. And for some reason (wine?) he decides the Bishop is the person he wants to tell this to. The Bishop’s response isn’t theological, though, and he doesn’t try to rescue the senator’s soul – instead, as we’d say today, he points out his privilege, and his condescension. Might this be insight into the Bishop’s conversion, which the narrator professed not to know about? He seems to have been this same sort of bon vivant before the Revolution. Perhaps the experience of sufefring in exile showed him problems with this sort of thinking?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 9. Le frère raconté par la sœur
entries.english_hapgood_title: 9: The Brother as depicted by the Sister
entries.companion_episode: Ep02 - I,1,i - ix - Why a Bishop?
entries.commentary_2025: Once again, our narrator insists that he’s reproducing an original document, that he has in his hands. He’s done this with the Bishop’s budget, and now, this letter from his sister. To be clear, this is fiction, and Hugo doesn’t *really* intend to fool anyone into thinking it’s not. This kind of claim in novels was a common device to lend a sense of reality to the story. So the things that he wants us to experience as the most real here are: the fact that the Bishop gave away everything he could, and his sister’s complete belief in and submission to him. 🤔Hugo lets us have doubts about things like what he did with the stolen goods two chapters ago, and the details of his life before he became a priest. But not these points. What’s the pattern?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 10. L'évêque en présence d'une lumière inconnue
entries.english_hapgood_title: 10: The Bishop in the Presence of an Unknown Light
entries.companion_episode: Ep03 - I,1,x - xiv - The Bishop, Builder of Bridges
entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is one of my favorites in the whole book! It’s also our first real dive into French history and politics: a Conventionist was part of the governing body that voted (in a slim majority) to guillotine Louis XVI, something like 22 years before this takes place. We learned from Baptistine yesterday that the Bishop is still very much a royalist, so that would have been a horrific event for him. It’s a while ago for him now, but it might be a bit like those of us who were adults at the time looking back on 9/11. Plus, the Bishop himself went into exile and lost quite a lot due to the Revolution. And this Conventionist was involved in all that, even if he voted “no” on the question of the d**th of the king. That’s the Bishop’s visceral reaction here. It’s uncharacteristic, but understandable. And he starts from quite a prejudiced place – compare this to how he accompanied the condemned man to the guillotine! What follows, though, is a conversation that exemplifies finding common values, even across vast difefrences of opinion, because the Bishop is willing to listen, and open to changing his mind. He’s still a royalist after his encounter with the Conventionist, but he has a better understanding of yet another type of person he’s expected to reject, but now doesn’t.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep03 - I,1,x - xiv - The Bishop, Builder of Bridges
entries.commentary_2025: This one is hard to follow if you don’t know a bit about the politics of the early 1810s in France, during Napoleon’s decline…. In the first half of the chapter, VERY basically, Hugo is describing the Bishop’s role in the power struggle between Napoleon and the Pope – it was minimal, but Myriel was very much not a supporter of Napoleon. The “restriction” in the title of the chapter is that Myriel had political opinions at all (and that they were difefrent from Hugo’s….) In a book that is clearly so political, especially later on, it’s interesting that Hugo (who was politically active himself) sees political opinions as a negative trait in a character (and this won’t be the last time either!) But he does clarify: wanting relief for the sufefring, believing in progress, or loving one’s country aren’t political opinions; he sees these as things everyone should share (see the previous chapter). He thinks there are higher things to think about than politics, and that’s what the Bishop was *usually* occupied with, so Hugo wishes he were occupied with it all the time.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep03 - I,1,x - xiv - The Bishop, Builder of Bridges
entries.commentary_2025: A few ideas about money, power, and status here, but just one about monseigneur Bienvenu: because he doesn’t have the first, he doesn’t have the other two. It seems maybe he likes it that way. The Church hierarchy is political like any other, and it’s hardly a surprise that our Bishop is not interested in all that. And because he doesn’t seek power, others don’t seek power through him. His solitude is an absence of hangers-on. Hugo observes that if people (even clergy) have money, power, and status, everyone assumes they deserve it – and how untrue that is. Monseigneur Bienvenu is proof – as if we needed it!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep03 - I,1,x - xiv - The Bishop, Builder of Bridges
entries.commentary_2025: We’re quite far from institutional Church dogma, aren’t we? The Bishop is almost a mystic or a contemplative here. Hugo loved animals, and like many of his Romantic contemporaries, experienced nature as spiritual. So attributing this to the Bishop is not a huge surprise. Through this, in combination with what we saw during his visit to the Conventionist, he ends up ofefring a very difefrent spiritual way of being, one that might appeal in a world where institutional religion fails to connect with some folks. Final note: the French in this chapter is quite poetic and beautiful to read; if you’re reading in translation, I hope it conveys that!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep03 - I,1,x - xiv - The Bishop, Builder of Bridges
entries.commentary_2025: This is sort of a corrective for yesterday’s chapter: the Bishop may not be particularly deep in Catholic dogma, but he’s not making up his own religion here! Our Bishop is humble, and accessing the Big Questions that would be involved in creating his own complex (and heretical) system of belief is farther than he’d ever dream of reaching. Instead, he’s simplifying. For him, it’s about love, kindness, and care. Maybe it’s the troubled times we live in, but I was particularly struck this time through by the image of the Bishop hiding in “Love one another” the way a pearl hides in an oyster. Not a bad plan! 🫣
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Le soir d'un jour de marche
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Evening of a Day of Walking
entries.companion_episode: Ep04 - I,2,i-v - How to Feed the Body and Soul
entries.commentary_2025: Hey, look who it is!! This way of introducing our hero, as he’s chased out of humbler and humbler places for reasons we’re mostly left to guess, tells us as much about his relationship to society as about him. All people in Digne know about him is whatever the innkeeper learned from city hall, as well as how he looks. Much of this is prejudice based on the fact that he looks poor, but his shaved head would have been a big clue to his past – which doesn’t make it NOT prejudice! Based on where he says he started his day, he walked just shy of 20 miles that day. He says “twelve leagues” – in French “douze lieues” – this word, when used by someone traveling on foot, was the distance one could walk in an hour, and so was quite variable. One way or another, it’s a LONG WAY, and he’s tired and hungry. As a hiker myself, I can feel in my bones (specifically, the ones in my feet) how awful this must be after a 20-mile day. With that, to my mind, the last ten lines or so of this chapter are our payoff for all of book 1. 🥹
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. La prudence conseillée à la sagesse
entries.companion_episode: Ep04 - I,2,i-v - How to Feed the Body and Soul
entries.commentary_2025: This is what’s going on while Jean Valjean is getting kicked out of every place he tries to stay for the night. These two chapters could be in split screen, like on “24.” The “duties” that the Bishop is writing about are clearly worth thinking about: the passages in the Gospel of Matthew that Hugo references are from the Sermon on the Mount. Check them out if you’re interested! They are quite unsurprising based on what we know about the Bishop, but given their placement at this pivotal moment, it’s worth a look. Meanwhile, Jean Valjean has created a stir in Digne, and the women have heard the rumors and are scared. The long descriptions of these two women make them relatable to us. Theirs is the typical way of thinking, and we can understand it. The Bishop, of course, is not typical, and isn’t any more scared by this than by any other possible threat that could come through his unlocked door. We were prepared for this in book 1, chapter 6, and he does here what he always does!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep04 - I,2,i-v - How to Feed the Body and Soul
entries.commentary_2025: Let’s count up the deeply needed things that the Bishop and his household gave Jean Valjean here, shall we? Food and lodging, clearly. As chapter 1 showed, he would have been satisfied with that, but it doesn’t stop there…. Acceptance: He invites him in, even after he knows who he is (while also saying that he wouldn’t have asked, because he knew he was a brother). Respect: He calls him “monsieur,” which signals a level of respect that Jean Valjean hasn’t had in 19 years *at least.* Compassion: He *sees* Jean Valjean’s sufefring, and asks to hear more about it. Trust: He puts all his silver out, even knowing that Jean Valjean was in prison for theft. And the women’s heroism, in the chapter title, lies in the fact that they cooperate despite their fears; had they shown Jean Valjean that they were afraid of him, it would have undermined these emotional gifts from the Bishop.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Détails sur les fromageries de Pontarlier
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: Details concerning the Cheese-Dairies of Pontarlier
entries.companion_episode: Ep04 - I,2,i-v - How to Feed the Body and Soul
entries.commentary_2025: Interesting that we once again have Baptistine’s as our narrator for this part of the story. Before, that seemed to be about an appearance of authenticity, especially about the Bishop’s generosity. Here I think the section where she tries to guess at his intentions is key. She knows him perhaps better than anyone, after all, and is in the best position to know his mind. And, of course, she’s fcitional – Hugo tells us this in her voice because he wants us to take the idea seriously: that religion and morality is not the most important thing that the Bishop has to ofefr here, and that in fact, preachiness in this moment would likely undermine what Jean Valjean really needs from him. He knows that more than anything else, Jean Valjean needs to feel like a normal person, and that’s what the Bishop is giving him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep04 - I,2,i-v - How to Feed the Body and Soul
entries.commentary_2025: A number of things happen here, which add up to Jean Valjean continuing to be trusted: with proximity to the sleeping household, with one of the silver candlesticks, and with information about where the rest of the silver is. But the chapter title draws our attention to the Bishop’s response to Jean Valjean’s provocation, when he asks how he knows he isn’t a k!ller. This seems to be the central event of the chapter. That response, which is hardly a surprise by now, is to proceed exactly as he was, and to refuse to mistrust him, as Jean Valjean seems to hope/expect him to.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This is a heck of a section to be reading today (note: Inauguration of the U.S. President in 2025…. ) The basics of Jean Valjean’s backstory are some of the best known parts of this story: the theft of the bread, the 19 years, the number 24601. (Don’t worry, we’re all singing a little here. 🎶) But we need to keep the thrill of recognition here from overriding the weight of the story he’s telling: this family had few resources, made the best choices they could at every turn, and it still ended in disaster. The Bishop seems to have been assuming a story along these lines, but let’s not forget the first chapter in this section: most people don’t. Most people learn that Jean Valjean broke the law, and they see how poor and uncouth he looks, and they’re comfortable assuming that his sufefring is deserved. Clearly, they’re wrong. I’ll have more to say about this day and the start of these next four years in a separate post – it doesn’t fit into the chapter-a-day.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Jean Valjean, tender-hearted but desperate when he was sent to prison, became the criminal they mistakenly imagined him to be. His sentence is self-fulfilling. The question of assigning blame, considering who is really guilty, has come up before: the Bishop said (I’m paraphrasing) that if a sin is committed in darkness, don’t look to the sinner, but to the one who made the darkness. Jean Valjean, in his way, agrees. But Hugo doesn’t neglect the emotional side that is at work here too – there is anger, hate, indignance, and he might not reliably direct it where it belongs. He is now a “very dangerous man” indeed. Who benefits from this system? Also striking in this chapter is the vision of all of society stacked up above Jean Valjean, at the very bottom. Hugo didn’t invent this physical representation of social hierarchy, but seeing it from the bottom is… rough.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter, y’all…. I find it to be one of the most viscerally, emotionally difficult ones in the book. The man overboard’s situation is so unthinkable, and Hugo’s description of it is so intense, it’s horrifying. I encourage you, if you’re at all able, to try to experience the original French. If you can read it in French, the efofrt is worth it for these few pages. Or, listen to this chapter in a French audiobook. Use a translation for any support you need, but the original here…! 🤯And, beyond the experience of the chapter, this will also be a central metaphor for the duration of the book. (I say lots more about it in the podcast!) How many people, then and now, live as the man overboard does – left behind, utterly without hope, trying to survive an existence that is only struggle and dread?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is a bit odd here, if I’m honest. It’s part of the flashback to all that happened to Jean Valjean before he arrived in Digne, but what do we learn? I suppose we learn financial details, which have already been important (remember the Bishop’s budget). But we already knew he faced prejudice, and that his release from prison didn’t mean freedom and wasn’t really a relief or a cause for joy. Perhaps it’s here simply to bring us back out of the intensity of the vision that was the metaphor for his situation in the previous chapter, and reconnect that to the rest: while you may be seeing something relatively mundane, if unfair, what’s happening beneath the surface is colossal and tragic.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep06 - I,2,x-xiii - The Bishop's Real Work
entries.commentary_2025: I’ve read this book numerous times, but I’m not sure I’ve ever stopped at the end of this chapter. It’s terrifying, after chapters 6-9. I think taking this section of the book fairly slowly is important, and something that we can forget to do, especially with how much is left 😳, and what we may already know from adaptations. We are, of course, encouraged to empathize with Jean Valjean, but he is also legitimately threatening here. The emotional landscape of what’s going on in the Bishop’s house tonight is complex. Which means that everyone involved faces real, weighty choices right now….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep06 - I,2,x-xiii - The Bishop's Real Work
entries.commentary_2025: This is one of a number of chapters in this book that are quite cinematic – more than 30 years before the invention of cinema! It uses light and sound masterfully. I wish an adapter would shoot this as Hugo wrote it. But in a sense, the ubiquity of adaptations has sort of ruined this part for us. What comes next is so well known, that it’s hard to feel the suspense that the original readers must have felt here. If you don’t know, though, lucky you! – I won’t tell. 🤐 Jean Valjean is at a decision point here; much hangs in the balance – Jean Valjean’s freedom, his soul, and maybe both of these men’s lives. So the suspense is also, I think, some of the payoff for ALL that time we spent with the Bishop. We’ve come to care about him, and about what happens to him – maybe more than Jean Valjean at this point!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep06 - I,2,x-xiii - The Bishop's Real Work
entries.commentary_2025: This scene, along with Jean Valjean’s backstory that we saw a few days ago, is also among the best-known parts of this novel. I love the detail, at the beginning, of the Bishop showing Mme Magloire the basket that was left behind in the garden. As if that’s what she was actually looking for. Smarty-pants Myriel is a superb touch. 😂 Let’s also not forget here that the Bishop is lying to the police! He is, and he isn’t: as he says to Mme Magloire, he really believes that the silver always belonged to the poor, that he (Myriel) was the one keeping it unjustly, and that it *should* go to Jean Valjean. The Bishop’s attachment to these items was more sentimental than monetary, as they were from his life before the Revolution, so let’s take a beat to note the personal nature of this donation! Also worth noting that we see very little of Jean Valjean’s response here. That’s for tomorrow….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep06 - I,2,x-xiii - The Bishop's Real Work
entries.commentary_2025: Well, this is…. timely. Maybe it’s the recent public conversation in the U.S., but what stood out to me on this read was Jean Valjean’s first instinct to see the Bishop’s kindness as an attack. He moves beyond that, and throughout the book it will become clear, I think, that that’s a testament to his character. But Hugo is pretty clear that it could have gone the other way, and that hardening against a gentle call to rise above base, cruel instincts is a terrifying turn indeed. This is another seminal chapter in the book (as it is in Jean Valjean’s life) – you might want to put a marker in it as you did chapter 8, because it will be worth thinking back to it often. I will say this, though: it’s tempting to try and “diagnose” Jean Valjean’s mental state here, from a modern perspective. I resist that, for three reasons: 1) I’m not qualified to make such a diagnosis; 2) Modern psychology wasn’t around in Hugo’s time, and so couldn’t have been his reference point, so 3) that’s not the important element of what’s happening here. What is important will become clearer as we keep reading! Meanwhile, this is another chapter where Hugo’s writing soars – savor it!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: First of all, congratulate yourself for bearing with this chapter. No one expects it to have been easy or fun! It probably was somewhat more fun for Hugo’s original 1862 French readers, especially those close to Hugo’s age, who remembered 1817, 45 years earlier. For them, this would be nostalgic, like someone 60-ish today looking back 45 years to 1980 when they were a teenager. (Hugo was 15 years old in 1817.) But for us, it’s ok if it’s hard to understand. I’ll leave it to you (again) to decide how many of these references you Google!! Meanwhile, a theme I see in this chapter is this: 1817 was the early phase of the Bourbon restoration, after the end of the Napoleonic Wars, when life had gotten easier, and royalism was at a high point. BUT, the 30-odd previous years –Revolution, Republic, Terror, Empire, war – loomed large. People thought all that was done, but it’s clearly not gone….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Here’s another character you’ve probably been looking forward to seeing! Hugo’s presentation of her probably seems a little judgey, but it’s the 19th century after all…. The four women here correspond closely to the character type of the grisette, a working class girl, typically a seamstress, who has love afafirs with young middle-class guys, usually students or artists. Hugo’s original readers would have recognized this right away, so he’s also dealing with their established expectations. A typical grisette character wasn’t *exactly* exchanging money for sex, but she wasn’t exactly *not* doing that: it was understood that they guys would support them for a while, but that the relationship wasn’t serious or permanent. Fantine, though, doesn’t seem to understand that… 😥
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This is the second chapter title in a row that emphasizes the number 4 – for reasons I discuss more in the podcast, this isn’t a great omen! And for the second chapter in a row, he emphasizes Fantine’s modesty, purity, innocence, beauty, and lovely hair and teeth in particular. 😰For the moment, though, it’s delightful to enjoy this day in the countryside with this group! And, given Hugo’s comments about the changes in the Parisian region between 1817 and 1862, this must have extended the nostalgia of chapter 1 for some of his original readers.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Tholomyès est si joyeux qu'il chante une chanson espagnole
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: Tholomyes is so Merry that he sings a Spanish Ditty
entries.commentary_2025: In the long, lightweight, summer dresses the women would be wearing here (picture the clothes in Bridgerton), swinging on a swing would likely show their legs. 😱 Fantine is too modest for that, but Tholomyès isn’t too polite to enjoy it when the other girls do it! So much so that he sings in Spanish about it. He’s a real piece of work, which we’ll, sadly, get to see more of. Hugo spent time in Spain in his youth, spoke some Spanish, and probably put a bit of himself into Tholomyès here… He also, surely, put some of himself into the lyrical passage about being young and in love in the summer countryside!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: As anyone who has a cat (as Hugo did) knows, a cat can be the laziest creature imaginable, and if necessary, turn into an absolute ball of fury. This analogy for the people of Paris in 1817 as they’re described in chapter 1, shows Hugo’s perspective much later in the century! Book 3 is also a similar time for Fantine – the calm before the storm.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: A in which They Adore Each Other
entries.commentary_2025: While the chapter title signals that this will be about love, the main thing we see is Favourite’s cynicism! She’s impatient with this arrangement she’s in, and it’s clear that it’s not for love alone. But she understands her role. 1817 is maybe a bit early, but by 1862, it’s reasonable for us to think here of bohemian Paris of the 1840s, most famously portrayed in the opera La Bohème. That opera was based on an 1851 novel by Henri Murger, and the tone and way we see our characters here are reminiscent of that novel. Hugo is once again connecting this group to known character types, from a genre that idealized the lives we see them lead. We’ll see if it remains ideal…
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: I hope your translation catches Tholomyès’s wordplay and allusions here! I discuss this type of monologue, typically from the educated characters we’ll see in the book, and typically when they get drunk, quite a bit more in the podcast. But simply: he’s talking about moderation and setting limits on joy and pleasure, but doing it in a way that the others, especially Fantine, won’t follow very well. If she did, she’d see the warnings embedded in this for her – even without knowing what’s in her future. For those of us who may know what’s coming for her, the foreshadowing is even more powerful. And it’s important to remember Tholomyès’s perspective here too: he knows, in his "wisdom", that he’s engaging Fantine in something that’s harmful for her, but his conscience doesn’t seem bothered by it…. 😡
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: So can we all agree now that treating empathy (for a horse, or for other humans) like it’s a bad thing is a massive red flag? Is that something we need to discuss further? 🚩🚩🚩The horse – noted specifically as female – also smacks of symbolism here. For what, we could discuss…. But she is old, exhausted, likely ill, and made to work until she collapses dead, which is understood (by everyone but Fantine) mainly as an inconvenience for her owner. Meanwhile, Tholomyès has continued to ramble on 🙄 about various pleasures, and it’s only this spectacle of death that reminds everyone to get on with the evening.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: And now we get down to the real problem, that has been brewing in the story for the last 8 chapters: Tholomyès is having a fling, and Fantine has given herself over to it entirely. The class dynamics that we mentioned a few days ago, when we talked about the character type of the grisette, come to the fore here too: these young bourgeois men have family expectations to return to, whereas the women have no families, and no other ties. The expectation for them is that some other young bourgeois will have wild oats to sow, and will replicate this same arrangement with each of them soon enough. All the other women seem to have known this was the deal, and with the men’s departure itself not being so much of a surprise, they can enjoy the theatricality of the way they do it. But Fantine will never be the same…. 😢 struggles. It presents us over and over, like Jean Valjean, with a choice about who we want to be in our world – which isn’t all THAT difefrent from his. It shows us political action that fails, but individual heroism that succeeds and empowers us to act, in our spheres, as we can, even when the political world seems hopeless. And if we could each make the difefrence that Jean Valjean, or Fantine, or Éponine, or Gavroche makes in one person’s life, how much better would the world be?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Une mère qui en rencontre une autre
entries.commentary_2025: Another major entrance into the plot for a character or two that you probably know! I talked a while back (Inauguration Day, as it happens) about Thénardier, and his inability to conceive of selflessness. His ability, and his advantage in many situations, is not being seen – and we see that at work here. Mme Thénardier is also somewhat in disguise here as, seated, she doesn’t seem to be the monster that Hugo is already telegraphing that she is. And, as with Tholomyès, Fantine misses major 🚩🚩that she *is* able to see. She’s simply innocent and trusting, but alas, that works against her. Otherwise, you can see here how much Hugo loved children ☺️ – nostalgia for his own daughters’ early childhood is just barely beneath the surface of his descriptions.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Première esquisse de deux figures louches
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: First Sketch of Two Unprepossessing Figures
entries.commentary_2025: Sometimes Hugo makes us wait and wonder about characters in this book, see things through a POV character and share their uncertainty. Not with the Thénardiers. The Thénardiers, we know from the beginning, are up to NO GOOD. With some people, it’s just obvious.* 🤷‍♀️Part of how Hugo shows us that is by making them evasive, hard to place. He tells us a lot of what they’re NOT, from which we get an unsettling, indirect picture of what they are. And it’s extra unsettling because they aren’t any of the things we expect them to be, or their opposites – they are in a strange void of NOTs. *But it clearly isn’t obvious to everyone – Fantine for example. It’s confounding to us that she doesn’t see them for what they are, but she doesn’t, and we’ll see what comes of that…. (This is a reference to U.S. politics.)
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The Thénardiers are above all else transactional. They give nothing without counting what they get in return, and are predisposed to conclude they haven’t gotten enough. They are the opposite of the Bishop, who refuses any accounting, apart from his “budget” of donations. And when it comes to the maternal love that Mme Thénardier has to give, the other side of the balance sheet is violence and abuse. As I explore more fully in the podcast (especially later on), Cosette’s life with the Thénardiers is a microcosm of a transactional society, where nothing is freely given, not even love or mercy. Cosette is now, oddly, where Jean Valjean was when we first met him: at the mercy of a merciless power, condemned to hard labor and sufefring, and deteriorating physically and psychologically as a result. 😢
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Histoire d'un progrès dans les verroteries noires
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The History of a Progress in Black Glass Trinkets
entries.commentary_2025: This stranger who’s come to town and done well in the costume jewelry business seems really important to our narrator – and weirdly familiar, when he’s described…. 🤔The honest source of his wealth is also really important, for reasons we can discuss even with what we already know. We’ve just seen (started to see) the consequences of Thénardier trying to get rich by dishonest means. We’ve seen theft become a theme already, via Cravatte’s stolen church goods, and via Jean Valjean’s original crime and theft from the Bishop. And we’ve seen the characters (the Bishop, as well as, implicitly, Tholomyès) come by wealth via inheritance or a wealthy institution, and we’ve seen generosity and charity. But this is our first example of innovation, honest exchange, and fairly compensated labor as a way to build wealth for a whole region – the best version of what was becoming the 19th-century economy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The name Madeleine in French is a common female frist name, which comes from the name of the biblical person known in English as Mary Magdalene. As such, it was associated variously with sin (especially carnal sins) and repentance (especially showy, exterior, or superfciial repentance), and a number of common expressions give it negative connotations. Interesting, then, that he’s so interested in the morals of his employees and others he may be in a position to influence! He also gives to the poor, the hospital, and schools, echoing the Bishop. This charity seems to be his main goal, which DOES NOT COMPUTE for the local gossips. Surely he’s up to something… 🤨 Still, he denies all honors and awards until he’s persuaded that he could do even more good as mayor. His character *seems* consistently altruistic.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The section on nettles here is a famous one, and served as an epigraph to Ladj Ly’s 2019 film “Les Misérables.” That film (not an adaptation of the novel so much as a re-exploration of its themes for 21st-century France) shares one element we’ve already seen: Montfermeil, which has changed quite a bit since Hugo set the Thénardiers there! It has, and it hasn’t, which is part of what the film is about – worth a watch, if you’re interested! https://www.amazon.com/gp/video/detail/amzn1.dv.gti.36b88ef5-d398-0a68-da08-15c414eb380d?autop lay=0&ref =atv cf strg wb _ _ _ _ Otherwise, there is more here that makes this Madeleine character feel familiar: his aim and some of his other skills, his candlesticks…. And we might wonder (if the rumors are true) why he has this arrangement with Laffitte (the big name in banking in Paris at this time, when modern banking was still very much in development). Could it be so that he can make a quick getaway?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The Bishop’s blindness at the end of his life calls to mind the trope of the blind seer, the person who has keener spiritual (in)sight without physical sight. We already understand the Bishop’s insight, of course! But we learn here that he’s been blind for “several years,” in 1821, so since shortly after his 1815 encounter with Jean Valjean. This suggests that perhaps something occurred around that time that completed his enlightenment – maybe giving up his candlesticks, his last valuable objects (and, as it happens, a light source)? In this way, he enters into the pre-paradise that Hugo describes so vividly here, of unconditional love and care. Meanwhile, his death is meaningful to M. Madeleine, and the townspeople sure are puzzled. Are we?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: JAVERT. He is first presented through his instincts – his instinct that there’s something unusual and familiar about this Madeleine fellow. And his instinct, it’s quite clear, is animal – if you have a minute, look back through the chapter for all the difefrent ways he’s compared to or connected with animals. But at the same time, he is the Law itself, inviolable and absolute. There is no grey area with this guy! Which, we also learn right away, is a problem for no one more than it is for him: he comes from criminals, but has a lawful instinct. By his own principles, he is a man without a place in the world – he can’t ever really escape his origins, but he can’t bring himself to do anything but reject them either. And so he must be only, fully, absolutely, a police officer.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Interesting that Fauchelevent not only starts off disliking Madeleine, but also, that it’s for reasons vaguely reminiscent of Thénardier: he’s failing financially, downwardly mobile socially, and bitter about others’ success. Of course, this also creates the opportunity for a transformation of bitterness into gratitude that echoes Jean Valjean’s – suggesting, perhaps, that even Thénardier is not beyond hope? Meanwhile, while Hugo hasn’t outright told us who Madeleine is, much of the drama of Javert’s presence in this scene depends on us having guessed…. Not all the drama of the scene though: focusing just on this one chapter today reminded me how suspenseful it is!!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: Fauchelevent becomes a Gardener in Paris
entries.commentary_2025: This short chapter is really a sort of odds-and-ends, cleanup chapter, to get us in position for Fantine’s story to continue (which is what book 5 is titled for). But, note the chapter title, which pertains to just one part of the chapter. It will matter much later! Also note the reiteration of Javert’s suspicion of Madeleine, and that it’s once again given via the metaphor of a dog protecting its master against wolves. 🐺🐶 I also notice how very bourgeois the concerns of this chapter are: Fauchelevent earning his living after the accident and “selling” his former assets, Fantine earning her living, the low cost of tax collection in Montreuil-sur-mer. Alongside Madeleine’s generosity and goodness, it is made clear that no one is an idle freeloader – lest Hugo’s more conservative readers start grumbling….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 8. Madame Victurnien dépense trente-cinq francs pour la morale
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: Madame Victurnien expends Thirty Francs on Morality
entries.commentary_2025: Here those town gossips become a problem – for Fantine, not Madeleine. And we see their motivation isn’t all that difefrent from Javert’s: Mme Victurnien, their embodiment, has a morally questionable past that she would like to cover up, so she persecutes others. And note that she spends money on it, and Hugo is sure to point out that it’s money that could have been spent on good deeds instead, like the Bishop’s or Madeleine’s. The movement of money is always important in this book! A number of important extended metaphors show up here: for one, they’re described as consuming those they gossip about, like a wood stove consumes wood. And, I talk lots more in the podcast, here and elsewhere, about mirrors – we see Fantine’s introduced prominently at the start of the chapter. And finally, we see a narrative technique here that we’ll see again: we already knew, from the Thénardiers’s POV, that Fantine fell behind on her payments. Here we get the same story a second time, from her side.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: One element stood out to me this time in the description of the woman who actually fired Fantine (on Madeleine’s behalf, but without his knowledge): she is described (I’m paraphrasing) as a generous giver, but not a generous thinker. That is, she is happy to give money, a sort of severance, but judges Fantine’s “misdeeds” harshly – and we see the result. Contrast this with the Bishop, who gave Jean Valjean material things of great value, but who also ofefred him understanding and respect. And, of course, she’s not the only one who is ungenerous in their thinking about Fantine now – which has the opposite efefct of the one that the Bishop had on Jean Valjean. Fantine is now following the emotional path that Jean Valjean followed in prison, into a defiant and bitter, instinctively defensive place. Of course, we understand. But will anyone else?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Oh, the irony of this chapter title! Two chapters ago, Mme Victurnien’s purpose was said to be “morality.” Did she in fact succeed? (Even by her own questionable definition of “morality?”) Direct, short-term efofrts (like hers) to enforce standards of behavior tend to go badly in this book. The only thing that changes people is the Bishop’s approach, which sees missteps as a symptom, not the real problem. And every step of Fantine’s story, all the way back to Paris and her time with Tholomyès, supports that approach. Her flaw, especially at the beginning, is naïvté: she trusts Tholomyès and the Thénardiers when there are many clues that they are not trustworthy. Hugo recognizes that maybe she didn’t always make the best choices, but given her background – without a family, money, education, or real allies – how could she know better? By now, whatever some one of these “moral” ladies might want to accomplish by a scolding is pretty redundant – Fantine knows the trouble she’s in. Isn’t it likely that compassion will go further?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Oh, buddy, is there stuff to say here. A lot of it is in the podcast, too, so don’t miss that. But today’s post could be a long one. 🤷‍♀️ First, a mild disclaimer, to both this post and the podcast: there is a movement, here in the 21st century, to destigmatize and decriminalize sex work, and emphasize the agency of sex workers. That is good; anything that gives people more agency and less stigma is a positive in my book. But I think it’s clear that Fantine is not part of that movement. And, I think discussing her situation in those terms would negate her story and the loss of choice and agency that brought her here. Should she be able to choose this profession without stigma if she wants to? Sure. Did she? ABSOLUTELY NOT. So let’s deal with that. Hugo is quite clear about – takes most of this short chapter to describe – how the real tragedy here is Fantine’s sufefring, and the erosion of her soul, not the “immorality” of her “choice.” It’s that she did not want this – any of this – and that it was all thrust upon her in a way that is so deeply violating. Hugo compares this moment to “society buying a slave” – in 1862, when slavery had been abolished in France, including its colonies, but the American Civil War was ongoing. That comparison to a hot-button issue goes right for the heart in his contemporary world: it’s an indictment of all of society for what has just become of Fantine. (I say a lot more about the systemic aspects of this, and why it’s all of bourgeois society and not just the men who patronize women in her position, in the podcast!) Meanwhile, the chapter title, which comes from Galatians 5, means “Christ has freed us.” In context there, Paul is encouraging freedom from religious law. But here, it drips with irony. This chapter – the title and the final lines – is not the last time that Hugo will tell us that God still sees and cares for Fantine. But is that enough? Do we not wish that people around her saw and cared for her too, perhaps on God’s behalf? Which is the second indictment of society here. They – we – fail to see and care for people who are sufefring.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep10 - I,5,xii - I,6,ii - Heroism and Complicity
entries.commentary_2025: This scene is the starting point for Fantine’s entire character and story. In a sense, everything we’ve seen about her up to now has been backstory. It is based on a real incident that Hugo witnessed in 1841 – I’ll say a bit more about that tomorrow when we read the second part of it, and a lot more in the podcast. At the time, the idea for Les Misérables was in an embryonic form in Hugo’s mind, and he had some notes about a man who stole some bread and about the Toulon galleys. Then, he saw a young bourgeois harass a woman in just this way, and the woman be arrested for it…. One difefrence, though, is that it happened in Paris. So everything we read here about Bamatabois being a provincial layabout and a sort of big fish in a VERY small pond, is added. Given that Bamatabois is connected directly to Tholomyès, we could see these two together as stand-ins for the man in the original story, difefrent manifestations of the same problem. And that problem is people having too many advantages over someone like Fantine, and too little compassion for her. Let’s count Bamatabois’s advantages (which are quite like Tholomyès’s): he’s male in a patriarchal culture, relatively wealthy, in good health, in line with social expectations, and thus favored by the legal system. He can get up to mischief with impunity, even if that mischief harms her disproportionately, because everything about their context allows him to. And if she responds in proportion to the harm, she faces consequences far beyond what he will ever face. Hugo saw all of this embedded in the brief scene that he witnessed, and placed it at the core of this character, which is at the core of his masterpiece.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 13. Solution de quelques questions de police municipale
entries.english_hapgood_title: 13: The Solution of Some Questions connected with the Municipal Police
entries.companion_episode: Ep10 - I,5,xii - I,6,ii - Heroism and Complicity
entries.commentary_2025: Yesterday, we said that Hugo witnessed this very scene in the street in 1841; what he did next was play the role that Madeleine does here. He wasn’t mayor, but he applied his name and his clout to a statement in favor of the woman. What did NOT happen to Hugo, that does happen to Madeleine here, is the woman spitting on him. So, when Hugo fictionalizes his own heroism, he immediately undermines it when she spits on him for being at the root of all the trouble he’s now getting her out of. I say a lot more in the podcast about how Hugo’s own biography connects to this section! Meanwhile, it’s interesting that both Javert and Fantine have difficulty understanding that the mayor wishes to set her free. Javert sees everything through categories and structures, and as such, misses their humanity. Bamatabois, and later Madeleine, becomes a stand-in for all of society, and Fantine for everything outside of it, that attacks it. So of course the matter seems simple to him, and it’s unthinkable that Madeleine would see it difefrently. Fantine, since she was fired, has so thoroughly rehearsed the story that has Madeleine at the root of her troubles that she can’t easily see him as merciful. It’s also interesting that Fantine has such a clear-eyed sense of the social and economic forces that led to where she is, and suggests to Javert that the police ought to look into prison labor if they want to prevent crime!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep10 - I,5,xii - I,6,ii - Heroism and Complicity
entries.commentary_2025: Three things happening at once here: Fantine’s worsening illness, the Thénardiers’ escalating demands, and Javert’s mysterious letter. We’ll see more about the last two soon. I’ll just point out now that Madeleine is not sure whether he’ll send someone or go get Cosette himself, and has Fantine’s letter reflect that ambiguity! As for Fantine’s illness, the reference to Laennec would have been recognizable at the time as implying that she has tuberculosis. René Laennec invented the stethoscope, and was a pioneer at exactly this time in the study of tuberculosis, of which he also died a few years later. Meanwhile, notice how receiving care (medical and otherwise), has remedied the terrible bitterness that we saw in Fantine before, to the point where she charms even the nuns, who are predisposed to judge her. This answers the questions raised by “Christus nos liberavit” – in exactly the ways we expected… Madeleine is for Fantine what the Bishop had been for Jean Valjean.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep10 - I,5,xii - I,6,ii - Heroism and Complicity
entries.commentary_2025: For all that descriptions of Javert are unflattering, and for all that he is, most of the time, an antagonist of our hero(es), he’s not a “bad guy” per se. He is, if you will, “lawful neutral.” Law and order are what matter to him – sometimes to a fault, and often to a point that is inconvenient for those around him. But he might not understand an alignment chart that puts lawful-chaotic and good-evil on separate axes. For him, lawful & orderly = good. So much so that he applies it even to himself. He must enforce law and order, even if it means the end of the career that makes it his job to do so. Having erred, it is by demanding his own removal from law enforcement that he… enforces the law. As for this Champmathieu situation, we’ll see more about it soon!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep11 - I,7,i-iv - The Truth About Madeleine
entries.commentary_2025: The insistence on Sister Simplice never telling a lie (in addition to mattering to the plot later), asks us to think about HONESTY. Always telling the full truth is… one definition of honesty. How healthy “brutal truth” is maybe somewhat beyond my purview here, but suffice to say, it’s an extreme position. Of course, we can all think of situations where we’d consider someone basically honest if they were less absolute about the truth than Sister Simplice. But to this point in the book, we’ve seen the French word “honnête” (lit. honest) in two conspicuous places. One was at the end of the previous chapter; Javert was called an “étrange honnête homme” – a “strange honest man.” The other, of course, was when the Bishop told Jean Valjean to “devenir honnête homme” – “become an honest man.” The phrase that is in both of those sections, “honnête homme,” has a more complex meaning, though. In addition to “honnête” meaning “honest,” or possibly something like “moral” or “upright,” the phrase “honnête homme” could refer to something like a respectable gentleman. That is, it may not have anything to do with truth-telling, or even really a deep sense of morality, but rather, conformity to social expectations of a respectable class. That will be worth keeping in mind….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep11 - I,7,i-iv - The Truth About Madeleine
entries.commentary_2025: The narration is the interesting thing in this chapter! We see Madeleine through very restricted and distant points of view: the passerby, then Scaufflaire, then the concierge, then the cashier. Each of these individuals has a small piece of information – the stop at the church, the planned trip to Arras, the preoccupation, the sleepless night. But none of them knows the whole story of Madeleine’s day (and night). Of course, we get all of it, as well as the conversations with Javert, Fantine, and the nuns and doctor about Fantine, in the previous two chapters. And we’re left with a mystery: what does it all add up to? Tomorrow, in one of the great soaring chapters of this novel, we’ll put it all together.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep11 - I,7,i-iv - The Truth About Madeleine
entries.commentary_2025: I hope you were sitting down for the revelation that Madeleine is Jean Valjean! 🤯 In seriousness, though, Hugo doesn’t seem to expect you to be surprised. The revelation comes now, not because you couldn’t figure it out before, but because we’re peeling back the surface and heading inside. For the first time since the field outside of Digne (January 27 on our schedule) we’re going to know what he’s thinking and feeling, see his humanity. And, the reveal comes now because the character can’t avoid it anymore either, and this wonderful operatic chapter shows us how he contends with that. I say operatic because this is one of the places where Hugo’s use of prose most resembles a master composer or conductor creating emotion out of sound through music – I hope your translation reflects that. What’s most remarkable here, I think Hugo says best. There is some context as well, that I explain in the podcast. But in this venue, I want to note that (contrary to expectations formed by the song “Who am I?” in the musical) he has not made a decision at the close of this chapter. We’ll see when he finally comes to one. This chapter, more than any other, is where this character becomes complex, and becomes one of the great characters in all of literature. I’ll also note the way Hugo narrates his train of thought here, allowing for twists and turns that could easily have escaped a rational, linear narration. This process is a little irrational in ways that wouldn’t be embraced about human thought for many decades after Hugo wrote it.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Formes que prend la souffrance pendant le sommeil
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: Forms assumed by Sufefring during Sleep
entries.companion_episode: Ep11 - I,7,i-iv - The Truth About Madeleine
entries.commentary_2025: After yesterday’s embrace of the non-rational elements of Jean Valjean’s decision-making, today Hugo prioritizes showing us a dream. Dreams have, in lots of cultures in history, been seen as another way to access truth – maybe a deity was speaking through a dream, or a person’s own mind was able to express things it couldn’t express otherwise. What Jean Valjean’s dream expresses is very much open to interpretation here. Hugo says it expresses something “funeste et poignant” – depending on your translation: macabre, gloomy, painful, poignant, harrowing. Maybe all of these. It’s unsettling and disorienting. It doesn’t, though, speak directly to his dilemma – to Hugo’s credit as a writer, I think. It feels the way he feels, but doesn’t continue his thoughts.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep12 - I,7,v-viii - On a Horse, With No Name
entries.commentary_2025: I always find this chapter so interesting for the detailed picture it gives us of travel in this era. For comparison, our hero’s (approximate) route here would take just over an hour by car today, per Google maps. Otherwise, what stands out on this read is his resistance to making any sort of decision. That means, of course, trying to get to the trial in Arras, because deciding not to go would be a decision. But while he’s underway, he keeps fighting back his anxiety by telling himself that he can just watch, that he won’t be recognized just by being there, that simply showing up commits him to nothing. And yet, at a deeper place, he seems to know that’s not all this trip is. We see this in his immense relief when it looks like the trip will be impossible. If he *physically can’t* get to Arras in time, the decision is out of his hands, AND it’s resolved in the way that’s more pleasant for him. But, alas (?), on he travels.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. La sœur Simplice mise à l'épreuve
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: Sister Simplice put to the Proof
entries.companion_episode: Ep12 - I,7,v-viii - On a Horse, With No Name
entries.commentary_2025: Sister Simplice doesn’t technically *lie* here… she says that Madeleine left, and could be back the next day, and Fantine does the rest… And the belief that results – that she will soon see her child for the first time in 5 years – transforms her. The efefct that emotions can have on health was more signifciant in medicine at this time than it is now (perhaps because other knowledge was more limited) – and we see that belief here. We hear a LOT of Fantine’s voice here, even as her caretakers keep telling her to rest and not to speak. Notably, she sings the song about cherishing and losing a child, which does not end happily…
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Le voyageur arrivé prend ses précautions pour repartir
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: The Traveller on his Arrival takes Precautions for Departure
entries.companion_episode: Ep12 - I,7,v-viii - On a Horse, With No Name
entries.commentary_2025: Have you noticed that the narrator hasn’t used a name for our hero for his entire journey? It’s quite awkward at the start of this chapter – perhaps on purpose, so we’ll notice. As he hasn’t decided what he’ll do when he gets into the courtroom, it is, in a sense (based on all his deliberations in ch. 3), impossible to know what name to use. He’s like Schrödinger’s protagonist, both Madeleine and Jean Valjean, or maybe neither of them – over 70 years before Schrödinger thought up his cat! This makes it all the more significant that, in order to get into the courtroom, he has to enter as Madeleine. We don’t have his thoughts as he heads down the stairs then decides to present himself by this name, but they must involve the fact that this is a more decisive statement of who he now plans to be than anything he has done yet.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep12 - I,7,v-viii - On a Horse, With No Name
entries.commentary_2025: As we witness the last (?) of our hero’s agonizing decision, what stands out to me in this chapter is the attention given to other things hanging in the balance. The room where he’s left alone, to enter the courtroom at his leisure, is a jury deliberation room. A place where life-changing decisions are made. There, he sees a letter describing officials held under house arrest by the Revolution – whose fates, we might imagine, also have yet to be decided. That letter is also interesting for what Hugo says about the date: it is written as a mix of the Gregorian and Republican calendars, and should read either 9 June 1794 or “21 Prairial an II” – not a mix of the two systems. The reminder of the Republican calendar – and thus of the Revolution’s attempt to remake everything about its society – reminds us that all systems are built, and are temporary. This includes the justice system that is so top-of-mind for our story right now. It was human-made, so it could, theoretically, be made difefrently.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 9. Un lieu où des convictions sont en train de se former
entries.english_hapgood_title: 9: A Place where Convictions are in Process of Formation
entries.commentary_2025: What a gloomy, absurd place, where “convictions” are formed. In French as in English, this can mean “convictions” in the sense of beliefs, or in the legal sense. Either way, the picture painted is deeply untrustworthy here. Arguments are absurdly long, myopic, and more interested in the formalities of language than in truth. The jury is uninterested, even as they decide a man’s fate. And by a remarkable coincidence, Bamatabois – the unserious guy who put the snow down Fantine’s dress – is one of them. With (in 1823) or without (at Jean Valjean’s original conviction in 1796) the crucifix on the wall, it’s hard to imagine anything truly good coming out of this place. Jean Valjean recognizes it as a faithful reproduction of his own trial 27 years earlier, and sees Champmathieu as if he’s seeing himself from the outside. For us, especially knowing that this is how Jean Valjean was sent to prison, this is all one more reason not to trust this system to tell us who the “bad guys” are.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: One of the clearest takeaways from this look at the justice system is just how outmatched someone like Champmathieu is. His defense lawyer doesn’t seem to be able to defend him (or particularly interested in doing so), and he certainly can’t defend himself. For us, if not for the others in the room, he does paint a vivid picture of a life on the edge of survival, with no education or advantages. Life has cut this man very few breaks. And without some minimal education, even if his lawyer had the best will in the world (which he doesn’t) how can Champmathieu be expected to efefctively communicate the information he needs? The ability to *really see* people is important in this book, and the one person in this room who *really sees* Champmathieu is Jean Valjean. Because he *was* him, 27 years ago, in a very similar room. Which means, – ready for a brain twister? – he is finally moved to show that Champmathieu is *not* Jean Valjean, because Jean Valjean *was* Champmathieu. And, a couple of chapters ago, he could only enter the room by being Madeleine. So all his efofrts to separate his identities were wrongheaded from the start: he needs, in a sense, to be all of these men at once here.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 11. Champmathieu de plus en plus étonné
entries.commentary_2025: This is one of the most dramatic and iconic scenes in the novel, and is the payof ffor all of book 7. What strikes me about it here is that Hugo puts Jean Valjean “on stage” in the courtroom, and then makes his language quite unpoetic – contrary to Hugo’s demonstrated ability as a playwright. I don’t know if this will come through in translation, but Hugo very much COULD have made this a theatrical-sounding monologue, and did not. The first moment when he announces himself, in the previous chapter, feels like theater, and *maybe* the line where he actually says, “I am Jean Valjean.” But the rest reads more like he’s talking to himself, or it resembles Champmathieu’s or (longer ago) Fantine’s defense of themselves – unselfconscious and a bit bogged down in details. Hugo was a master of dramatic rhythm, as we see elsewhere in this novel, but he doesn’t give us much of that at all in Jean Valjean’s “lines” in the courtroom. Perhaps because making this moment seem like theater would diminish it. This is not a spectacle, it’s a much more profound type of tragedy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Dans quel miroir M. Madeleine regarde ses cheveux
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: In what Mirror M. Madeleine contemplates his Hair
entries.commentary_2025: Of course, the chapter title points us toward thinking about this mirror… the mirror used to detect a faint trace of breath in someone who might be deceased. “Madeleine’s” white hair – turned from gray to white as he awaited the moment of truth (so to speak) in Arras – is that sign of life, the surprising bit of white in the mirror. The ambiguity between life and death in the Champmathieu afafir reminds us of the end of the dream he had the previous night, when he was asked if he knew he’d been dead for a long time. He might well wonder if his confession in Arras was a kind of death for him, for his Madeleine persona – or even, if it might lead to a literal capital sentence for him. But he sees in this mirror that he’s still alive. Perhaps it was the confession that kept him alive, kept him from becoming less human by letting Champmathieu sufefr in his place, and kept him on the path of meeting the Bishop’s call. Perhaps the white hair, in addition to being an efefct of stress and a sign of life, is a transfiguration.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Fantine is happy here, per the chapter title, and we see Hugo express it in the same way he did when he first introduced her: he says she “is” joy. And, as in that first glimpse of her, she’s subject to illusions. She believes she watched Madeleine all night, while we know where Jean Valjean was. She believes – is allowed to keep believing – that he has brought Cosette back with him. She believes she hears Cosette in the courtyard. / All of this, even Madeleine himself, is an illusion. Fantine was joy, is joy, but it seems that, in her tragic life, the only joy she can have is based in illusions. 😢
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Yesterday, Fantine’s happiness was based on illusions. Today – in a chapter with an obviously parallel title – Javert’s is more complicated. On one hand, it’s the opposite – it’s based on a revelation of the truth, and the confirmation that he was *not* experiencing an illusion in thinking that Madeleine was Jean Valjean. He’s happy to have been right, not only because it confirms what he thought he knew, but because it confirms everything about himself and his identity as a police officer that he doubted a few chapters ago. But at the same time, there is illusion mixed in with his happiness too. He sees himself allegorically, not as one police officer arresting one criminal, but as a Law triumphing over Chaos. This illusion is part of what creates the social damnation that so much of this novel is about.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: 😭 After we cry it out, what killed Fantine at this moment is interesting to think about… The emotional shock, for one thing, was understood to be dangerous for her. They’ve gone to great pains to prevent just that. But beyond that, just a few chapters ago, she said she only lived when Madeleine was there, and Javert declaring, so abruptly, that he doesn’t exist, proves that. She also said she was healed because her daughter was there; learning that she was not also reversed any real benefit of that good news. Javert is horrifically cruel here. But we see how he justifies it to himself – he believes he’s setting the world right, and “fixing” this strange place where convicts and prostitutes are treated humanely. Nevertheless, he knows that Jean Valjean has a kind of power – sheer physical strength, and something else as well – that he can’t match.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: I think this is the first time we see just how clever Jean Valjean is at escapes! And while most of the town, for reasons of prejudice, has turned against him already, it helps that those closest to him haven’t. (It also stood out to me this time how Hugo included the royalist who was glad that Madeleine’s unmasking would somehow stick it to the Bonapartists….) The payoff for Sister Simplice’s uncompromising honesty, which he’s reiterated several times, is interesting too. She has always been as inflexible about telling the truth as Javert has been about respecting authority, and here, because we know that, we fear she will give Jean Valjean up. But she doesn’t, to our great relief. It’s the person with the more flexible rules, who can evaluate morality on a case-by-case basis (as the Bishop did), who earns our respect, and wins out. And finally: Is this in fact a suitable tomb for Fantine? Based on what we know about her – her dignity, courage, love, sacrifice – no. She deserves honor. But it will become clear in this book, if it hasn’t yet, that what people deserve is not what society gives them. So, her tomb resembles her life, not just her bed – it gives her as little as possible, and nothing really of her own. Congratulations on finishing Part I! Tomorrow, we head to Waterloo….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Ce qu'on rencontre en venant de Nivelles
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: What is met with on the Way from Nivelles
entries.commentary_2025: Here we go… Since we're going to be at Waterloo for almost 3 weeks, let's spend some of that time thinking about why on earth…. (We’ll keep doing this throughout!) Hugo wrote this digression at the very end of the composition of the novel. He knew what the book was about by then, knew the plot beats, and thought this was important to it. (Regarding plot beats – remember that these 5 volumes were originally published separately, the first two about 6 weeks apart. So there was a natural pause before this section.) He also started several chapters in Part I in 1815, and has mentioned Napoleon quite a bit. He clearly sees this as connected to Les Misérables. So we should at least consider that he might have had a point! We see him here approaching Hougomont across an idyllic spring countryside, and, after noticing one subtle scar left by the battle, he’s surprised to learn where he is. Time (between 1815 and 1861) has nearly erased the monumental and tragic events that took place here – so maybe we’re not all that far from Fantine….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo probably liked that this place sounds like it’s connected to him, but the connection to the Hugo name that he gives has no basis in reality! This tour of a ruined monument reminds me of his novel Notre-Dame de Paris (The Hunchback of Notre-Dame in English), and Hugo’s support of historical preservation. He takes us on a tour of the place, seeing into the past through it, and subtly laments the way historical events get overwritten in places like this. Incidentally, the Hougomont Farm is a museum today – so the historical preservation that Hugo seems to crave here has taken place, as it did at Notre-Dame after he wrote about it! If you’re interested, a Google search of Hougomont will provide pictures that bring this description to life. There are also some details in this chapter that stand out as symbolically connected to other parts of the novel. The courtyard is guarded by a dog, which is compared to the English on the day of the battle. Guard dogs (Javert…) are important in this book! Also, the well where legend said some soldiers may have been “buried” alive creates a situation like the man overboard that we saw early in Jean Valjean’s story, an important image of his state as a convict.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo does two things here that seem contradictory: he ofefrs a physical, tactical explanation for why Napoleon lost the battle, and then says that sort of thing isn’t his main interest or his expertise. (Wha? Hugo admits he’s not the expert?? 😲 His modesty might be a tad false.) But it isn’t really a contradiction: in discussing the rain that prevented moving artillery earlier in the day, he says “Providence” was at work. He isn’t interested in HOW Napoleon lost at Waterloo, but WHY. And not the physical, tactical, earthly “why,” but the cosmic one. He’s interested in why history progresses – or regresses – in the way that it does, in the “chance” events that change everything, and in the human lives that get caught up in it. This book has been, and will continue to be, full of all of those things, albeit on a smaller scale. In examining Waterloo, he’ll examine why the Big Moments show up and change the course of lives.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo is more or less right about the “A” here. He is going to tell us a story where this general orientation of the battle will matter, but once again, the other parts of this chapter carry more meaning than the part it’s titled for. We have here the first real reflection on Napoleon’s legacy – for Hugo, it’s mixed. As a kid, Hugo saw Napoleon as a hero, and the way he describes the glory surrounding him reflects that. While it seems inexplicable to many of us now, this was not an uncommon feeling in France at the time. Napoleon was supposed to be picking up the torch from the Revolution, and carrying the French nation, now freed from the monarchy, into the future. With the benefit of hindsight, adult Hugo can see that’s…. not how it went. But, as ever, Hugo sees the whole picture at once: the brilliant military mind, the initial intent to lead France forward, the violence and the unacceptable tyranny that came later. The image he uses for this, of history as a bright light that both illuminates reality and casts shadows, tells a basic truth: light does this, and light and shadow usually exist together. Seeing the truth clearly makes heroes into human beings, and human beings have a shadow side..
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Once again, a bit of straightforward battle narrative, a bit of reflective commentary, and – as he told us – Hugo is better at the latter, even if his evocative descriptions do give a good “feel” of the battle itself. What he describes in the last long paragraph of this chapter sounds very much, to this humble humanities professor, like chaos theory. I’d love to see what someone who knows more about chaos theory than I do thinks about this section! Except, when he completes the Latin phrase in the chapter title, he shows that he doesn’t believe in true randomness. Quid obscurum – what is obscure – is the chaos he describes. Quid divinum – what is divine – is, for Hugo, hidden in that chaos. He’s already given us the rain on the battlefield as an example: we could see it as random (and weather systems are actually a frequent example in chaos theory! – I think). But Hugo said then, and reiterates difefrently now, that he doesn’t believe that.
