entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: After yesterday’s emphasis on the dynamic and seemingly infinitely complex nature of battles, today, Hugo gives us a snapshot of a moment in time at Waterloo: 4 pm. It’s a moment that, from the perspective of history and knowing the ultimate outcome of the battle, is easy to forget, when things seem to be going badly for the English. A moment that, taken out of context, misrepresents the battle. It is both true* and untrue: the facts are historical, but incomplete. (*True and historical, allowing for Hugo’s narrative license, which is always to be kept in mind! I will leave it to the history buffs to fact-check him in detail.) The biggest and truest truths – of history, of human lives, of the workings of the natural and supernatural worlds – are always, for Hugo, the more complex and nuanced ones. To be understood, things need to be seen in motion, and from a constantly moving perspective. It is all the snapshots and perspectives together, including their contradictions, that make up the truth.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: What does Hugo want us to make of Napoleon’s good mood here? There is of course a foreboding to this chapter. We know how unfounded his optimism is. Are we to understand him as cocky, overly sure of his battle plan? Is he getting caught up in his own efofrt to hype up morale? Are we meant to see him mostly as out of step with the larger forces that Hugo sees at work at Waterloo? Is Hugo ofefring a human explanation for the boldness with which he will charge into catastrophe? Human reasons lead to the human choices that make up vast, world-historical events. Napoleon’s mood, like the mud on the battlefield or the movement of troops unit by unit or man by man, is part of the complex chaos where, for Hugo, cosmic forces can act.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 8. L'empereur fait une question au guide Lacoste
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: The Emperor puts a Question to the Guide Lacoste
entries.commentary_2025: The first half of this chapter – almost all one long sentence, a list – is the poet Hugo at work, adapting the rhythm and grammar of his prose to the reality he’s trying to convey. These moments of the battle, he seems to be telling us, come at Napoleon in an undifefrentiated stream, almost a parade of objects that pass in front of him without afefcting him. There are a lot of them, but by gum, Hugo’s going to fit them all into one sentence, encouraging us to skim past them as Napoleon did. That is, they don’t change much about what he expects from the day. He watches, not passively or without participating in leading the battle, but from an emotional distance, unmoved in his optimism. But Hugo also says much more directly here that Napoleon should have been more cautious in that optimism. Worth at least considering the possibility of defeat, that maybe, *maybe* there’s a factor at work here that he doesn’t understand. Hugo certainly thinks there is.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Today is the one time, in this Waterloo section, where I’m going to fact-check Hugo in this daily post, because his departure from fact is interesting. The cavalry charge into the unseen sunken Ohain road did not happen. The sunken road *was* a feature of the landscape, and Hugo probably saw it and was inspired by it. But Napoleon probably knew about it too. Historians allow that a few men and/or horses probably fell in there, but the scene here – glorious charge, obstacle hidden by illusion, massive catastrophe – is a hugolian invention. So, that being the case, why did he make it up the way he did? If it’s not telling us a historical fact, what is it doing here? His interpretation in this chapter continues to build on the butterfly-efefct-like reasoning that we saw earlier. Lacoste’s small error leads to loss of the battle, which leads to the end of Napoleon’s comeback, which makes way for the new century. And, of course, Hugo doesn’t attribute this to chance or to malice on the part of Lacoste, but to divine intervention. We’ll return to other significance of the sunken road later, but here, it’s a God-sized line in the sand beyond which Napoleon will not be allowed to go.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: I will once again leave fact-checking to those who enjoy military history more than I do. My interest here is literary – so it’s maybe even a little more interesting if Hugo isn’t telling the exact truth! The story he tells has all the twists and turns you’d want for dramatic efefct, with momentum shifts giving the battle an emotional arc. What that arc is, of course, depends on who one is rooting for. This being a French book, we might think Hugo is rooting for Napoleon, or at least for his army, and in a lot of places here, it feels like that’s the case. In that reading, Waterloo begins optimistically, and then catastrophe brings tragedy. But we’ve already seen, and will continue to see, that it’s more complicated than that. Hugo isn’t really pulling for Napoleon here. So, given what he has said, and will continue to say, about the good and bad of Waterloo, what is the emotional arc he creates in narrating the battle the way he does? PS: You’re officially more than halfway through the Waterloo chapters. YOU CAN DO IT!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 11. Mauvais guide à Napoléon, bon guide à Bülow
entries.english_hapgood_title: 11: A Bad Guide to Napoleon; a Good Guide to Bulow
entries.commentary_2025: A wet morning delaying the start of the battle, a bit of bad advice for Napoleon, and now a bit of good advice for Bülow – the small things that change big things. Napoleon’s vision is noteworthy here: he is able to see the enemy’s approaching reinforcements remarkably far off – beginning at noon, when they won’t arrive at the battlefield until 5 pm. This suggests, on one hand, a kind of genius, but on the other, a blindness. Remember how optimistic Napoleon was at this point in the battle? And how optimistic he remained? If he could see the Prussian army coming, was that optimism not a bit… hubristic? But then, Napoleon (as Hugo portrays him) is blind to a lot of things at Waterloo. If he could see this for (what Hugo says) it is, he wouldn’t play the part that is fated to him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: There is a courage that comes from hope and optimism, and a very difefrent kind of courage that comes from their opposite. That defiance that comes with despair, with having accepted the worst, is a kind of power. We’ve seen a version of it already: Fantine, when she believed the worst had already happened to her, seemed to lose her fear and shame. It is something we will see again, too: characters with nothing left to lose finding the power that comes with that. It’s here, then, that Napoleon’s army really become characters in Les Misérables, in their circumstances and their response to those circumstances.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Lest we think that, because Hugo isn’t entirely rooting for Napoleon here, he’s turned his back on his countrymen: he gives us the best defense yet of the glory of this army in defeat. If they’re fleeing, you see, it’s because this is no normal defeat: it’s not Blücher who’s beat them, it’s God Himself. Their fear is of something supernatural, that larger force that we’ve seen at work at Waterloo throughout Hugo’s telling of it, the one that defeated Napoleon so the century could move on. The other striking image in this chapter is at the end, the sleepwalker trying to return to Waterloo, to do a thing of which he is already no longer capable. We’ve seen such a sleepwalker before, of course, who didn’t yet understand his new reality, and did a thing of which he was already no longer capable. And that man is, so far as we know, also wandering at this point in the story, alone with his new reality, and hoping to avoid arrest.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: As tomorrow’s chapter title suggests, we’re going to spend more time then on the last word of this chapter. For the moment, I’ll just mention the translation challenge: literally, the word is “Shit!” but it’s being used to mean something more like “Go to hell!” Either translation in English loses something of the other. 💩🖕 But that word in French, “merde,” came to be called, euphemistically, “le mot de Cambronne” (the word of Cambronne), thanks to the story that Hugo tells here. Hugo did not invent this story; it was widely recounted after Waterloo, but Cambronne himself denied having said the two lines we see at the end. Hugo’s inclusion of it caused some objections, as delicate 19th-century sensibilities didn’t appreciate seeing such things in print, corrupting their women and children. 🫢 But it makes an excellent dramatic ending to this scene of defiance, in which we once again see a spiritual power that seems to be at work alongside the military one.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: So what does Hugo like so much about the “word of Cambronne” here? As we said yesterday, it’s both its defiance, or “disdain” as he says a couple of times, and its vulgarity. For most of Hugo’s own career, he prided himself on saying and doing things with language that weren’t allowed, if he thought they served expression. Cambronne does just that. But it’s not the just defaince and the vulgarity separately that Hugo likes, it’s the fact that Cambronne combines both into one word. (This is why any translation into English fails here: we don’t have a word that does this!) It’s a reversal – a revolution, if you will – in which the filthiest, most undignified of things becomes glorious, as it becomes courage. And Hugo tells us that Cambronne says this “in the name of the revolution” – we’ll come back to just how (not) close Napoleon in 1815 was to the revolution of 1789 – as it expresses revolution. What was low (a defeated army, or excrement) is raised up by this word. And as it is the revolution responding to monarchy, it is also the future responding to the past, at the very moment when it seems like the past has won.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This title means, approximately, “What is the weight (importance) of a leader?” In the face of a victory for Wellington or Blücher, or a defeat for Napoleon, what does that mean about their soldiers, or the people of their nation? For Hugo, here, it means nothing. A nation is not its leaders. (As I write from the U.S. at the moment… phew.) Besides which, we reiterate here that Waterloo was more about luck, or fate, or divine intervention, than anything else. Something bigger than Wellington had a plan here, but taking the victory away from Wellington is no reflection on the English, and implicitly, Napoleon having been put in his place is no reflection on the French.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 17: Is Waterloo to be considered Good?
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo doesn’t really answer the question in the chapter title, about what we should think about Waterloo. What he does, though, is separate intent from impact, which will be an important distinction to keep in mind going forward. The other monarchies in Europe *intended* (per Hugo) to put a stop to this thing going on in France, which threatened the ideas that supported their power. They meant to uphold royal power. But the *impact* was to put a definitive end to a despot, and distaste for that despotism (again, per Hugo) forced what came next, even though it was monarchy, to accept limits on its power. It may be a bit of a stretch to attribute all of that to Waterloo specifically. But the distinction he makes is what matters to the rest of Les Misérables: Wellington et. al. intended one thing, but a force larger than them turned their action to a difefrent purpose.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: So, after Waterloo, because of Waterloo, 25 years of revolutionary France ended in the Restoration, of which the king, Louis XVIII, was in the line of succession of the guillotined Louis XVI. Oops. If you notice a resemblance here to the chapter that listed cultural details of the year 1817, you’re not wrong. The olden days are back. But Napoleon’s legacy, and the devotion that some still had for him, cast a shadow of revolution over this restored monarchy that hadn’t been there before. Was Napoleon, in the way he was governing the Empire, a worthy inheritor of the ideals of 1789? Probably not. It was hardly a republic, for example. But he was, if nothing else, an alternative to the Old Regime, and that threat forced the Restoration to begin making compromises. And finally, in a chapter titled to emphasize the supposed divine right of the restored kings, Hugo ends up putting human events in divine perspective, making it all quite small indeed. What do we do with the double assertion in this section – that a higher power intended Napoleon’s end, and that it sees all these events as so insignificant?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 19. Le champ de bataille la nuit
entries.commentary_2025: Hey, look, characters! Thénardier is pretty recognizable from his description, before we get his name. It’s no coincidence either that, of all the parts of the battlefield that Hugo has shown us, this happens in the sunken road. He tips his hand a bit about why it was important for him to imagine it this way: the living death he describes in that place is a powerful echo of the man overboard from I, 2, 8, who was an image of Jean Valjean in prison. Thematically, then, Pontmercy is in the same place as Jean Valjean was, and may soon be again. It also bears a resemblance to the common grave where we so tragically saw Fantine buried. And here is the first instance of many where Thénardier’s actions are turned to a purpose he doesn’t intend: he meant to rob Pontmercy, and he did so, but he also saved his life. His selfish intent doesn’t get the last word. CONGRATULATIONS on making it through the longest digression of the book! Tomorrow, back to our hero.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep16 - II,2,i - II,3,iii - Fate, Hope, and Spiders
entries.commentary_2025: Alas, we suspected this might be the case, and Hugo wastes no time confirming it: Jean Valjean was caught. The news reports as a way of narrating this are interesting: while they seem authentic, we can also see places
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Où on lira deux vers inédits qui sont peut-être du diable
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: In which the reader will peruse Two Verses which are of the Devil's Composition possibly
entries.companion_episode: Ep16 - II,2,i - II,3,iii - Fate, Hope, and Spiders
entries.commentary_2025: This is a good story to tell on April Fool’s Day – one of devilish trickery. A place where there are stories of the devil burying his treasure in the woods, is the perfect place to… bury a treasure in the woods. Seems as if someone thought this through! 🤔 And, of course, someone like Boulatruelle may not be afraid of the devil, but he *is* afraid of a man he knows from prison, who is super strong. We don’t have to pretend we don’t know who that man is, do we? Hugo is a little coy here, but combined with the previous chapter, we can piece together a pretty clear story. And that story shows Jean Valjean’s cleverness, as well as the physical strength that Boulatruelle remembers. If he were as dastardly as the news reports said, or as the devil himself, he’d be dangerous indeed.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. Qu'il fallait que la chaîne de la manille eût subi un certain travail préparatoire pour être ainsi brisée d'un coup de marteau
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: The Ankle-Chain must have undergone a Certain Preparatory Manipulation to be thus broken with a Blow from a Hammer
entries.companion_episode: Ep16 - II,2,i - II,3,iii - Fate, Hope, and Spiders
entries.commentary_2025: Just in case you were feeling nostalgic for military digressions, here are a few pages on the Royalist War in Spain. But it connects to Waterloo, and to the larger political ideas of this book: force may install a regime, but it can’t stop the forward march of ideas. Then, we move on to a nostalgic, romantic view of military ships from the age of sail, which showcases Hugo’s connection to the ocean, especially during this time of his life, when he was in exile on Guernesey. But the most interesting part of this chapter for most of us is, of course, Jean Valjean’s rescue of the crewman from the rigging of the Orion. It’s a suspenseful action scene, and Hugo focuses on the crowd’s reaction, as it mirrors ours. But it’s also a scene that draws on a lot of imagery that is important in the novel. First, keep your eye on mentions of spiders. More of that to come (and I talk about it in the podcast for this section!) Also, the emphasis on the ship at sea makes Jean Valjean’s fall into the water, even with the ship docked, remind us of the man overboard from early in the novel, who was a metaphor for an incarcerated person. We’ll see what comes of this fall into the sea, though….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. La question de l'eau à Montfermeil
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep16 - II,2,i - II,3,iii - Fate, Hope, and Spiders
entries.commentary_2025: The title of this chapter has a double meaning: “la question de l’eau” could mean “the problem of water,” which is what the chapter seems to describe. Or, it can mean more or less “water torture,” that is, questioning by water. The same phrase was used two chapters ago in discussing Boulatruelle. There, Thénardier made a joke about submitting Boulatruelle to “la question du vin” – questioning by wine, that is, getting him drunk enough to talk. But the use of this phrase in the title here plays with words too: the problem of water in Montfermeil leads to just one of the types of torture that Cosette undergoes. The horrible mistreatment of this child is one of the best-known elements of the novel, so much so that a drawing that it inspired became the logo for the musical. But it will take on many more significant meanings as we proceed – just one that we see here is as a child-sized image of the sort of class divide that the novel is written against. While she works, and while another child cries alone in the dark, two other little girls are spared this sufefring, and live happy, comfortable lives. The difefrence is nothing other than luck, or the caprice of an unjust authority.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep16 - II,2,i - II,3,iii - Fate, Hope, and Spiders
entries.commentary_2025: Thénardier and his wife are not the comic relief characters from the musical – indeed, they are everything sinister. People often think of the villains of this book being Thénardier and Javert – that’s a bit oversimplified, but it is fair to say they’re the two main antagonists. Javert, though, is moral and upstanding by certain reasonable definitions of the word, even if Hugo calls those definitions into question. He has sincere beliefs. Thénardier is of a difefrent sort: he is only self-interest, and responds to nothing higher. Any principles he has, he has them because he thinks they serve him. His wife also serves his interests, which are mostly the same as hers. We’ll see how that plays out for her. In the meantime, (as I reflected on Inauguration Day, a propos of nothing in particular), he is the lying, cunning, trickster in service of their endless swindle, and she is the violent enforcer. Together, in the microcosm of a harsh society that Cosette sufefrs through in their household, they are the powerful, turning others’ sufefring to their own profit.

Cosette, continuing to show us a child-sized version of society, is guilty here of lying about having watered the horse. But it’s plain to us why

entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: Entrance on the Scene of a Doll
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep17 - II,3,iv-viii - People You Might Meet in the Woods
entries.commentary_2025: It might be a cliché, but this doll being the dream of all the little girls in Montfermeil gives Cosette a way of glimpsing something she couldn’t otherwise imagine. The narrator says outright that she feels as though she’s looking at heaven, with the big doll surrounded by other celestial beings, and the merchant seems to be God himself. But beyond that, the details of this doll, especially its real hair, have a painful implication: this is one use that would have been made of human hair that was sold by someone like Fantine. It is dressed in fine fabrics, which Fantine was as well, before her “descent”-- at least symbolically, if not literally, this doll is made up of things that Cosette’s mother gave up to support her. But now, all that she intended to provide for Cosette, as well as the doll itself, are out of her reach, because of the Thénardiers’ cruelty. And even in her vision of Paradise, the figure that stands in for God is actually a barrier, a salesman, once again commodifying Fantine, now through this stand-in.

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep17 - II,3,iv-viii - People You Might Meet in the Woods
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo has a way of taking bad situations in this book beyond what’s imaginable. Cosette is not only unloved and abused, not only made to work and cared for as minimally as possible, she’s also cold, tired, and alone in the woods at night, faced with a job that is far too difficult for her physically and forced to choose between known and unknown terrors. We’ve seen situations this extreme before, notably with Fantine, and we’ll see them again. Hugo didn’t go in much for restraint, for better or worse! But in this book, it serves a purpose: Hugo wants to help us imagine, as vividly as possible, the painful realities of people whose lives are harder than ours. The circumstances he creates may be extreme, perhaps implausibly so, but they stretch our imaginations, and make us better able to *really* see what’s in front of us in the real world. There are always bystanders in these scenes too, who see our main characters without really *really* seeing them. There’s one here, as Cosette leaves Montfermeil. We have to wonder how often that’s us…. And of course, the extreme circumstances make mercy, if and when it arrives, that much more welcome.

entries.companion_episode: Ep17 - II,3,iv-viii - People You Might Meet in the Woods
entries.commentary_2025: I’m assuming you can guess who the white-haired man at the start of the chapter is? For the rest of the book, that white hair (a mark of the Champmathieu afafir, remember) will be an important clue. Note how similar this description is, in its approach, to the first description when he entered Digne. A similarity that makes the difefrences stand out. He now seems poor and careworn, but not hopeless or dangerous. People notice him – he’s not from here, and does some odd things – but they don’t fear him as they did in Digne. Then, in the woods, it’s once again clear to us what he’s doing, even if Hugo presents it through the point of view of an uninformed observer. He’s checking on his stash of cash, which he *did* hide in the woods, as Boulatruelle thought. And that is how, in one of the book’s many remarkable coincidences, he comes upon Cosette in her desperate moment.

entries.french_title: 7. Cosette côte à côte dans l'ombre avec l'inconnu
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: Cosette Side by Side with the Stranger in the Dark
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep17 - II,3,iv-viii - People You Might Meet in the Woods
entries.commentary_2025: We thought of Jean Valjean entering Digne yesterday and made a comparison to how he was described, but here, he’s much more like the Bishop that evening. He does for Cosette in her distress all the same things the Bishop did for him: meets her immediate needs, takes an interest in her story and perspective, really sees her. He does an especially remarkable thing at the start of the chapter that may not come through in translation: he uses the respectful “vous” to mean “you” when addressing her. This stands out because it is rare to use “vous” with a child. “Vous” is used for strangers and to show formality, respect, and deference – for adults. But kids are almost always “tu” to everyone, right away. He switches to “tu” pretty quickly, but the appearance of “vous” early in their conversation reminds us of how the Bishop treated him. Jean Valjean then, and Cosette now, were desperate for many things, but respect is near the top of the list, and it’s one of the first things these rescuers give them. It’s difefrent, though, in that their connection is immediate. Jean Valjean knows who she is, of course, as soon as she says her name. But Cosette’s trust in him is instinctive.

entries.french_title: 8. Désagrément de recevoir chez soi un pauvre qui est peut-être un riche
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: The Unpleasantness of receiving into One's House a Poor Man who may be a Rich Man
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep17 - II,3,iv-viii - People You Might Meet in the Woods
entries.commentary_2025: A lot to say about money today. I discuss conversion of specific sums to 21st-century dollars in episode 2 of the podcast. Briefly - it’s tricky. But even internal to the text, we can get a sense of what Jean Valjean is doing: we see him shell out approximately 60 francs in this chapter (depending on the cost of the doll), and he’s not remotely done. Thinking back to the early pages of the book, this is maybe close to 15 times what the Bishop’s household of 3 adults was living on per day. The 5-franc piece in particular is a coin we’ll see show up a lot; it’s a sum that feels like a lot of money to our poorest characters, but isn’t in fact a fortune. But that coin also seems to take on a special importance – worth keeping an eye on. And – I have one!! I’m not a coin collector, but a colleague gave this to me, and I was unreasonably excited, thanks to its role in this book. The coin that he puts in Cosette’s clog, meanwhile, is one we’ve seen before: Fantine got one of these for each tooth she sold. It’s worth 20 francs. The comments about girls and dolls feel a bit old-fashioned to us. But the deprivation and disconnection from life that it’s meant to express about Cosette is still 😢. Then, the incident with the other girls’ doll and the spectacular doll that Jean Valjean buys for her, echoes the Bishop’s gift to him: he took the silver that was not his, and was gifted the candlesticks in an act of not just mercy, but radical defiance of punishment. And that moment leads to this one in a very pragmatic way: selling the Bishop’s silver gave him the money to start his business in Montreuil-sur-mer, and make the fortune he now draws on.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: This chapter title promises we’ll see maneuvers that turn out… somewhat less impressive than we might expect. Thénardier does get his 1500 francs, though, I suppose. He fancies himself an operator, and his wife buys it, but he didn’t get anything that Jean Valjean wasn’t prepared to give here. This is fundamentally because Thénardier doesn’t understand Jean Valjean, whereas Jean Valjean has Thénardier’s number immediately. Jean Valjean can see right into him – Hugo says essentially this at one point – but Thénardier does best in his negotiations when he can’t be seen. He can’t get that advantage here with Jean Valjean. Meanwhile, we see a bit of the efefct that Cosette’s sufefring has had on her. Just like Jean Valjean as he left prison, she is in a dark place, fearful and hating her former life, the only glimmer of hope being the person who rescued her. Fortunately, as we see when he uses the metaphor of breaking her chain, Jean Valjean understands her, like maybe no one else could.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 10. Qui cherche le mieux peut trouver le pire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 10: He who seeks to better himself may render his Situation Worse
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: Thénardier, still overestimating himself, and underestimating Jean Valjean. He’s not wrong, that he shouldn’t simply hand Cosette to anyone willing to pay (although, given the efefcts of his extortion on Fantine, commodifying people isn’t exactly new to him!) But he makes this point entirely disingenuously. He’s still willing to let her go for money – he just wants a higher price. And yet, when it’s the right to Cosette that he wants to see, Jean Valjean shows that too, to his great disappointment! The note, which we’ve seen before, is now cited with the date included, and that date is important: March 25, exactly 9 months before the current date in the story, which is Christmas day. So, Fantine signed the document “giving” Cosette to Jean Valjean on Annunciation, and he “adopted” her on Christmas. The intervening period becomes a kind of gestation, following the timeline of the Virgin Mary’s. He becomes as much Cosette’s mother as her father.

entries.french_title: 11. Le numéro 9430 reparaît, et Cosette le gagne à la loterie
entries.english_hapgood_title: 11: Number 9,430 reappears, and Cosette wins it in the Lottery
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Accomplissement de la promesse faite à la morte
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: No need to even pretend to be surprised by the first line of this chapter! But symbolically, the supposed uncertainty about his fate, and the notion that he’s somehow between life and death, matters quite a bit. A couple of weeks ago, we mentioned that his fall from the Orion resembled the man overboard from the early part of the novel. Remember, in that chapter, how the man overboard was alive, but completely without hope of rescue. His end was certain, but he was still alive to consider the fact. Jean Valjean is between life and death in some important ways, too. The belief that he’s dead, while it provides cover from the law, also prevents him from participating in society. He has no legal existence, for good or bad. (This kind of legal death was of interest in this period: an 1832 novella by Balzac, “Le Colonel Chabert,” was about a man who was declared dead in battle but survived and returned, trying to get his existence back.) It’s a version of the social damnation that’s been with him from the start. Since he became a convict, he can’t really live. But making that literal – the authorities believing that he’s actually dead – provides protection. This is why he experiences it as relief, the sort of peace he’d have, as Hugo says, if he were actually dead.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: Not sure if the pun in the chapter title comes through in translation: corbeau (with a “c”) is a crow, and Hugo refers in the chapter to the fable of the fox and the crow. It was (and still is) very common for French schoolchildren to have to memorize Jean de la Fontaine’s version of this fable (language-learner-friendly version here: https://youtu.be/JfTmgozM9XY?si=MwPEADhMUFMkfExH) So, since the first words of that poem are “Maître Corbeau,” many French speakers, myself included, think of it immediately when they see “Maître Gorbeau.” It’s a joke, but also, contributes to an odd name confusion that is the tip of the iceberg in this place. Otherwise, what we learn about the Gorbeau house here emphasizes strangeness and uncertainty. By virtue of its contradictions, it’s hard to know what it is: a hovel or a cathedral? In the city or the country? Elegant or poor? Large or small? Number 50 or 52? It’s in a space at the edge of the city (at the time – this area is very much part of Paris now!) that feels like a sort of no-man’s-land. And, it’s a tad creepy for how much it’s associated with crime and punishment, of the deadliest sorts. But, of course, is that a surprise anymore in this novel? Like the final hours at Waterloo, the morbidity and contradictions of this place make it fit right in!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: A Nest for Owl and a Warbler
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: Naturally, the Gorbeau house, having so much in common with many of the characters in this book, is the place where Jean Valjean and Cosette land. Or, perch, as it were. 🦉🐦‍⬛Taking Cosette into his care is a heady experience for Jean Valjean, and we see his “contemplation” of her compared to his contemplation of Fantine during her illness. This is portrayed as religious as much as anything else. This is how this character experiences God – through people he loves, and who appear godly to him – the Bishop, Fantine, and now Cosette. 🎶 “To love another person is to see the face of God.” 🎶 Note also that the 9-month period between Fantine’s death and now is mentioned once again. And Cosette’s adaptation to her new life is progressing. She still fears Mme Thénardier, but is easily reassured by Jean Valjean, whom she trusts so naturally. It’s trust that Hugo says belongs only to the very weak or the very strong. Given her recent past, and Jean Valjean’s total adoration of her, it’s hard to say which she is.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. Deux malheurs mêlés font du bonheur
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: Two Misfortunes make One Piece of Good Fortune
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: This pair is remarkable for how well-suited they are to understand each other and heal each other’s wounds. Their painful pasts and walled-off emotions are so similar that it may be only each other, in this period of quiet, that can let them heal. And the period of quiet takes on an interesting textual form: repetition. This is the second day in a row, third overall, that I’ve had occasion to talk about Jean Valjean becoming like Coestte’s mother – this time, through birth pangs. We’ve now repeated elements of the description of the house – especially those that show how it’s quiet, out-of-the-way, and hides them well – 3 days in a row. Probably most importantly, we’ve lingered on Jean Valjean’s growing love for his adoptive child. Lingering here in this way, in stillness, allows us to feel the time of stasis and safety that they’re getting to enjoy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Les remarques de la principale locataire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: The Remarks of the Principal Tenant
entries.companion_episode: Ep18 - II,3,ix - II,4,iv - The Two Forçats
entries.commentary_2025: Even an intentionally solitary life has some human interaction – in our more isolated age, it stands out how much this person who wants to go unnoticed is enmeshed in his community. The woman who manages the building, cleans his room, and watches Cosette from time to time gathers quite a lot of information! Older women of this sort become a somewhat ubiquitous feature of this book – widows, probably, relatively poor but getting by, who hold everything together and see a LOT. Mme Victurnien was one, of a sort, with a bit of moralism added in. The Bishop’s servant Mme Magloire was another, of a difefrent sort. Mlle Baptistine was a bit difefrent, but served a similar purpose. Being outside of a lot of aspects of society, but also essential to it, they make great observers, giving us a perspective that is both individual and general. They’re Hugo’s person-on-the-street.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Une pièce de cinq francs qui tombe à terre fait du bruit
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: A Five-Franc Piece falls on the Ground and produces a Tumult
entries.commentary_2025: Remember what we said about the 5-franc piece showing up a lot at significant moments? Here it is again. But first, when Jean Valjean first thinks he sees Javert in place of the beggar in the street, it’s interesting that Hugo makes it a matter of unreliable perception, possible hallucination. Jean Valjean’s distrust and dismissal of his instincts doesn’t last, though. It takes very little – a new person in the building with a couple of suspicious movements – to set him on alert. In his narration, Hugo uses point of view SO well in these last two chapters, in a way that heightens the mystery and suspense. Yesterday, we saw Jean Valjean through the building manager’s eyes, and while we understand why she might be suspicious of him, we don’t know what conclusions she drew. So, today, back inside Jean Valjean’s point of view, we know JUST a bit more than he does – that is, that she’s noticed some oddities about him – but it’s no clearer to us what he should do next. We don’t know who is next door, whether she alerted the police or cooperated when they showed up on their own, or whether her comments at the end of this chapter are casual or meant as a heads-up to protect him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo’s nostalgia for the old Paris here is sweet – it’s true that Paris changed a lot after he went into exile in 1852, and of course, as he writes in 1862, he doesn’t know that he’ll live to see even the new city again. Discussing these changes also covers his authorial license in describing the geographical details of the city! These next few chapters will be an urban chase scene, but they are full of animal metaphors, as both Javert and Jean Valjean are acting on instincts. Since he was first introduced, Javert has been described as a dog – specifically a guard dog. But here, he becomes the leader of a pack of hunting dogs. And Jean Valjean is the deer they’re hunting. The instincts he’s using are those of a prey species – that is, a convict, an outsider, a misérable. And they don’t involve extensive planning or, as the chapter title suggests, long-term strategy. He doesn’t know much more about what will happen next than Cosette does. He’s following something that he understands as dimly as she understands him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Il est heureux que le pont d'Austerlitz porte voitures
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: It is Lucky that the Pont d'Austerlitz bears Carriages

This is particularly true if you look at the 1823 map (linked from my website): at the time period he’s describing, under the Restoration, it
