entries.french_title: 3. Voir le plan de Paris de 1727
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: To Wit, the Plan of Paris in 1727
entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: Don’t bother to follow the instructions in the chapter title. You won’t find what Hugo says you’ll find. 🙄 (If you like old maps, though, have a look at the Turgot map of Paris – it won’t help with this chapter, but it is from the early 18th century, and it’s beautifully drawn!) Ultimately, the Petit-Picpus neighborhood that he describes, and the convent that will bear its name, are fictional. There is, however, a location in this general area of Paris that is likely to be up Hugo’s alley (so to speak) and that is evoked here: the Picpus Cemetery, which had been a convent seized by the Revolution, and where over 1,000 guillotine victims were buried during the Reign of Terror. The Marquis de Lafayette is buried there too. But there is no map, not even the one Hugo recommends or the ones on my website, that will give you a better sense of Jean Valjean’s experience than Hugo’s description will. The police are closing in around him in this labyrinthine old city, which they know better than he does. His options are running out.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: This, once again, is a fictional spot. But Hugo has imagined it down to its minutest details, because it’s on those details that Jean Valjean’s fate will hang. Like rain or bad directions at Waterloo, this window being barred, or that wall being in light or shadow, will make ALL the difefrence. Jean Valjean has his usual advantages here: he’s smart, quick, strong, and has the skill set of a convict who made multiple escape attempts. But he has even more disadvantages. He doesn’t know the neighborhood. Anyone that he startles might lead the police to him. And he has a child with him, who is the purpose of all of this. He has to escape with her, or escape is useless, and she makes it that much more difficult.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Qui serait impossible avec l'éclairage au gaz
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Which would be Impossible with Gas Lanterns
entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo once again draws our attention, in the chapter title, to the fact that we’re in a bygone Paris here, one before the installation of gas lamps. This ends up mattering to Jean Valjean and Cosette, of course, because of the ropes that allowed lamplighters to raise and lower the old lamps. And drawing our attention to that rope creates a whole other meaning…. Remember when Jean Valjean rescued the crewman on the Orion, the image of one man suspended on a rope below the other was compared to a spider and its prey. I gestured here then to spiders having symbolic value for Hugo. Specifically, they signal an inevitability, a larger force at work, and not generally for good. (Check out the podcast for more explanation of that!) Here again, we see the person he’s rescuing dangling below him on a rope, just as the crewman man did on the Orion. But there, and again here, with Jean Valjean as the spider, it’s turned to the positive, an image of rescue, not predation. He is the force that works against the inexorable predation of life in this world.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: Gardens and the plants in them matter a lot in this book. We saw the Bishop’s garden: it was a place of contemplation, and he insisted on dedicating a portion of his to plants that were for beauty, not food. Jean Valjean has not (yet) had a garden of his own, but Madeleine knew quite a lot about cultivating plants, and making use of what was seen as useless. And now, he’s found himself in another garden. It’s grim, and it seems utilitarian. For a garden in spring, it’s a bit lifeless…. And the heavenly singing is a strong contrast to the garden! No wonder it feels like a riddle. In a sense, this reproduces the contemplation-garden combination from the Bishop, but without the garden reflecting any of the beauty – that’s all reserved for whatever is the source of the music.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: Throughout book 5, Hugo has been playing with genres of fiction that were popular, and relatively new, at the time. The chase scene in the streets was reminiscent of crime or detective fiction, which were gaining popularity in this period. And this chapter calls to mind gothic horror or “contes fantastiques” (lit. “fantastic tales”), both of which were popular in this period as well. But we’re not properly in either type of story here. In a typical detective story – think, a bit later, Sherlock Holmes, or today’s TV police procedurals – the lawman is the protagonist, and he catches his criminal in the end. And in horror stories or contes fantastiques, the monsters are real – or at least, they might be, as in contes fantastiques, the uncertainty on that point is a hallmark of the genre. We don’t yet know what Jean Valjean saw through the window, but we do probably know enough about this book to guess that it isn’t the other-worldly creature of his horrified imagination!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: It’s getting even stranger: aside from the bleak-looking garden, the heavenly singing, and the hellish vision of a body lying on a floor, now there’s a man wearing a bell as if he were livestock. What kind of place has all of this within its walls? Not knowing that makes it difficult to know what to do next – and the cold makes it urgent to figure it out. All the more so because Cosette has become as much the reason for his existence as she was her mother’s; he must protect her and provide for at all costs. In fact, the clothing he had to shed to get them both into this place and keep her warm – his hat, socks and shoes, tie, and now coat – remind us ever-so-gently of Fantine’s gradually increasing sacrifcies. The difefrence, of course, is that these sacrifices are reversible.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: And, the mystery is solved! We’re in a convent – specifically, the convent where Madeleine had sent old M. Fauchelevent to be a gardener after he rescued him from under his cart. This was in I, 5, 6-7; February 14 & 15 for us! It seemed like a detail at the time, an example of Madeleine’s generosity and a cause for Javert’s suspicion of him. But in one of this book’s more extraordinary coincidences (I know…🙄), Jean Valjean finds the right man at the right time: someone who can help him, and is willing to do anything for him in particular. He approaches him with an ofefr of money, but finds a much more powerful motivator: gratitude, and mutual generosity. A transactional situation à la Thénardier is replaced, in this scene, by a benevolent one à la Myriel, and that makes it far more trustworthy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 10. Où il est expliqué comment Javert a fait buisson creux
entries.english_hapgood_title: 10: Which explains how Javert got on the Scent
entries.french_book: Livre 5. A chasse noire, meute muette
entries.commentary_2025: A lot of adaptations show Javert as obsessed with Jean Valjean, and that always bothers me. This chapter is key to understanding why. Javert is exactly one thing: the quintessential police officer, the personifciation of the law. He is relentless in pursuit – hence the hunting and predator metaphors – and sees lawfulness as the bright line between those he must pursue and those he must protect. But none of that applies uniquely to Jean Valjean. It says right here that, when Javert doesn’t have a reason to think about him, he doesn’t. He’s just the guy that *this book* is about. I think adaptations add the weird obsession element because Jean Valjean keeps having to deal with the same policeman from one end of the country to the other. And I agree, the coincidences in this book are a LOT. But in their attempt to “fix” that, they lose something important. The relentlessness of Javert is a way of figuring the inexorable damnation that the law imposes. He’s merciless because it’s merciless – not just to Jean Valjean, but to everyone like him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The deep sequestration of the nuns of this convent will be an important theme in the coming pages – we’ll be in a digression about them until mid-May. We’ll see what Hugo thinks of this. It’ll be a little like Waterloo in that it will matter more thematically than it does for the plot. I hope you’ll bear with it in the same way! Still, plot-wise, the layers upon layers of barriers that separate the convent from the outside world are a great benefit for Jean Valjean. They’re not there for him, of course, or for Fauchelevent. In fact, Fauchelevent has already hinted that the nuns are just as eager to avoid him as to avoid the rest of the world – that’s why he wears the bell. But, for starters, they’re an important part of what’s stopping the police from pursuing Jean Valjean into this place: even if they could get in, they’re assuming that he could not have.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Let’s just be clear: this order is made up. A lot of the elements of it are real, but this combination is a product of Hugo’s imagination. He has imagined an extremely strict religious order here, in which the nuns’ asceticism and sufefring atone for the world’s sins, so it must be as great as they can stand. Of course, sufefring as payment for misdeed is not new in this book – it’s the assumption behind the penal system as well. But here, it’s assumed willingly, and mostly for others. These nuns share much with our other characters in fact: they are isolated, poor, have their identities stripped away, and sufefr physically. But at the same time, they’ve been presented to us so far as strange, mysterious, and something entirely new to this book. We’ll see if we can figure out how these similarities and difefrences add up.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo learned a lot of what he knew about the inner workings of convent life from Juliette Drouet, his longtime official mistress, who was educated in a convent. Convent education was common in the days before universal public education for girls – rich families paid the convents for this service, and some poorer girls were educated as an act of charity. As this chapter reflects, it didn’t mean the girls took vows (although some went on to do so, and the nuns probably hoped some of them would) – it was just a place for them to get a good, respectable upbringing. Protecting girls from the “dangers of the world” – read, horny young men – was a significant preoccupation, in the 19th century in particular. Hugo (who knew a thing or two about what men wanted from women!) was certainly protective of his own daughters. It seems patriarchal to us today, but it was what any good father at the time would have done. Fantine has already shown us why the world might be considered a danger, and while it may boil down to prudishness and social stigma, those things also did real harm. So, being behind convent walls was a sure way to avoid all of that until it was time to begin looking for a husband.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: There are a few occasions in this book where Hugo takes a moment to revel in the delight that is childhood, and this is one. They’re always lovely. Hugo adored children – his own four children and two grandchildren, and other children in his orbit as well, even hosting regular “poor children’s dinners” at his home on Guernsey. Later, after his grandchildren were born at the end of the 1860s, he would also write a poetry collection titled “L’Art d’être grand-père” (“The Art of Being a Grandfather”), that is full of similar themes and images. But even such descriptions of innocence can have dark corners, and they certainly do in this book. The first one we saw was when Fantine first met the Thénardiers, and Cosette played with their children. We know how that turned out. Here, too, innocent childhood play masks harsher realities. Spiders – those predators that represent the inevitable – appear again. Hidden in these adorable vignettes, there’s a child who lost her mother, the uncertainty of a future rooted in troubled French history, wordplay that alludes to a loss of innocence. We’re still in Les Misérables!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: In novels in this period and earlier, retreat to a convent, maybe after a scandal or heartbreak of some kind, was a fairly frequent trope. When the exciting action of the novel ended badly for a female character, going to finish out her days in a convent (perhaps without taking vows), was an alternative to dying – but just as definitive an end to her story. Like the ceremony of taking vows that we saw a few days ago, it was a symbolic death. The convent is a(nother) place of living death for this book. But the unusual thing that we’re doing here is seeing it from the other side. Mme. Albertine and “Auguste” could well have been characters in a novel that’s ended, and we’re seeing past that end. And inside the convent walls, as it turns out, things aren’t all that difefrent. There are still miniature dramas and scandals, on the scale of the young girls – not permanent residents of the convent – who are living them. The girls, as we saw yesterday, are not persisting in this living death. They are very much alive, and bringing life into the convent means bringing curiosity, intrigue, and just the teensiest bits of trouble!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: He doesn’t put it this way, but we see quite a lot of the efefcts of the Revolution in his chapter. The nuns who are here as “refugees” of other orders are one – the Revolution sought to eliminate the influence of religious establishments. And the events in the life of madame de Genlis that most likely scandalized the sisters of the convent (beyond the actual novels she wrote) had strong associations to that time as well: both her husband (from whom she was formally separated) and her lover (Phillipe Égalité, father of Louis-Phillipe who would become king in 1830) were Girondins, executed in 1793. But Madame de Genlis’s presence here points, perhaps more optimistically, toward the idea of education – she is known, among other things, for her writings on the education of children. This is of course a mission of the nuns as well, and Madame de Genlis was hardly Revolutionary herself – she emigrated, like much of the nobility, to avoid the danger that the Revolution posed to her own life. But she is quite difefrent from the nuns, and yet Hugo keeps showing us how various factions in society can make common cause around shared values.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: We finally learn a bit about the nuns as people – significant, given their beliefs and their vows, that Hugo provides us with their “real” names. Even with the severity of their lives and the strict rules they follow, the nuns have distinct personalities, and it’s worth it to Hugo to sketch them for us. A couple of the (again, fictional) names are interesting within the novel, though: Marguerite shows up twice, as Mère Innocente’s name, and as the name of one of the sisters. This was an early name of the character who would become Fantine, and Tholomyès connects it to her in his drunken monologue. As he says, the word, as a common noun, is from the Latin for “pearl.” It is also a French word for “daisy.” And, of course, there is also a sister Euphrasie, which is Cosette’s real name!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Now, we return to a description of the building, after getting an understanding of the mini-culture it contains. This is more or less what the chapter title means: literally, “After hearts, stones.” What’s interesting here, I think, are the ways Hugo conveys an image of the structure, largely envisioned from above, as he also had us do at Waterloo. The main building forms much of two sides of a trapezoid – and he describes it as a gallows, presumably resembling one in one of Hugo’s drawings. He describes the spider webs that form in the small door that opens to the public, because it is used so infrequently. The walls that enclose it are compared to prison walls. It’s a grim place, even in its physicality, which was also our observation when we first saw it through Jean Valjean’s eyes. But he notes at the end that flowers bloomed here first.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This character exists not only to provide historical memory by virtue of her age, but to take us back to a time that is even more gone than normal, as the Revolution intentionally erased it. The chapter title gives us a bit of a pun: “a century in a guimpe” can, of course, mean that she’s been a nun for a century (although she technically hasn’t been one for all of her long life). But it can also mean that she embodies a century – namely the 18th – and that in her, that century is wrapped in a guimpe. And what we see of the 18th century here is not just found in historical names (including Louis XVI), but also in a lightheartedness that the regular nuns of Petit-Picpus definitely don’t share! This is not the last time we’ll see this distinction, between a frivolous 18th century and a serious 19th!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This other convent, based more closely on a real one, does something that we often see with (human) characters in this book: it serves as a double. Many significant characters have (often less significant) doubles. Champmathieu has been a notable example already. We could see the fact that there were two Thénardier daughters this way. And there will be many more. So the convent also gets a double. Which means, if the distinction between the two convents here is a tad confusing or unclear, perhaps that’s the point. It might also be the point *for the very reason* that the nuns see it as significant. How many divisions among groups of people, which they see as absolutely critical, are difficult to understand from the outside? Not that such difefrences are never meaningful, but seeing them through untrained eyes can help keep them in perspective….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This harsh, old-fashioned, ascetic community couldn’t survive in the modern world (and we’ll read a lot more about that in the coming days!) But we start to get a bit of Hugo’s opinion on it here – serendipitous that this falls in our reading schedule on a day when a new pope has many people thinking about religious tradition. Hugo is not a religious traditionalist, but nor does he mock religious tradition. He has respect for the human need for religion without buying into dogma. He calls prayer and contemplation “needs” of humanity, even if the forms they take might change. He worries about the vacuum left when religion goes away, and what might fill it. But as society moves forward, he also warns against “superstitions” and “hypocrisies” as cheap knock-offs of what was. We’ll need to find our own ways of meeting that need.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Convent as an Abstract Idea
entries.commentary_2025: This book is so rooted in social themes, it’s a bit surprising when Hugo declares that humanity is only its second-most-important character. So how can we understand “the infinite” as the main character here? We’ve seen moments that seem like divine intervention, mostly in Jean Valjean’s story, and Waterloo was certainly presented in those terms. But is that “the infinite”? I suspect he means something bigger than an “infinite” force nudging events one way or another. Let’s keep thinking about that as we keep reading. Meanwhile, monasticism, or religion in any form, is figured as simply a tool, an optical device, used to “see” the infinite. Personally, I love this image. Because what is a device? It’s something that humans, and (almost) only humans, use to accomplish a task. Often, it’s possible to use any one of a number of difefrent tools to accomplish a given task, and so long as it’s efefctive, the tool doesn’t matter much. It’s not the point. This seems consistent with how Hugo has seen religion so far. It’s fine if it does what it’s intended to do, but pointless at best if it doesn’t. And if someone (think of the Conventionist) gets to the same point a difefrent way? Also fine. It’s the connection to the infinite that matters.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: The Convent as an Historical Fact
entries.commentary_2025: Yesterday’s respect for the “tools” of spirituality, which might include monasticism, was a prelude to this counterpoint. While he allows that some of the practices he describes here may give some practitioners access to “the infinite,” he seems to feel that the harm outweighs that potential good. So what is the harm? If people want to dedicate their lives to a form of asceticism like this, step out of “normal” life and into a practice this extreme, what harm does that do to anyone else? This will come into sharper focus, but we see it compared here to blockages in circulation, to a parasite, to a growth. That is, the harm is to society at large, in lost potential. Energy, life, is drawn away, and to no purpose. The harm is waste. Remember that, we’ll see it again!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. A quelle condition on peut respecter le passé
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: On What Conditions One can respect the Past
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo continues to think about monasticism, and forms of religion generally, in terms that implicate life and death. In the first lines of the chapter, he says this with a reference that is particularly striking in this book: in the French, he calls it a “phtisie” – your translation may vary, but the most literal English word for this is phthisis. This is an old-timey medical word for tuberculosis, and while the disease was extremely common in this era, in this book, it will always make us think of Fantine. But there’s another striking image early on too: castration. Monastic life, and its accompanying celibacy, mean renouncing participation in the flow of life that carries humanity into the future. This is a practical concern, as he notes that it “depopulates,” but it becomes a spiritual one as well, as we saw in the Waterloo section that bringing the future into being is an imperative of “the infinite.” This relic of the past, then, is not on the side of life. From this, what he says next follows too: if it is a dead thing, it can be respected as part of the past, but shouldn’t persist in the present. And yet, here it is, in this modern, social book. The convent becomes another thing in this book that is hovering between life and death, a zombie institution. 🧟‍♀️
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Le couvent au point de vue des principes
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: The Convent from the Point of View of Principles
entries.commentary_2025: It’s odd – yesterday, monastic life was synonymous with stepping outside the normal folw of life, impeding it, limiting its potential. Today we’re back to positive potential. He seems to be suggesting that monasticism, historically, has had its flaws, but the possible, ideal convent or monastery is a place of radical community. He makes a connection that is both odd and hard to argue with, between monastic life and forms of community that we see, even today, as modern and progressive: a commune and a republic. Equality and fraternity – two thirds of the French Revolution’s motto “Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité” – are without a doubt, features of the ideal monastic community. Maybe two out of three ain’t bad? 🎶
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter answers a question posed yesterday, and so it’s connected to the “ , Égalité, Fraternité” ____ way of describing monastic life. Prayer takes the place of liberty. So perhaps it’s fitting that Hugo takes up an argument that we’ve already glimpsed in this book, way back when the Bishop met the Conventionist. The Conventionist said a version of a lot of this. Context is important for both of these sections: the Revolution, still France’s reference point for democracy at this time, was aggressively atheist. Exception: briefly, in the summer of 1794, Robespierre’s Cult of the Supreme Being was the Convention’s official “religion,” but this didn’t outlive Robespierre. Apart from its actual violence, the thing that left the worst taste in folks’ mouths after the Revolution was probably the elimination of religious practice. The Conventionist and now Hugo both reject that absolute atheism, while at the same time not insisting on traditional religion. Their goal – whether you think they succeed or not – is a spirituality based in reason, because they see spirituality of some sort as an inherent part of humanity.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Beyond rejecting an absolute atheism, as we saw yesterday, Hugo also rejects a philosophy – any philosophy, even if it’s a religion – that doesn’t seek to make the world better. Ideas or beliefs must lead to action, and that is how all of this starts to connect back to this book. Whether it’s a philosophical position or a religious conviction, if it doesn’t move toward something higher, it’s useless. Some of the last words Hugo ever wrote, “Aimer, c’est agir,” (“To love is to act”), are perhaps more quotable than this chapter, but express a similar sentiment. Here, it’s more “Penser, c’est agir,” or “Croire, c’est agir.” (“To think is to act” or “To believe is to act.”). But each version is very much at home in this social novel.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Précautions à prendre dans le blâme
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: Precautions to be observed in Blame
entries.commentary_2025: There are things about which Hugo expresses straightforward opinions. Death penalty: against. Universal education: for. Exploitation: against. But religion in general, and monasticism in particular, it’s complicated. Religious dogma and judgment, religion as a political force or power structure: against. But spiritual life, the search for higher meaning, connection to the infinite, and religion as a force for good in the world: for. So when we see religious people and institutions in this novel, the analysis is almost always a mixed bag. The Bishop was *almost* an exception, but even there, there was a “restriction” (I, 1, 11). In thinking about monastic life, he sees both sides of that coin at work. The dogma, rules, constraints, judgments are SO imposing, so intense, that they impede the fullness of life, and prevent the practices’ spiritual benefits from improving the wider world as they could. But he can’t help but commend their focus on spiritual life, and their deep connection to what lies beyond our world.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: An interesting element gets added in this chapter: protest. Hugo has made an argument up to this point *against* stepping away from the world and the fullness of life, but there’s just one pesky little problem…. That’s exactly what he’s doing. When this book was published in 1862, Hugo had been outside of France for 10 years, despite having been included in an amnesty and allowed to return in 1859. In his public response to Napoleon III’s amnesty, he wrote, “Quand la liberté rentrera, je rentrerai.” (“When liberty returns, I shall return.”) His exile (and you may have noticed this word in this chapter!) is by this time a well-known voluntary act of protest. He suggests that people, especially women, in monastic life have good reason to be doing the very same thing – opting out of a world that they object to. He didn’t have our modern language available to describe it as a feminist act, but here, and in the coming chapters, we see hints of that idea. And in that context, perhaps the spiritual work they’re devoted to (like his own) in the place and for the sake of those who seem to do none at all, is in fact worthwhile.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Où il est traité de la manière d'entrer au couvent
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: Which treats of the Manner of entering a Convent
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.commentary_2025: Having finished our deep dive on monasticism, you’ve made it through your second major digression, and your reward is one of the most entertaining parts of the book. We’re already feeling the tone shift here; Fauchelevent will consistently bring the story a much-needed lightness. It makes for a nice contrast with the heaviness of the setting, and the headiness of the questions we’ve been dealing with for the last few days. The stakes, as we see from the bits of this chapter that are told through Jean Valjean’s eyes, remain high. But it *feels* like a comedy. There are puns, cracks about the nuns’ prudishness even after death, and an overall sense that we’re about to cook up a wild scheme….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Fauchelevent en présence de la difficulté
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Fauchelevent in the Presence of a Difficulty
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.commentary_2025: As is often the case in this book, in the presence of people and places that seem *in particular* to belong to it, things become strangely inverted. Such is the case with Fauchelevent in the convent. What were negatives for him outside are positives in here. There, he was downwardly mobile, and bitter about falling from the lower middle classes to the peasantry. Here, his simple country style serves him well, and masks a cleverness that he can also put to use. There, his age and bum leg (and, if they were real and not metaphorical, weak sight and hearing) would have sentenced him to misery and death. Here, they’re his main job qualifications. For all the convent’s harshness and flaws, this person who would have been abandoned outside is valued, and he’s a changed person because of it.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.commentary_2025: We learned about Mère Innocente’s erudition a couple of weeks ago, and we see it put to use here. The floods of words that Hugo sometimes has his characters pronounce are of two basic types: emotional overflow, like Fantine in the police station, or displays of (often superfluous) knowledge. This is the latter, and it’s rare that this type is attributed to a woman! But Mère Innocente is not typical, and perhaps because she’s a nun, Hugo doesn’t quite treat her like a woman. Similarly, Mère Ascension, thanks to her strength, is assigned to help Fauchelevent lift the large stone in the church floor that covers the crypt, also (to Fauchelevent’s chagrin) filling a role that would usually be occupied by a man. These women, by virtue of their vocation, seem to take on characteristics of men. Meanwhile, what Mère Innocente applies her intellect to is another notion that resonates with the rest of Les Misérables: a law higher than human law, namely respecting the wishes of the saintly dead. And yet, alongside this most serious of subjects, she still gets trapped in the who’s-on-first-style slapstick dialogue with Fauchelevent. We somehow, inexplicably, remain in a comedic parallel universe to Les Misérables!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Où Jean Valjean a tout à fait l'air d'avoir lu Austin Castillejo
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: In which Jean Valjean has quite the Air of having read Austin Castillejo
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.commentary_2025: The reference in the chapter title, which is explained in the chapter, makes a connection to another Hugo work, the 1830 play Hernani. In that play, the character of Don Carlos, as he is learning that he will become Holy Roman Emperor Charles Quint, undergoes a dramatic change of heart/character while hiding in a tomb. The details of that scene are not as similar to this as is the one Austin Castillejo is said to describe, but the basics – images of death, resurrection, hiding, transformation – are there. Meanwhile, even as Jean Valjean is cooking up this grim and risky idea, drawing on some of the darkest and most desperate times of his life, his lightheartedness is uncharacteristic. He even SMILES. 😁 And, just like that, they have a plan. And any plan that includes getting a guy drunk under the table is clearly foolproof!!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Il ne suffit pas d'être ivrogne pour être immortel
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: It is not Necessary to be Drunk in order to be Immortal
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.companion_episode: Ep23 - II,8,v-ix - Death and Other Happy Endings
entries.commentary_2025: Of COURSE this plan was going to go sideways. A couple of interesting details stand out in this complication, though. First, Gribier mentions having seven children to feed as a reason why he must be serious about his work – 7 children to feed, exactly, was the reason why Jean Valjean stole that fateful loaf of bread. Then, he mentions that his other job is as a public scribe. A public scribe – and one that didn’t have his scruples about drinking – told Fantine’s secrets to the gossips in Montreuil-sur-mer. So, as inconvenient as it is for Fauchelevent, this character reverses, in a sense, two ill-fated moments from earlier in the story. All of this as Jean Valjean uses his prison-break skills to ultimately get INTO a place of confinement. Up is down and down is up in this section, which is perhaps why, even as the danger starts to be real, the tone remains light.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.companion_episode: Ep23 - II,8,v-ix - Death and Other Happy Endings
entries.commentary_2025: For a writer for whom the visual, and even visionary, elements are so salient, an entire (short) chapter in total darkness, with only descriptions of other sorts of sensations, is remarkable. It conveys a point of view (so to speak) of a burial that no one gets to experience first-hand – that of the corpse. And Jean Valjean takes on the role of the corpse in more than one way. Early on, in the dark and relative quiet, he is said to experience something of the peace of death. But later, when things become more serious, his loss of consciousness also mimics the grave. This loss of consciousness probably doesn’t yet come from lack of air, as the air holes had just been covered up, but rather, from terror of being buried alive. This was a widespread fear in the era before advanced methods for being medically sure of death, even giving rise to the invention of elaborate “safety coffins!”
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Où l'on trouvera l'origine du mot: ne pas perdre la carte
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: In which will be found the Origin of the Saying: Don't lose the Card
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.companion_episode: Ep23 - II,8,v-ix - Death and Other Happy Endings
entries.commentary_2025: And everything works out ok, just like in a comedy written for the stage! You can almost hear the audience's laughter after the chapter’s final line. Their bonkers, dangerous idea of burying Jean Valjean alive ended with nothing more than a little stiffness, nothing he couldn’t walk off. (Even though that stiffness is compared to rigor mortis….) Gribier, for whom this could have been the start of the kind of downward spiral we have a way of seeing in this book, ends up happy with the outcome. (Even though his family seems to have had a pretty bad evening as a result of all this.) The chapter title is a pun as well: “ne pas perdre la carte” is an idiom meaning something like “don’t get confused” or “don’t get disoriented.” The stakes were real, but all is well in the end, and everyone will look back on it and laugh.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.companion_episode: Ep23 - II,8,v-ix - Death and Other Happy Endings
entries.commentary_2025: We saw a while back the phenomenon of characters getting doubles in this book; with Jean Valjean already involved in it once. Here, the two “Fauchelevent” “brothers” do the same, with their matching limps (remember Jean Valjean’s, from his ball and chain) and bells on their legs. And during their interview with the nuns, they become interchangeable, to the point where the nuns don’t even seem to notice that Fauchelevent is speaking for his “brother.” This pair also continues a phenomenon we’ve seen before, of saintly older men in gardens. Notably, the model for this was the Bishop. Both Jean Valjean and the Bishop have had words of wisdom about gardening as well: the Bishop, on flowers, and Jean Valjean, on weeds.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les cimetières prennent ce qu'on leur donne
entries.companion_episode: Ep23 - II,8,v-ix - Death and Other Happy Endings
entries.commentary_2025: A refuge and a prison aren’t all that difefrent – an enclosure that someone can’t leave, often that they didn’t choose and where they can’t control the conditions of their life. Jean Valjean is always under the threat of prison, and his only way to avoid it has become to stay in this place, which so closely resembles prison. In Hugo’s comparison between his former fellow prisoners and the nuns, an interesting grammatical thing happens that can’t really be rendered in English: Hugo begins by referring to the nuns as “êtres” (“beings”), which is grammatically masculine, so the rest of the description of their conditions refers to the nuns using masculine pronouns. This makes them even more indistinguishable from the men in the prison, including Jean Valjean himself. BUT. Here, he can do good – for Cosette, and for his own soul. He can almost live the life he had before that fateful loaf of bread, but with more economic security. He’s safe even from the physical and spiritual dangers that have threatened him since he was a peasant tree-pruner near Faverolles. (Congratulations on finishing Part II!!)

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: The last short paragraph of this chapter is one of my very favorites in the book. I hope your translation does it justice. The vast city of Paris is mother (“city” is grammatically feminine in French, so the image becomes a feminine one) to this odd little creature, which resembles her. The “gamin” (that’s the French word for the child being described here – your translation may, again, vary) was not invented by Hugo, though. This is a character type that would have been recognizable. He’s a wild child, poor, possibly orphaned or abandoned, surviving as he can off the city. Unruly but pure, or even pure *because* he’s unrefined, not unlike the “noble savage” that this period so loved to imagine as well. But he’s deeply Parisian, especially in Hugo’s rendering. Which, of course, makes translation here difficult. He’s not just any street urchin, he’s *Paris’s* street urchin.

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: It’s clear Hugo expects that a Parisian of this period would recognize this type of child, fluttering through their day-to-day life. What he seems to be giving us is a sort of field guide, a way to recognize the difefrent varieties that exist within this species, and what makes up its essence. And as we become naturalists trying to recognize the gamin, the gamin is a naturalist too, but of the bits of nature that he finds in the city. He knows his city down to its every bug and mystery amphibian, and masters it like a scholar. But he applies his mind to wit as well as nature, and can produce barbs with the best of them. These are signs of an intellectual as much as they are signs of a gamin!

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: A lot of what Hugo tells us about the gamin and the arts here might require some cultural explanation. Perhaps the chapter title is enough to help you draw this conclusion, but it’s all designed to position him as sympathetic. The bit about the theater makes more sense if you know that “le Paradis” – Heaven or Paradise – was the nickname of the cheap seats, way up high. The gamin here becomes like an angel in Heaven. And the “quantity of regret” that Hugo feels about his tastes not being classical or academic is more or less zero – those were (quite famously) not Hugo’s tastes either! The gamin is the audience that Hugo wants (needs) for his own work: appreciative, with an artistic sensibility, but not delicate or easily given to fear or disgust.

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: So the gamin is a sub-type of the people (broadly, people living in poverty) that this book focuses on, so he definitely belongs in this book. And, as we’ve already seen, and see again here, he’s uniquely Parisian, so as the plot takes us definitively into Paris proper, we learn about the city through him. But he *really* shows his “useful”ness and earns his place as the gateway to the second half of the book in this chapter. A revolutionary spirit is part and parcel to what Paris is, and the gamin expresses that aspect of it too. That spirit might not always be a threat – he may just be a wide-eyed child now – but this little guy will grow up!

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: Back in the middle of April, we talked about the Gorbeau house, and how strange it is – sort of hybrid, not fitting neatly into any of its descriptors. The outskirts of the city, where the gamin frequents, is like this too. Where the countryside meets the town, it’s both and neither. While these types of spaces may seem strangely deserted to some, and maybe a bit scary, to Hugo, and to the gamin, they’re abundant in inspiration. Then, we mentioned that many of our characters are hard to define in this same way – Jean Valjean is probably the best example. It’s deep in the DNA of Les Misérables. But partly, the gamin likes these spaces because they’re the closest he gets to nature, to a difefrent environment. Being attached to Paris by his nature and the city’s, a true departure from the city is impossible.

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: We said a few days ago that the gamin was a well-known character type who appeared in art and literature at this time – famously in Delacroix’s “Liberty Leading the People.” In those representations, he was a romanticized figure, happy, and not a real kid whose well-being you needed to worry about. In this section, Hugo is engaging in a bit of double-speak. We recognize the happy-go-lucky character type, and he says he doesn’t want to take away from that. But he also shows us the real social problem of abandoned and uneducated children, and the moral problem it is for that to be turned to the state’s benefit. Remember that, in the Preface, “the atrophy of children in darkness” was the third “problem of the century” that is central to this book. The first two were also social problems that were turned to the benefit of the powerful. The exploitation of men’s labor (in prison, and through unfair wages) benefited the powerful people they worked for. And the desperation of women like Fantine benefited the powerful by entertaining men and preserving the “purity” of “virtuous” women.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Le gamin aurait sa place dans les classifications de l'Inde
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: The Gamin should have his Place in the Classifications of India
entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: Not only is the gamin a class, or caste, unto himself, the population of gamins has internal hierarchies. And what distinguishes a gamin is, at least here, witnessing the most extreme parts of Parisian life, especially those that could provoke horror. Perhaps it makes them seem brave, or gives them an impressive story to tell. But it also brings them closer to Hugo’s other books, beyond the one (Claude Gueux) that he mentions here. Seeing a man fall from the top of Notre-Dame reminds us of the end of Notre-Dame de Paris (The Hunchback of Notre Dame). And watching executions and recounting their details reminds us of The Last Day of a Condemned Man, which mentions many of the same names of notorious convicts that we see here. These are also the novels of Hugo’s that were published around the time that our story takes place, potentially taking his contemporary readers back to a specific moment in their own experience of the city’s past.

entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: In which the Reader will find a Charming Saying of the Last King
entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: In a 19th century that was constantly changing, the gamin’s basic role in Paris was the same. This meant adapting to the changing times and cultures, to remain what he was: antagonistic, but not really a threat, to the authorities in place. It will be worth comparing this relationship with the police to that of more serious criminals that we’ll see later. These children are another miniature version of adult society. The gamin has learned to watch out for the police, to know what they need to about various officers, and to warn each other, just as real criminals would do. But just as the gamin isn’t much of a threat to the public order, so the “trouble” they might get in is mostly about keeping childish hijinks under control.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 9. La vieille âme de la Gaule
entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: The spirit of the gamin can go beyond the strict and literal defni ition (a pre-adolescent male street kid in Paris). Hugo finds it in irreverent laughter, in defiance. The names he mentions here are almost all associated with laughter in one way or another. The major exceptions, Camille Desmoulins and Joseph Bara, are closely connected to the Revolution. Of these, only Bara is actually a kid – he died at 14 in a battle connected to the Revolution. The others express “gaminerie” in other ways. In the end, as Hugo says here, the gamin has fun because he is miserable, and turns the world upside-down with a smile on his face.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: There has been tension for all of this section between the picturesque idea of the gamin and the sad reality of the abandoned and uneducated child. Here, he resolves it. The gamin may be all that he’s said, but if that delightfully mischievous creature comes at the cost of a child’s quality of life, Hugo knows how he’d choose. Connecting this clear social statement to the rest of the chapter is tricky, but here’s how I understand it: if the gamin expresses Paris, the social problems that result in the gamin are Paris’s problems, and Paris’s problems are the world’s. That is, the gamin – both the joyous idea and the harsh reality – is above all humanity’s child, perfected (according to Hugo) in its Parisian form.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: This is a strangely appropriate chapter to read on Barricade Day – a day that was also about DARING. (If this is your first time through and you don’t yet know what June 6 means in this book, you will find out in the fall!) And, we’ll come back tomorrow to how this connects to the gamin, if you haven’t guessed already. But, for today, I want to help us forgive the ever-so-slight soupçon of jingoism that’s happening in this chapter. Perhaps we can do that by remembering that, when Hugo published this, he hadn’t seen his home city in a decade, so we can think of this as him loving and missing Paris. Add to that the fact that the reason for his absence was an authoritarian regime at home that at first did not welcome him, and that even at this point, he could not tolerate. From where he sits in 1862, Paris needs to rekindle the revolutionary spirit he describes here. It’s not real, at this moment, so much as aspirational. He’s not bragging, he’s desperately hoping.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 12: The Future Latent in the People
entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: So why have we been talking for all this time about the gamin? Because the gamin is the perfect image of the people of Paris (especially the faubourgs), the people of Paris express its spirit, and the spirit of Paris is a kind of distillation of humanity. The gamin personifies the popular revolutionary spirit as much as Javert personifies the law. (A note about translation: if your chapter renders “faubourgs” as “suburbs,” that could be misleading. We’re not talking about middle-class, 1950s-style suburbs. The faubourgs are very much working-class/poor areas!) As he draws this digression to a close (tomorrow, we’re back to plot and character), he asks two things of our response to the gamin, and all he represents. First, education, for both the wayward child and the adult he will become – this call goes especially to those who hope and work for progress, to give the people enough education to participate in that work. Second, attention: that we see them and their perspective, and allow it to inform how we understand the world, and how we work for progress.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. Paris étudié dans son atome
entries.companion_episode: Ep24 - III,1,i-xiii - Child of Paris, Child of Misère
entries.commentary_2025: Gavroche is a big fave in this book (for me as well!) – and here he is, presented as the representative of Paris, of the people, and of humanity that is the gamin. Except, Hugo says, his heart is darker and emptier. His sadness comes from being neither orphaned nor really abandoned, but rejected. He has a home with his parents, but he’s not welcome there. His parents didn’t die or give him up (which, as with Fantine, can be done with great love), they simply don’t care about him. We’ll see more of this “Jondrette” family, after a little flashback to get to know their neighbor. But clearly, they’re up to something – the father has multiple identities, as multiple difefrent nationalities – not a harbinger of an honest person!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: After spending two weeks reading about the gamin, Gillenormand is a bit of an abrupt change! – Even if, as the end of the last chapter said, this is our way into Marius’s story. He is everything the gamin isn’t: old, rich, powerful (at least, relatively – we’ll talk more about him and actual power!). Where the gamin is the spirit of the people, and of rebellion, Gillenormand is backward-looking, from an era before the Revolution. He and Gavroche are also presented difefrently relative to the phenomena they represent. Gavroche is one example of a type (the gamin), and we spend most of our time learning about the type, with Gavroche’s name only showing up in the last chapter. Gillenormand is also an example of a type (a grand bourgeois), but we start with specific information about him, and we’re explicitly told he’s unique by the time he’s old. On lots of occasions in this book, including this one, individuality is harder to come by for les misérables.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Interior decoration was important to Hugo, made his home on Guernsey a site of artistic expression, and said that if he hadn’t been a writer, he might have been a decorator. https://www.maisonsvictorhugo.paris.fr/en/guernesey So it’s little surprise Gillenormand’s home is, as the title suggests, an expression of its owner. It’s also one of the only homes we see in this novel where the inhabitant is well-off enough to make design choices. And what it expresses is a person deeply attached not only to the past, but a specifically royalist past. Many of the details here hearken back beyond Gillenormand’s own youth, to the era of Louis XIV, the height of absolute monarchy in France. His clothing and behavior are more reminiscent of the era before and during the Revolution, when he would have been a young(er) man. But the home provides a glimpse of what will become his defining characteristic: legitimist politics.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is probably particularly puzzling for those who don’t have Hugo’s familiarity with 18th- and 19th-century French culture. Broadly, this chapter is showing us Gillenormand’s place in the social hierarchies of his youth. That place was, quite specifically, NOT among the elites, and he plays an active role in keeping it that way. As a teenager, he rejected the famous dancers in favor of a cute girl his own age. He’s shocked, after the Revolution when he’s older, to find that people with middle-class names like his are government ministers. This hierarchy, and accepting one’s place in it, was a hallmark of the pre-revolutionary regime. After the Revolution, it becomes another way in which Gillenormand clings to the past.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Another one with lots of cultural references. All of the anecdotes in this chapter are designed to show us one thing: Gillenormand is a ROYALIST. The person who is likely being referred to as the duc de Nivernais here was a relative of two people (Madame de Montespan and the cardinal Mazarin) who were close to Louis XIV. So his memory of this prize is Gillenormand’s six degrees of separation connecting him to the Sun King. The bit about Poland seems to refer to Catherine the Great having supported (because they were lovers) the last king of that country, who failed to maintain royal power. She “repairs” this by purchasing the anti-love elixir that’s mentioned, but is otherwise the sort of monarch he can respect, having opposed the French Revolution and the Enlightenment ideas that led to it. And of course “93” – that is, 1793, the year associated with the Reign of Terror in France, when the Revolution sought to expunge all traces of royalty most violently – is a nightmares memory for him. 93 holds such acute horror for him that he (probably, mostly) jokes that he doesn’t want to live to that age, so as not to “see 93 twice.”
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This is the other side of that hierarchy we were discussing a couple of days ago: while it’s important to Gillenormand that he remain “beneath” nobility and royalty, there are people beneath him too. Specifically, he disdains women and the working class. While he does things here that benefit his wife and his servants – specifically, he buys them off – he does so to remain above them. He “passionately loves women,” meaning he has mistresses, so he keeps his (allegedly) unpleasant, nagging wife busy by letting her do whatever she likes with his money. His servants even seem to be less than human to him, as he renames them when they come to work in his household, like pets. All of this, from the point of view of mid-19th-century France, smacks of pre-Revolutionary culture; it’s what his place in the social hierarchies looked like in his youth. Of course, the financial cost to him is real. The extra pay for “Nicolette” is a decision on his part, but the financial complications brought on by his second wife are beyond his control. But he gave up that control, for the sake, essentially, of maintaining a set of cultural codes that had fallen out of favor (even as gender and class hierarchies still very much existed!)
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. Où l'on entrevoit la Magnon et ses deux petits
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: In which Magnon and her Two Children are seen
entries.commentary_2025: Don’t forget about Magnon and her boys. They’ll be back. But for now, the importance of this is, in an odd way, a positive characteristic of Gillenormand: generosity. It can seem odd, since he’s pretty mean otherwise, and he’s contrasted with his brother, a miser who’s also a priest. And in this chapter his generosity is all wrapped up in his womanizing and wanting people to know he *could* father a child at 84, even though he *didn’t*. But in the end, he provides a pretty substantial sum for these boys. For reference, Fantine got 40 francs for her two front teeth, and he’s sending these boys twice that each month! He’s less ofefnded by the suggestion of illegitimate children than by a bonapartist in the family, less ofefnded by being cheated than by being disrespected by the cheater.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Règle: ne recevoir personne que le soir
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: Rule: Receive No One except in the Evening
entries.commentary_2025: The more time moves forward, the more Gillenormand clings to the past. “His” century (the 18th) had its ways of doing things, he insists on them more the more things change around him. In the early Restoration, the second half of the 1810s, Hugo describes the culture as generally backward-looking – remember the chapter about 1817 at the beginning of Fantine’s story. So Gillenormand was in line with that for a while – he shared his horror of the Revolution and longing for the time before with a lot of other people. But, time marches on, and as it does, he becomes an ever-more-unusual relic of another time.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 8. Les deux ne font pas la paire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: Two do not make a Pair
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo compares Gillenormand and his elder daughter to the Bishop and his sister, but it’s clear he does not hold the two pairs in the same regard! Where we’ll remember that Baptistine’s main characteristic was saintliness, to the point that she was almost ethereal, Mlle Gillenormand is the opposite. Her hope in a husband was for money and status, not feeling. Despite being (he emphasized) a virgin, she is very much concerned with her physical body, a concern which manifests through prudishness. She is a material being where Baptistine was a spiritual one. Gillenormand and the Bishop, apart from being old men who live with old maid relatives, are also quite difefrent. But they do share the trait of generosity, of being known for giving their money away, which is significant in a book where so much – even human life – comes at a price.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: Salon culture was an important social marker in Paris at this time – salons were gatherings, in homes, for intellectual, literary, and political discussion. Which salon(s) a person attended – and which one(s) were willing to receive them – provided a great deal of information about their status, ideas, and politics. (It was also an important way that women could exercise power – the hostess crafted the group and guided the conversation in the salon she hosted, and that determined much about which ideas took hold.) The many (possibly obscure) references in this chapter add up to this salon being one that is chiefly about being extremely politically conservative, and looking back fondly on the pre-Revolutionary era. They lament the existence of the Charter that limits King Louis XVIII’s power, and they consider him (literally a brother to Louis XVI) a political radical for accepting it. They pronounce “Buonaparte” with an Italian accent to emphasize Napoleon’s Corsican origins, and suggest that he’s not really French. And, we’re back in that same period that we saw as so reactionary at the beginning of Fantine’s story, around 1817. We already know this illusion won’t last, but this salon is deeply invested in it!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Un des spectres rouges de ce temps-là
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: One of the Red Spectres of that Epoch
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: A lot of things come together in this chapter! Georges Pontmercy is, by my count, the 4th (relatively) solitary old man with a garden, and in his case, this is his defni ing characteristic. At least, by the time we meet him it is. Earlier in his life, of course, he was defined by his military heroism, including at Waterloo. But the early reactionary years of the Restoration took that glory from him. They also took his child from him, and we can’t help but remember Fantine when we see this parent separated from a child he adores. And, even as he sneaks into Paris, to attend mass at Saint-Sulpice and try to glimpse his son from afar, he is compared to a parole-breaker, bringing to mind another parole-breaker in this story… And so, in Georges Pontmercy, we find most of the “good guys” of this story – from the Bishop to the French soldiers at Waterloo, and from Fantine to Jean Valjean. Could it be clearer that our narrator thinks Gillenormand is in the wrong here??
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: The chapter title is the Latin word for “rest” in the phrase “requiescant in pace” or “rest in peace.” Which – and I say this as we too have prominent parts of our society seemingly competing for who can turn back the clock hardest – feels like a good wish to make for this salon. But what is interesting here is the imagery of death and darkness that accompanies this funerary phrase. This is a world that lives inside a tomb, and does so as little as possible. We’ve already seen something similar: the convent, where life was also described as a kind of living death. Monasticism, like ultraroyalism, was a thing of the past, continuing to live beyond its natural death, like a zombie. And in each of these places, there is a child (or children), making their start in life in a place that reeks of death. How will they grow up in these places, and what will they become?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: We’re once again reminded of Fantine, who also wanted nothing more than to see her child before she died, and also wasn’t able to. 😭 And Marius’s cultivated indifefrence to his father twists the knife, because it delayed his arrival. (Where the travel is concerned, remember Jean Valjean traveling to Arras, and the many resources available to a traveler who wishes to hurry!) It’s important to note that the absence of love for his father and his belief that he was abandoned by him is the salient reason for his feeling of distance. The political opinions don’t help, but they’re not as important to him as they are to Gillenormand. Marius is a kid, after all, and has no memory of the violent and divisive periods of the Revolution and Empire. But he does remember growing up without his father. That is, and will continue to be, what matters!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Utilité d'aller à la messe pour devenir révolutionnaire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: The Utility of going to Mass, in order to become Revolutionist
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: For the original readers of Les Misérables, this chapter title would have been every bit as ironic as it seems today, maybe more. We saw in the early pages of this novel, when the Bishop visited the Conventionist, that the Church and the Revolution were opposing forces. But there, Hugo wrote their interaction to the point where we saw that tension resolve, when the Bishop realized that their values and goals weren’t that difefrent after all. For now, we don’t know what efefct this has had on Marius. He “paled” when he realized that Mabeuf was talking about him, but from then on, we haven’t seen inside his head. But presumably, this interaction is going to make a change in him!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. Ce que c'est que d'avoir rencontré un marguillier
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: The Consequences of having met a Warden
entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: In any other context, it would be a strange leap that Marius makes here: his father loved him and wasn’t a monster, so his whole outlook on politics is revised. But, it’s Gillenormand who frist connected these things, made a person’s goodness or badness entirely tied to their politics, and raised Marius with a false horror of his father as a result. It’s clear that his father was the first part of the equation: if he did in fact love him, then perhaps he was good after all, and… could it be that what he believed in was worthy of him? This opens Marius’s mind, and then what convinces him can be described as an ecstatic vision. He acquires information, certainly, but ultimately, his conversion is emotional, not rational, and it even leads to a (slight) change in name and identity when he adopts his father’s title. And Hugo can see that this is all a bit dramatic, but Marius can’t. It’s often speculated that Hugo drew on his own experiences and character as a young man to write Marius, and the narrator’s attitude toward him here certainly gives that impression.

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: Many characters in this book have less significant doubles, a bit like an echo. We talked about Jean Valjean and Fauchelevent or Champmathieu. Thénardier had Boulatruelle. His two daughters were doubles of each other. And now, Marius gets his double in Théodule. And, if we reach back a bit further, Mme Victurnien gets a double too, as Marius’s aunt pries into his business just as that other nosy old lady pried into Fantine’s. The situation is a bit difefrent, as the consequences are likely to be as well. But the echo is unmistakable. The other people in Marius’s life are likely to be quite surprised to learn where he’s been going. But we aren’t: his father’s memory *is* his new illicit passion.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 3. Le grand-père et le petit-fils
entries.commentary_2025: I always find this chapter a bit funny, which might be inappropriate, but I think I’m going to stand by it, at least a little. First of all, Gillenormand is a character ripped from the pages of Molière, and it’s the character type who is always the butt of the jokes and whose fits of rage are meant to be funny. Then, Marius faces a dilemma here, but it’s like a mini version of the novel’s great dilemmas, with a silly resolution – and I think that comparison also makes me chuckle. Plus, he’s so SERIOUS about it. Should he betray his father’s memory by appeasing his grandfather out of respect, or disrespect his grandfather by defending his father and his new beliefs? This is weighty, in its way, but it’s not like Champmathieu’s life or the fates of Fantine, Cosette, and an entire town hang in the balance. And the solution that Marius finds – defaintly insulting a king who has been dead for years – is hardly Jean Valjean’s tempest in a skull or appearance in Arras. And just as Marius is hardly Jean Valjean, Gillenormand, while he’s been compared to the Bishop in passing, is no Msgr Myriel. Remember that the Bishop was also confronted with a challenge to his beliefs about the Revolution – and he ended up asking for the Conventionist’s blessing. But Gillenormand is too stuck in his sharply divided and categorized view of the world to make such a change.

entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: A Group which barely missed becoming Historic
entries.french_book: Livre 4. Les Amis de l'A B C
entries.commentary_2025: One of the things that is SO much better in the book than in any adaptation is the individuality that Hugo brings to the Friends of the ABC. Even the best adaptations only have time to hint at it. I hope your translation conveys the pun in that name, but if not: “ABC” when pronounced in French, sounds just like “abaissé,” or “downtrodden.” To be clear (since our narrator insists otherwise), this group and its members are fictional, even though the event we’ll follow them into was real. Some of these individual personalities (Enjolras, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Bahorel) seem created to personify an aspect of the revolutionary spirit. Others (Jean Prouvaire, Joly, Bossuet), are less allegorical, and just seem to humanize the group. Their personality – the puns, the range of interests and expertise, the lack of focus (in all but Enjolras) will be what makes this group fun. And – by now I may not need to tell you this – it’s what will make them a playground for Hugo, as he’ll give them monologues and songs on a range of topics. There’s a bit of the author in each of these guys too!

entries.french_title: 2. Oraison funèbre de Blondeau, par Bossuet
entries.french_book: Livre 4. Les Amis de l'A B C
entries.commentary_2025: In the side of Bossuet and Courfeyrac that we see here, Hugo is reflecting a widely known and romanticized element of Parisian life at the time: bohemia. https://youtu.be/xTvhS5d1kn8?si=VBzWL39QdQ z7HQe _ The origins of what we think of as “bohemia” can be found in Paris in the 1830s, later made famous by Henri Murger’s book “Scènes de la vie de bohème.” This was then adapted, most famously, into the opera “La Bohème,” and a century after that, into the musical “Rent.” A lot changed as those stories were adapted across time and space from one culture to another to another, but the essence that stays the same is the one we see here too: rejection of bourgeois values; choosing today over tomorrow; lighthearted whimsy in the face of adversity (which is often at least partly brought on by those first two elements). It’s a culture of youth, artistry, cheerful poverty, and easy friendship. It romanticizes all of these things, as well as the actual hardships that can come with them, including disease and even death. In fact, the “grisette” is a Romantic trope associated with bohemia, of whom the most famous example is Mimi from La Bohème. Mimi, like Fantine, dies of “consumption” (TB), but unlike Fantine, her death is elegant and romantic. Bossuet mentions chasing “grisettes” here, and Courfeyrac, in the previous chapter, was compared to Tholomyès. All of which is to say, this is just one moment when Les Misérables has close connections to bohemia, simultaneously drawing on its cultural appeal and signaling its real problems. And in the end, its take is nuanced: some things that bohemia rejects are worth rejecting, but the consequences of this are also real, and for some, returning to the safety of bourgeois life is not an option.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 4. Les Amis de l'A B C
entries.commentary_2025: Marius has been living in a world built on binaries. Young vs old. Revolution & Empire vs monarchy. But it’s all about to come apart. First, he’s shocked that Courfeyrac has to ask what his political opinion is. Then, he finds that some of these young people disagree with each other, and maybe even with him. He may have parted ways with his grandfather’s ideas, but he hasn’t yet challenged the frameworks they’re in. All he’s done so far is switch sides – that’s the easy part. The world he’s found is like the legacies of Napoleon or Rousseau: complex.
