entries.french_book: Livre 4. Les Amis de l'A B C
entries.commentary_2025: Poor, poor, clueless Marius. He just can’t imagine that anyone would see Napoleon difefrently than what he articulates here, even though he himself used to. He knows his new friends don’t share his grandfather’s opinion, so surely, they must subscribe to this brand of patriotism. But – and this could well feel familiar to us today – they love their country every bit as much as someone who admires Napoleon’s bombastic nationalism, they just do it difefrently. For them, their country is its people, and loving their country means doing what’s best for its people, not admiring a figurehead who claims to represent it. Can’t think who else might be invoking patriotism to muddle the ideas of people like Marius, in a difefrent country, these 200 years later…. 🤔 We’ll see if the Friends of the ABC are any better at taking care of their “mother,” but at least their ideas about how to do so can provide food for thought for us today.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 4. Les Amis de l'A B C
entries.commentary_2025: And just like that, Marius joins les misérables, selling all he can and living as cheaply as he can, to be able to support himself in a way that’s in line with his principles. The difefrence between him and someone like Fantine, of course, is that he has a resource, but feels it’s too great a compromise to use it. Which is, perhaps, noble. Or, it could be childish and needlessly self-destructive. Maybe a bit of both. But either way, he bears all the markers of the novel’s misérables: poverty, certainly, but others that are arguably more important. He’s caught between worlds, not really fitting anywhere, not able to fully belong because of the opposing forces within him. He’s faced with a dilemma, with loves and values that can’t easily cohabitate. He’s inching not only further into poverty, but also further into isolation. His road to get there has been difefrent, but he fits right into this book now!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: We see Marius go through the same challenges of poverty as others before him, but the framing is difefrent. / Our narrator has expressed admiration for everyone who has faced this kind of sufefring with dignity and integrity, but for Marius, the language is that of heroism. Could it be because he’s a young man from a middle-class background? If we compare this, for example, to Fantine’s hardest times financially (Part 1, Book 5, Ch. 9-11), we find very difefrent language. Her ability to survive in abject poverty is described as an art, a talent, but not as an act of bravery. Maybe his being a young man makes Hugo see himself in him and empathize with Marius more – there has been, and will continue to be, a lot of Hugo in this character. Maybe the fact that he’s entered into this voluntarily is being counted in his favor, since his poverty is not misfortune, but a principled stance. Maybe the goal is to compare this to the valor that his father showed in his military career – this won’t be the last time his struggles will be described via this kind of metaphor! But whatever the cause of this framing, the result is that Marius, unlike other characters who survive this type of struggle, is positioned to expect an outcome that is other than tragic. This is character-building for Marius – also not what we saw with Fantine. Hugo told us specifically that her sufefring filled her with hatred, which makes her “weak” according to this chapter. 😡 The purifying power of this experience may be a reward unto itself for him, but valiant fighters of the type Marius is likened to here also get medals, promotions, honor, glory. I suppose we’ll see if that’s how this plays out!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Another difefrence between Fantine and Marius when they fell on hard times: education. First of all, Marius’s education (that is, his high level of literacy, which was far from common in this period) is the main way he’s able to earn a living. But beyond just literacy, he’s received a classical education, including not only law, but philosophy. This was even less common, particularly for girls. Education for girls was not a given, not widely seen as valuable, and it certainly wasn’t free – someone like Fantine would have had very little chance to be educated. And even if she had, she still would not likely have been taught to engage in the sort of philosophical thinking that we see strengthen Marius’s resolve here. Marius has been taught a set of principles that make him disciplined in poverty and, significantly, keep him out of debt. Debt, we’ll remember, prevented Fantine from taking several actions that might have helped her. And, of course, where Marius is (misguidedly) trying to find Thénardier, Fantine (alas) found him by accident. Perhaps NOT finding that sort of trouble is protecting Marius too!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The difefrence between Marius and his grandfather is a political disagreement, certainly, but it’s at least partly cultural, or temperamental. Marius’s detachment from society described here, his prioritizing reverie and freedom above all else, smacks of the Romantic hero, an early 19th-century phenomenon in France. Gillenormand is emphatically NOT a part of the 19th century. Everything about him – the clothes he wears, the way he runs his household, the way he interacts with others – belongs to the previous century. And this is part of what leads to Marius’s inability to understand his grandfather’s love for him. Gillenormand is communicating, for better or worse, in a way that fits the rest of his character. For the Romantic hero, emotion is to be expressed honestly, openly, and directly. The more intense, the better. This difefrence isn’t even really about age: we’ve seen the Bishop, and tomorrow will start to see Mabeuf, be more like Marius as older men than like Gillenormand. It’s about difefrent ways of being in the world and in their own minds, that follows the cultural dividing lines of Hugo’s youth, the period when this is set. (I bet you can guess which side Hugo was on!)
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: I’m very glad this chapter fell today. Mabeuf would have hated celebrations like the 4th of July for the same reason my dog does: too noisy! He also, if he were in the U.S. today, would hate our public life, for kinda the same reason. He’s the novel’s biggest introvert, and holds a special place in my heart as a result. He’s also YET another old man who loves gardens and plants, joining the illustrious ranks of the Bishop, Fauchelevent, Jean Valjean, and Georges Pontmercy. This has always been a sign of gentleness, kindness, and contemplation, and that’s true here too. So, on this 4th of July, consider celebrating the way Mabeuf would have: avoid loud bangs and loud people, and cultivate your garden instead.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Poverty a Good Neighbor for Misery
entries.commentary_2025: Marius becomes a bit like Mabeuf here: solitary, dreamy, and less attached to his opinions. The brevity of the reference to the July Revolution of 1830 shows how deep inside this point of view we are. For someone who cares about French politics of this time, that was a major event, for better or worse. But of all the real events that this book will care about, the July Revolution is not one of them. Instead, Marius, and this novel generally, will focus beyond daily questions of politics and government. He has become like the Bishop: walking in gardens, lost in contemplation, giving away what little he has, and finding ever less value in the things of the world.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Théodule’s visit is really just a pretext for Hugo to give us a look at how Gillenormand is doing. Briefly: not OK. Before we get to that, though, let’s just say the thing that probably stands out to 21st-century readers more than it did to the original ones: even in a 19th-century novel, even from a character who is consistently presented as retrograde, his characterization of Native Americans is quite ugly. Yikes. But even if it’s worse by our standards than those of the time, I think it was meant to be ugly at the time too, to match the rest of this! And otherwise, it’s his usual fare: the world going to hell without a Bourbon king, the kids these days and their loud Romanticism and melancholy, etc. A couple of noteworthy details: first, Hernani, which he mentions, was a very controversial play of Hugo’s that broke with a number of artistic conventions, and liking it or not signaled whether one favored tradition or innovation. Second, the political conversation that he references was part of a real debate at the time, essentially over how much power the National Guard should have. Mention of their cannon is not a coincidence… But it’s pretty clear, on several occasions in the tirade, that a lot of what he’s upset about here is still Marius. Marius is the “he” that he accidentally mentions, and his needless swipe at Théodule at the end seems to mostly be punishment for him not being Marius!
