entries.french_title: 1. Le sobriquet: mode de formation des noms de famille
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Sobriquet; Mode of Formation of Family Names
entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Whoever could this be, the mysterious man with white hair, a kind, sad, stoic, taciturn personality, and a young teenage “daughter” in the late 1820s who is dressed in mourning?? 🤔 I don’t think Hugo really expects you not to know (but if you don’t, I won’t tell!) But what matters, and what will matter in the coming chapters, is Marius’s point of view, and *he* doesn’t know. What he knows is that this is one of the two women in the world that he’s not ashamed to have see his poor clothing. The other one is an old lady whom he sees as too old to matter, and this one is too young to matter. In addition to being a skinny, awkward teenager, the narrator makes her seem sort of brazen, like how to be demure is among the things she doesn’t yet understand about womanhood. This is an interesting connection to other hints at her character (if we knew who she was 🤷‍♀️) that often get left out of adaptations!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Let’s talk about something that is going to continue to matter for a while here: the fact that this girl is a teenager. By our modern standards, it’s a bit uncomfortable to think of Marius at 21 seeing a 15-year-old girl in the way this chapter describes. Even if, as this seems to imply, these are mostly aesthetic observations, and Marius is not feeling much of anything for her here, this is a LOT of attention to someone who’s quite young. The difefrence between our modern standards for such things and the standards of past eras often gets exaggerated, but there is *some* distinction to be made. At this time in Paris, the median age for people’s first marriage was in their 20s, and long relationships before marriage weren’t the norm as they are today. (The super-young arranged marriages we associate with times past were mostly for the rich and powerful, and were mostly political arrangements.) So 15 was still, mostly, considered too young for an adult relationship, and girls especially weren’t given information about love and associated matters that they weren’t expected to need yet. Plus, it was normal for parents (especially fathers) to control their daughters' lives much more than is normal today. All this adds up to: a girl like this is still considered young and is probably quite innocent, and her father is likely to try to keep it that way. The difefrence, I think, is down to our reaction to the male gaze, and our absolute division between child and adult: we think of childhood, which lasts until 18, as sacrosanct in a way that makes the male gaze here shocking. They didn’t. A young person’s interest in love happened when it happened, and there was nothing magical about the 18th birthday, for men or women. What mattered, above all else, was the parents’ permission, judgment, and guidance – which, for an orphan like Fantine, or for anyone with cruel or neglectful parents, raised obvious problems. We will see more about how all of that works as this story progresses!!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Welp, so much for the distant, aesthetic observations we saw yesterday. I hope your translation, if you’re using one, conveys just how dramatic and flowery Hugo’s language is here. It’s rather a lot. But he’s describing something nuanced too, and his ability to do so while also keeping us inside the emotional experience of the not-so-nuanced Marius, is worthy of recognition! He’s NOT just describing seduction, or lust, or an encounter with a femme fatale. Neither of the people involved here is entirely in control of what’s happening. It’s a force of nature, beyond them both, happening *to* them both. The idea of light not only entering the eye but being produced by it goes back to Plato (Timaeus), for whom sight was also as much metaphysical as physical. This was no longer scientific belief by the 19th century, but it’s meaningful here, where seeing and being seen are intensely powerful, and seem to go beyond the natural, normal ways we think about them.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: We mentioned a couple of weeks ago that Hugo wrote a lot of himself into Marius. For example, he was a young royalist whose father was an officer in Napoleon’s army and whose politics evolved as he grew older. I think people who (like me) have to look back a ways to find our 20-year-old self can also recognize a sort of self-reflection in this chapter. The omniscient narrator here is also, thanks to his tone, easy to read as an older version of this young man, looking back at just how ridiculous he was about his first love. Don’t we all kind of remember this rite of passage this way? We hadn’t the first idea what we were doing, but we were doing it SO DRAMATICALLY, and with so much emotion. Meanwhile, (and I hope your translation renders this) note the military language that appears again to describe Marius mustering his courage. Before, it was to face poverty, now it’s to face love. One wonders which was harder for him….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Divers coups de foudre tombent sur mame Bougon
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Divers Claps of Thunder fall on Ma'am Bougon
entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: The expression in this chapter title that is probably translated something like “thunderbolts” (“coups de foudre”) is a bit of a joke. You see, that’s also an expression in French that means “love at first sight” – as if mame Bougon is the one having that problem here! Marius still doesn’t seem to know what his problem is, which is interesting. We’ve seen other characters (Jean Valjean, especially) act without understanding why, although usually in very difefrent sorts of crisis. He just gets up every day, puts on his best outfit, and hangs out in this out-of-the-way corner of the Luxembourg gardens for hours. As one does. (Actually, that sounds pretty great…) He doesn’t have any particular plan or goal, he doesn’t seem to work toward meeting the pretty girl or communicating with her in any way. He just seems compelled to hang out nearby.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Today, as Marius is “taken prisoner,” you get to join me in one of my favorite super-niche Les Misérables jokes. I have been SO alone in this until now, and I’m really excited for you to join me. Ready? This is Marius in this chapter (seriously, down to the smallest detail, and the tone): https://youtu.be/Sj 9CiNkkn4?si=-PiuAyguWTorIcu2 PLEASE tell me you get this. I find it so funny. _ Aaaanyway…. In addition to the continued military language (which supports this joke), we see a lot of what has characterized his life for the last little while reversed. He’s laughing, eating, socializing, spending money, and talking about politics again, where he had been solitary, thrifty, and lost in reverie. It’s like he’s been brought back to life. Also, take note of the (extremely 19th-century/Industrial Revolution) machine metaphor we see at the end. It will be back, but for now, note how similar love is to poverty – you get caught and fall in ever deeper, and it either makes you much better or much worse.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Aventures de la lettre U livrée aux conjectures
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: Adventures of the Letter U delivered over to Conjectures
entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Now let me see, who do we know who has white hair and a “daughter” about this age, and was last seen going by a name with the initials U.F.? 🤔(It seems like Hugo tells us that this is the “father’s” handkerchief so that we’ll figure that out, if we haven’t already.) If this is indeed Jean Valjean and Cosette, then Marius is in WAY over his head, thinking he can hide behind various objects in the garden and be seen by her and not him! He has no idea who he’s dealing with. But, the power of young love compels him. She has a somewhat better idea of her “father’s” skill set, but probably also overestimates what they can get past him, as teenagers almost always do with their parents. What they both certainly understand is that, once her “father” is on to them, the obstacles to their feelings will only increase. But at the same time, nothing ventured, nothing gained….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 8. Les invalides eux-mêmes peuvent être heureux
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: The Veterans themselves can be Happy
entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: In a book that doesn’t lack for Marius-induced eyerolls, this might be the eyerolliest. This is another moment when Hugo wrote himself into Marius: at about the same age, he became testy in a letter to his future wife Adèle for the same reason. So Hugo may well fni d it at least somewhat ridiculous as well – we’ve certainly seen, and will see again, that he pokes gentle fun at his silly younger self in Marius. But he also understands. Part of the deep empathy at the heart of this book is the way it can hold both gentle ridicule and understanding for the pain and seriousness of a feeling like this, often in the same sentence. It’s not all that difefrent from the way other characters are treated, in other difficult moments. For example, Hugo affirms that Jean Valjean was as dangerous as his yellow passport said when he first left prison, while also explaining how he got that way, and seeing his pain. And while it seems a bit silly, love and its related feelings (jealousy, heartbreak) are no less a driver of desperate behavior than hunger, say, or rage against injustice. It very much fits in this book!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 6. La conjonction de deux étoiles
entries.commentary_2025: Poor Marius, got a little too daring. This feels a bit like stalking to us, but this is another area where standards at the time would have been difefrent. He would be expected to pursue her more aggressively then, and this is really the only way he has to do it. Plus, everything they’ve communicated through their eyes suggests the young lady here has no objection to his pursuit. It’s her father who objects. And in fairness to Marius (assuming, as I think we can, that the “father” is Jean Valjean), he would have no reason to expect her father to be this easy to spook. But, of course, *we* know why he is. We’ve seen him move at the drop of a hat (or, a coin) before when he thought he was being followed. Following these two, and asking the doorman about them, was the WRONG MOVE, but Marius has no way of knowing that! Now that he’s lost her trail, and she’s the only thing he seems to think about, what will become of him?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: We’re leaving broken-hearted Marius and heading into a mini-digression for the next four days, and this one is a bit more abstract and metaphorical than the others. But it’s important. It’s been clear from the beginning that Hugo’s overarching goal in this book is to show his readers a world they don’t know, that’s hiding from them in plain sight. He assumes, based on the fact that they have the education and free time to read a book like this, that his readers are comfortable, middle-class – that is, not the people who make up most of this cast of characters. And what he’s been showing them (us) so far is how, and more importantly why, the poor sufefr: to a great extent, because of the harshness of laws and social judgment – with Jean Valjean and Fantine as examples. He’s also shown us principled, bohemian poverty through Marius; it’s already more complicated, and probably also poorly understood by his imagined reader. Now, if he wants to show these same comfortable middle-class readers other parts of the social world that they don’t typically see, he has to do something trickier. He has to distinguish between types of law-breakers, between types of disturbers of the peace – between types of underground. That’s what this digression will do.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: There’s quite a lot in these few pages that is important to how the whole book works – and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that it’s about halfway through page-wise. The overarching image here is of a “mine” or “sap,” the siege tactic that consisted of digging under defensive walls to weaken them. The type of underground described yesterday (and, as he says explicitly, in Book 4 – the Friends of the ABC), and this one both do this. The difefrence, though, is intent. The upper mines work for progress, for others, whereas the lower mines work for personal gain only. It’s not an accident, I think, that “mining” also refers to the practice of extraction of minerals for profit. (And this relationship is even closer between the French words, where “mine” and “undermine” are the exact same verb.) So, the action in this metaphor can be a purposeful attack, or a search for personal gain, and in the lower mine, it always involves personal gain. But both weaken what is above. Also: this “lower mine,” the “bas-fond” or “lowest depths,” is home to beings that are born of two “mothers”: ignorance and misery. We’ve seen this combination before – it’s a combination signifciant enough that it made the single-sentence preface that articulated Hugo’s goal for this whole massive work. It is, in one way or another, the state of most of the characters we’ve met, and it’s also the source of the worst human impulses. He puts it another way here too, grouping ignorance and misery into one idea, saying that “darkness” is the only social peril. But we still, even in the lowest depths, need to take care with blame. As the Bishop said, the guilty one is the one who created the darkness.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This is not our first foursome in this book, and the previous ones were no more encouraging: the four young men and their four girlfriends that made up the group where we frist met Fantine. What is the signifciance of the number four? It could be the seasons, the winds, the elements… the number is commonly associated with nature thanks to these associations. Or – and this is the answer that resonates for me here – the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse: War, Plague, Famine, and Death. Each occurrence of a foursome has been foreboding. These four don’t correspond precisely to those allegorical figures, but they seem to function the same way. They each represent a difefrent face of violent crime. And while the numbers don’t line up, we also think back here to the descriptions of the Friends of the ABC, with whom the previous 2 chapters put this group in direct contrast.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: A few characteristics of the criminal world of Les Misérables show up strongly in this chapter. First, the slipperiness of individuality and identity. These aren’t four distinct men with clear identities, at least in the poetic way they’re described here. They’re a four-headed monster, one being, a crowd, or all three at once. None of their names are real, and they can change them at need. Second, and relatedly, there’s the theatricality of this “troupe.” Their changeable identities are roles they can slip into and out of. The names of the four leaders (if you can call them that) as well as the minor players that Hugo lists, may or may not consistently apply to the same individual person. Nothing we know about how people are named applies here. Otherwise, for the list of names, I recommend really listening as you read it. Hugo is playing with sounds here as much as anything else, and reading the list aloud is meant to feel monstrous. Also, note that we find in this list one of the very few moments when Hugo mentions a character’s race – and he gave the character a name that resembles his own, and Homer’s.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Marius, cherchant une fille en chapeau, rencontre un homme en casquette
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: Marius, while seeking a Girl in a Bonnet encounters a Man in a Cap
entries.commentary_2025: Oh, for heaven’s sake, Marius, don’t follow that guy AGAIN. At least he didn’t think of it in time. The party his friends take him to was a well-known elegant afafir, and figures prominently in a Balzac novella as well. It would have borne very little resemblance, but I wondered if it was what inspired the ridiculous
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: We’ve seen characters have echoes and doubles before, and now, as it happens again, Marius sees it too. These two girls are not only doubles of each other, they’re doubles of Cosette. Except they’re explicitly her inverse, like negatives of a photograph. Victor Hugo’s son Charles was a photographer, and photographed Hugo in the 1850s. So Hugo was probably familiar with the early versions of negatives used at the time. It’s interesting to view this scene through that, er, lens. Like in the Luxembourg gardens, these girls appear, then disappear, along a tree-lined walkway. Only it’s winter not summer, dusk not day. Cosette’s grace, beauty, and apparent comfort are replaced with signs of poverty and crime. What was light has become dark.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Another (apparent) four-headed monster. Four difefrent identities, but with the same characteristics (spelling errors, paper, handwriting, odor) giving away an underlying unity. And, in addition to the probability of a single author for these letters, what underlies them all is poverty, lack. Hugo gives us all four letters in their entirety, so it’s worth thinking a bit about them. Each one showcases a difefrent origin story for poverty that (the author seems to believe) will be acceptable to its reader. There’s the royalist refugee from Spain, the abandoned mother, and two artists. All “good” reasons to find oneself lacking resources, in that the person writing is noble, or at least faultless. But of course the illusion only holds up when the four letters are separated from each other. Together like this, they seem to show something else entirely….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: As the chapter title suggests, this character is another example of the poverty that this book is about. And she bears all the signs: her clothing and body reflect living on the bare minimum, and she’s taking on characteristics of someone older, and even of a man. There’s also something new here: suggestions, suited to 19th-century prudishness, of a level of experience that also doesn’t suit a girl of her age. The confdi ence with which she enters a young man’s bedroom, the letter’s promise that “my daughter will await your orders,” Marius’s suspicions of what else the girls might do to earn money… What Hugo was forthright about with Fantine, now that it’s a father profiting off his daughters, becomes unspeakable. He can nevertheless reflect on the morality of the situation, and he’s clear that, because the girls have no freedom, ideas like virtue, responsibility, good, and evil don’t apply. But she’s keen to show that her current circumstances aren’t the only thing about her; she can read, write, and take a political stance. Still, there’s a kind of veil over her thoughts and actions. We can guess what she’s thinking and feeling, but even she doesn’t seem to know all the time. And, she describes hunger contorting her perception in a way that’s striking in its surrealism. She’s complex in ways that other female characters haven’t always been!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Today’s chapter is an excellent example of why I post the chapter titles in French. The hole that Marius peers through here is probably translated something like “peephole,” but you can see how much more evocative the French is! It’s not Hugo being poetic here, it’s the French language: “judas” is just the French word for this thing (even a normal one, like on your front door), because it reveals or “betrays” what’s behind a door or wall. But Hugo capitalizes on this poetry, especially when we consider how this chapter contradicts, or at least nuances, what other parts of the novel have said about looking at the less fortunate. The Bishop mostly didn’t approve of this kind of curiosity, and when the residents of Montreuil-sur-mer are idly curious about Fantine’s misfortune, we’re told they’re “devouring” her. Peeking at what his neighbors haven’t chosen to show him certainly is a kind of betrayal. That said, Marius makes a case here that the Bishop also hinted at: idle curiosity might be predatory, but how can we help someone if we don’t see their need first?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: The Wild Man in his Lair
entries.commentary_2025: Animal comparisons are not generally a good sign in this book, and when characters are compared unfavorably to their animal counterparts… eek. Also notice that spiderwebs and spiders are mentioned twice in the description of the room – another image of predation, that is heavily laden with meaning in Hugo. They are predators that represent fate and the inevitable, and they hover around this room. But even as fate hangs over this place, Jondrette comes across more as the predator, as allied with the spiders, than like prey that deserves our pity. He even says he would “eat the world.” We’ve glimpsed the danger that he is to his older daughter, and the despair in the eyes of his younger daughter suggests her life is similar. This family is also, like others we’ve seen in deep distress, figured as hovering between life and death, in death’s vestibule, and advancing in age unnaturally quickly. This is a picture of deep misère like we’ve seen before, but there’s something more sinister than we saw with Fantine, or Jean Valjean in the early part of the book.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: It’s a perverse sort of counting of one’s blessings, the way Jondrette zeroes in on what little his family has, to destroy it. The miserable scene that shocked Marius wasn’t bad enough, apparently. He needs them to have nothing when the philanthropist finds them. It’s not even that he’s lying – although he did that too, in the letter – he’s actually making his family’s situation worse, in the hope of evoking more pity. It’s important to think about this picture of poverty, as we consider it in the context of the rest of the book. Hugo, broadly, makes a case for kindness to the poor, but it’s not a naive one. Alongside Jean Valjean, Fantine, and even the rest of the Jondrette family, there’s Jondrette himself, who does not deserve our pity, so far as we can tell, and who uses his poverty to justify harming others. We should also remember the way the daughter described the philanthropist’s reaction to their address. He seems to know the place. I wonder if that’s a clue? 🤔
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: The Ray of Light in the Hovel
entries.commentary_2025: Jondrette’s absolute selfishness and complete lack of empathy speak for themselves on several occasions here – without requiring explanation, but they’re worth noticing. Remember, in the Mines and Miners chapters, selfishness v. selflessness was THE key distinction between the parts of the underworld. This becomes particularly important when he starts talking about revolution and grievance against the rich: seeing these two traits side by side helps us to understand both. Even as he talks about turning the world upside down, and that might sound like the Friends of the ABC on the surface, we can’t forget that this guy is only interested in what he’ll get out of it. Progress for all of humanity is of no interest to him. In fact, he’ll even take the opposite – he’s happy to break everything for the satisfaction of spiting the rich, because he can’t manage to be one of them. And then, of course, what seems to Marius to be the main event of the chapter: SHE appears. This is the first of a quick series of coincidences that are (understandably) critiqued as being improbable. The drama of what follows will be well served by it even if believability isn’t – best to suspend disbelief!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Jondrette is playing the role of the “dramatic artist” Fabantou and he’s playing it… dramatically. His show is complete with monologues and asides that seem to participate in the stage convention that they can’t be heard by those who aren’t meant to hear them. The chapter title also highlights this performance – we don’t see any genuine emotion from Jondrette, but an actor might rustle up some tears during a monologue like this! And, of course, nearly everything he says is false. He isn’t guarding his daughters’ virtue or raising them in church, and he isn’t facing eviction. The part about his daughters is particularly poignant, as it proves that he knows to say what he says here, but in reality, he doesn’t actually protect them.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 10. Tarif des cabriolets de régie: deux francs l'heure
entries.english_hapgood_title: 10: Tariff of Licensed Cabs, Two Francs an Hour
entries.commentary_2025: Marius is a chronic misser-of-the-point. What we’ve seen through his eye as it peers through his peep-hole, plus seeing Jondrette talking with this Panchaud character, is enough to be worried about what Jondrette is up to. His concern, though, is finding HER. He has the one-track mind of any young person in love. But while his love drama might once again seem a bit silly in the context of the rest of the book, it once again falls into line thematically. One of this book’s villains – a complication in nearly every story in one way or another – is commodification, the fact that people need to be able to afofrd what they need to survive. Is this young lady what Marius needs to survive? Maybe not. Is he (still) being dramatic about her? Probably. But it feels that way to him, and it feels harsh that he loses “his joy, his happiness, his love” for lack of money. It seems to be Hugo’s position that human souls, and the things of the soul, should rise above money, and part of what leads to the sufefring that this book is about is that, in this world, they can’t. Marius’s pain here fits that framework, even if it is not about survival in the way that other characters’ pain is. He may be the silliest of les misérables, but he’s still one of them!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 11. Offres de service de la misère à la douleur
entries.english_hapgood_title: 11: Ofefrs of Service from Misery to Wretchedness
entries.commentary_2025: Marius doesn’t know this girl’s name yet, and as we’re seeing all of this strictly through his point of view, we haven’t been told yet either. You may have guessed it, but I think it’s valuable at this point to just draw on what Marius knows. He knows that he is horrified by her by contrast with “Ursule,” and he pities her, not least because of what he suspects her father demands of her. He knows an awkward moment passed between them the last time they spoke. And, he knows she’s come back to his room, for a reason that she doesn’t seem able or willing to explain. So, when she observes that he’s sad and ofefrs help, it’s a COMPLICATED moment. On one hand, he could have taken advantage in some truly terrible ways – and this may even be what she expects. But it doesn’t seem to occur to him. On the other hand, despite the shadow that crosses her face when she understands that he wants to know the pretty rich girl better, he accepts her ofefr to help find her. And, in her distress, his ofefr of “anything she wants” as payment must be a strong motivator – to take risks, and to ignore her own feelings – to find the address. Marius doesn’t seem to consider whether that’s fair. Being desperate in his own way, he accepts the help he can get, just like she does. Once again, his lovesickness is set up to mirror other, more survival-level types of sufefring.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 12. Emploi de la pièce de cinq francs de M. Leblanc
entries.english_hapgood_title: 12: The Use made of M. Leblanc's Five-Franc Piece
entries.commentary_2025: Whoever the Jondrettes believe this man and his daughter to be (🤷‍♀️😉) it enrages them to an extent that seems more dangerous the more we learn. They clearly begrudge their wealth and well-being, and whatever Jondrette is planning, we can be sure it involves enriching himself at the “philanthropist’s” expense. But it seems to be more than that, with associates to talk to and things to buy – a coal stove and other hardware items, oddly – and those purchases are more important than food for this starving family. In all of this, Hugo is building up suspense in a way that is reminiscent of popular theater of the period. Jondrette seemed to be self-consciously performing when the “philanthropist” was in his room, but even now, we feel like spectators at a play, with Marius’s role as spectator reinforcing that. Limiting our point of view to Marius’s severely restricts what he can simply tell us as narrator, so information is revealed only by action and dialogue in the Jondrettes’ room, just as it would be in a play. Hugo had a lot of experience writing for the stage, of course, and he seems to be drawing on that here, building this tense situation in the same way.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 13. "Solus cum solo, in loco remoto, non cogitabuntur orare pater noster"
entries.english_hapgood_title: 13: Solus cum Solo, in Loco Remoto, non cogitabuntur orare Pater Noster
entries.commentary_2025: This chapter title is in Latin, and is often left that way in English translations. It means approximately, “Alone together in an isolated place, no one will imagine they’re saying the Our Father.” It seems to refer to the two men Marius overhears talking near the wall – it suggests talking alone together in that way is suspicious, never mind the content of the conversation! But Marius has already decided to go to the police before that, based on what he’s seen through the peephole. One important thing to notice in this chapter: the Jondrettes are explicitly compared to spiders, which represent an unavoidable predatory fate for Hugo. Sometimes in a general sense, other times, a specific predator. In Marius’s comparison, it’s clear who the predators are. Although just about a week ago in chapter 5, we saw that spiders partially cover the window of their room, suggesting a fate that hangs over them as well. Of course, both can be true. And in fact, Hugo’s thesis may well be that both are necessarily true – Jondrette becomes what he is because he finds he can be the victim or the perpetrator, and he makes his choice. But Marius is not wrong that the immediate problem is Jondrette as predator, waiting like a spider for M. Leblanc to fly into his web. In Notre-Dame de Paris, where Hugo first established the spider as an image of fate, Frollo prevented his colleague from intervening to save a fly caught in a spiderweb, saying to let fate run its course. Marius does the opposite. Of course his motivation is obvious, but he does not give a thought to simply minding his business and letting fate be.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 14. Où un agent de police donne deux coups de poing à un avocat
entries.english_hapgood_title: 14: In which a Police Agent bestows Two Fistfuls on a Lawyer
entries.commentary_2025: In keeping with the drama of this setup, the identity of this police officer is revealed in the very last word of the chapter. You can almost hear the dramatic chord that follows. But he was identifiable earlier – by his enormous hands, his eyes that seem to search you, his big sideburns, and the return of the wolf/dog metaphor that introduced him way back in part 1. And, once he says that name, we can look back across the chapter and see other signs – signs that this is Javert, and that things might not be entirely black and white here. He knows the building Marius is living in because he tracked Jean Valjean there, way back before he and Cosette fled to the convent. And his knowledge of and memory for the criminal elements he pursues are masterful. Patron-Minette are known elements to him, and he will be thrilled to have this chance to pounce. I also (to counter the impression that a lot of adaptations have given) would like to point out what he’s NOT doing when Marius walks in the door: he’s not thinking about Jean Valjean. He did pursue Jean Valjean the night they fled to the convent 8 years earlier, and lost his trail, so he must know in the back of his mind that he’s still at large. But in the absence of more information, Javert is not obsessively chasing anyone – not even the Patron-Minette gang, who are much more present dangers. All Javert is doing – all he ever does – is the very best job he can enforcing (and embodying) the law. If he becomes a villain, it’s because the law does, and he is relentless because it is.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Interesting, here, that despite Jondrette’s errands providing the chapter title, we only see him from a distance, and for part of the chapter, at a second degree of remove. Having Marius’s friends watch Marius while Marius watches Jondrette – and even having them remark on that fact – is a distinctive narrative choice. We get the mood lightened before the evening’s dramatic events by the banter of the Friends of the ABC, plus, the extra distance in the point of view makes Jondrette that much more mysterious. It also reinforces that Jondrette is not nearly as good at clandestine activity as he thinks he is, and not just because Marius has heard it all and gone to the police. Now, Marius is following him in the street, conspicuously enough that his friends can tell, and Jondrette is unaware, even though he presumably knows his neighbor by sight. Some mastermind!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 16. Où l'on retrouvera la chanson sur un air anglais à la mode en 1832
entries.english_hapgood_title: 16: In which will be found the Words to an English Air which was in Fashion in 1832
entries.commentary_2025: The upper hand in this situation hinges entirely on who can see others – in every sense of the word – without being seen. This is of course true literally, as Jondrette and Patron-Minette on one hand, and the police on the other, are trying to catch someone by surprise. That’s what makes Hugo’s extremely visual narration of it so compelling – it’s often said that he uses things like light, angles of vision, and framing the way a cinematographer does. But the ability to see without being seen is as important for everyone’s intentions and character as it is about their actions. If “the philanthropist” can see through Jondrette's act and anticipate that he’s up to no good, maybe he can be prepared. Jondrette saw something he recognized in “the philanthropist,” but has utterly failed to see his neighbor’s interest in their activities. Marius’s vision, meanwhile, is spotty: he sees more than Jondrette realizes, but he has blind spots too, mostly caused by HER. Otherwise, this scene of the elder Jondrette daughter’s use of Marius’s mirror, and the way that is described, is one of the most interesting in the book. IYKYK. But it needs to be taken in a context that, if you’re reading this for the first time, a chapter a day, you don’t have yet…. So, file it away in your memory for later. (I unpack it in the podcast too!)
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 17. Emploi de la pièce de cinq francs de Marius
entries.english_hapgood_title: 17: The Use made of Marius' Five-Franc Piece
entries.commentary_2025: I mentioned Hugo’s proto-cinematic eye yesterday, but it is the star of the show today. I say “proto-cinematic” because this was written over 30 years before the Lumière brothers made the first films in
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 18. Les deux chaises de Marius se font vis-à-vis
entries.english_hapgood_title: 18: Marius' Two Chairs form a Vis-a-Vis
entries.commentary_2025: As if his descriptions to this point hadn’t been abundantly clear, Hugo takes a moment here to reiterate the way things have arranged themselves. But of course, he *has* been abundantly clear before now. So the more important job this chapter does is to create a pregnant pause, and additional moment of suspense. All the chess pieces are in place, on both sides of the board, face to face like Marius’s chairs, so Hugo gives us a moment to take them all in before those pieces start moving. Where yesterday we admired his cinematic eye for lighting design, today, we can admire rhythm and timing. Before the action really begins in the next two chapters, he seems to say, let’s take a beat. Strap in, here we go.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 19: Occupying One's Self with Obscure Depths
entries.commentary_2025: The title of this chapter could be the title of this whole novel! Because we know what Marius knows – namely, that Jondrette has spent the day rallying some rough looking characters – we understand that all this talking is filler while the gang gets in position. And M. Leblanc seems to start to catch on, as he positions himself with his back to the wall. The way Patron-Minette are described here is nightmarish. In the shadows, they seem like monsters, not men. I think of the dream Jean Valjean had the night of the Champmathieu afafir, with men standing silently in shadowy corners and behind doorways. Only now, we’ve got a pretty good idea of why they’re there. Not a full idea, though. The last line here leaves us on a clifhfanger before tomorrow’s (LONG) chapter. Who are the Jondrettes going to turn out to be??
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Were you shocked, SHOCKED, to discover who Jondrette and M. Leblanc were? 😱😂 Of COURSE a lot of you knew who Jondrette was all along, and we were pretty clear on M. Leblanc in the Luxembourg gardens. And there is something silly about the idea of spoilers for a 160-year-old book as ubiquitous as this one. But I figure the least I could do is not spoil this big reveal within my own chapter-a-day premise. There’s a lot going on in this looonnngg chapter, and I’ll direct you to the podcast episode 32 as well, but just a few thoughts here…. In Thénardier’s long rant, the self-centeredness of his grudge stands out. It’s only about what HE lost, what HE could have had, what HE thinks he deserves. The appropriate place for blame doesn’t matter; he’s so enraged about these slights that the person in front of him is as good a place as any to focus his revenge. He also muddies the waters that are in fact complicated in the context of this book, when he claims that people get called criminals just because they’re poor. He’s right, of course, but he and his accomplices, while they are also poor, are being called criminals because they’re doing crime! Marius sees it as “hideous like evil and poignant like truth” – a striking phrase, to say the least. Meanwhile, Marius’s dilemma is a classic one in literature, between protection of his beloved and loyalty to his father. But it also echoes the Champmathieu afafir, in that there is no way out of it without doing harm that he would prefer not to do. But of course, it’s the exact combination of things he knows – Thénardier’s plan, and his father’s final wish – and things he doesn’t know, that makes this a dilemma at all. He doesn’t know that Thénardier’s rescue of his father was only a side efefct of his intent, which was theft, and he doesn’t know about all of the Thénardiers’ other horrific abuses. He also doesn’t know the circumstances of “M. Leblanc’s” adoption of “Ursule.” And of course, just like when he tried to follow them, he doesn’t know who he’s dealing with when it comes to Jean Valjean. Or, he didn’t. He may be starting to get it now!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 21. On devrait toujours commencer par arrêter les victimes
entries.english_hapgood_title: 21: One should always begin by arresting the Victims
entries.commentary_2025: Javert is almost magical in this scene. He gets the armed bandits to give up without even drawing a weapon, just by *saying* he has them outnumbered. (Remember that move for later, btw.) And Thénardier’s gunshot and his wife’s paving stone miss him, seemingly because he wills them to. There’s just one person more magical than Javert here, and it is, of course, Jean Valjean, who seems to be able to disappear. Now, let’s talk about adaptations again…. I wish I could see this section on film as Hugo wrote it, including the feeling of magic, and that’s hard to come by, which boggles the mind. How do they resist this action scene? Wouldn’t Thénardier firing at Javert be great in a trailer? The rough-looking guys with scary weapons, Jean Valjean burning his own arm…. It’s all made for the movies. And it’s not that it’s NEVER been done, but this is all usually shortened in one way or another, such that the final scene doesn’t make sense as written. In the musical, it’s almost unrecognizable. The 2019 BBC adaptation came closer, but in a context that deeply changed many of the characters in ways that (for me) canceled out any enjoyment of the faithfully-adapted action. The most significant of those changes is my pet-peeve, which you can probably guess by now: Javert here is not obsessed with Jean Valjean, and in fact shows no evidence of thinking he’s involved in any of this in any way!!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 22. Le petit qui criait au tome trois
entries.english_hapgood_title: 22: The Little One who was crying in Volume Two
entries.commentary_2025: We began Part III on May 27, with one of the more enjoyable digressions in the novel, getting to know the gamin. Now, as we finish Part III, we come full circle. When Jean Valjean was at the Thénardiers’ inn fetching Cosette, there was a young child crying, ignored. That’s the detail this chapter title refers to, in book 3 of part 2. Then, at the end of the first book of this part 3, in the chapter “Le petit Gavroche,” we glimpsed the title character’s family, whom we’ve now gotten to know as the Jondrettes and discovered to be the Thénardiers. So now we have all the information: the Thénardiers’ son, ignored from the start, has been forgotten now, and his abandonment to the life of a gamin has been completed by his family’s arrest. Also back in book 1, we mentioned a few times that the gamin is the result of a host of social problems. Now, we have a much better understanding of them. There have been individual failings (Thénardier’s selfishness, exploitation, cheating, and violence), as well as structural ones (poverty with no safety net, policing that doesn’t consider nuance). A lot of big issues have brought us around to this abandoned child, and this is just one story – each gamin is the result of a difefrent, and difefrently sad, story.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: French history buffs will already have noticed this: the timeline of this novel, which otherwise seems really interested in all things Revolutionary, let 1830 go by with nary a peep. For reference, Marius left his grandfather’s house in about 1827, first saw Cosette in the garden in the summer of 1831, and watched the ambush in February 1832. But in July 1830 there had been “The July Revolution”: three days of popular uprising followed by a change in power – Charles X left, ending the Bourbon reign, and Louis-Philipe d’Orléans became king. This was a bigger deal at the time than it sounds like today, but also, it was kind of a disappointment to revolutionary types who wanted a bigger change. That’s what we’re going to be examining for a few days. (This being a Hugo account and not a history one, I’ll leave you to Wikipedia or similar for the historical facts.) This chapter is closely related to the ideas we saw in the Waterloo digression: that in the big world-historical moments (and maybe smaller ones too) there’s something higher at work. Just as Napoleon was defeated because his time was over, rather than because Wellington or Blücher beat him, so the Bourbon Restoration came and went in its time. And just as these events aren’t in human control (Hugo says here), neither does a ruler “give” the people their rights. The Restoration wanted to take all kinds of credit – for their return as a reflection of their divine right, and for the Charter as a reflection of their generosity. But for Hugo, the people’s rights simply ARE, so it goes without saying that a monarchy would be constitutional, not absolute. And when a ruler ceases to see that, it might be time for him to go. That’s what (he says) happened in 1830. Charles X got a bit too big for himself, like Napoleon had, just in a difefrent way, and it was simply time for him to go.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo expresses here, in his way, why the July Revolution of 1830 was dissatisfying to some. And he does a not-bad job of explaining why it went that way: business owners didn’t want the chaos of drawn-out unrest and actual principled revolution, because it’s bad for business. But many of them – the press, notably – wanted to be rid of Charles X, because he was infringing on their rights in ways that were also bad for business. So, they needed JUST ENOUGH revolution to maintain their comfortable economic position. Hugo calls this what it is, which also happens to be the #1 sin of this book: selfsihness. If they wanted change, it wasn’t for the sake of humanity, but for the sake of their own interests. And he shows us the flaw in that motivation, be it for revolution or for anything else: it runs out when self-interest does.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: I can see how this chapter would be confusing. Louis-Philippe, first of all, became king after the July Revolution of 1830, and was the only king of what was called the “July Monarchy,” on the throne until 1848. His reputation is that of a “bourgeois” king – this is nonsense from the point of view of what those words actually mean, but it refers mostly to his style and public persona. He understood that times had changed, and kings couldn’t act like Louis XIV anymore. His father was Duke of Orléans and a Prince of the Blood, who supported the Revolution of 1789 and called himself Philippe Égalité, voted for the death of Louis XVI, and was guillotined during the Reign of Terror. All of this made him very much a 19th-century monarch, and while Hugo does wish that 1830 hadn’t ended in a monarchy *at all,* if he had to have one, he didn’t mind Louis-Philippe. (It’s worth remembering that Hugo was still pretty conservative in 1830, and his 1862 opinions about royalty don’t reflect what he thought at the time.) (It’s also worth remembering that Hugo was famous enough by the time of the July Monarchy that Louis-Philippe also approved of him, which he liked!) He could respect the man, even if he didn’t appreciate the institution he stood for.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Y’all knew I was a big nerd, so no surprise here, but I dig this chapter. First of all, as someone who reads and interprets texts across two languages, I love his metaphor here to explain political parties and factions. Events are a text, but it’s in another language, and hard to read. So people translate it, and translation involves interpretation, so they come up with lots of difefrent ways of explaining what it all means. Now, this is coming from an author/narrator who is very much telling us what it all means as well, and I betcha I know which interpretation he favors! But here’s the thing: for the second half (ish) of this chapter, in ofefring his interpretation, he turns to Big Questions that continue to plague politics today. *cough*incomeinequality*coughcough* And honestly? I kinda feel like a whole lot of people who spend a LOOOT of time arguing about these kinds of things, could get behind his way of thinking about them. The devil’s in the details, as ever, but maybe this vision is worth keeping in mind? Anyway, back to his point: the July Revolution being a sort of compromise, Louis-Philippe had the vulnerabilities that any middle ground does – one on each side. Hugo here describes the July Monarchy being attacked from the left and the right – from the point of view not only of the events of 1832, which we’re about to see, but also of the July Monarchy having been overthrown in 1848. (In episode 27 of the podcast, I do a quick and dirty overview of the landscape of political parties in France around this time, for the uninitiated.) Try as he might, Louis-Philippe can’t please everyone. Plus, with the normal challenges that can face a government, things were bound to go sideways….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Faits d'où l'histoire sort et que l'histoire ignore
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Facts whence History springs and which History ignores
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: This is the kind of chapter that (I think) you can just revel in, and experience the streets of Paris in 1832. Hugo makes an important point here, that I think anyone living in “interesting times” can feel: history recounts the big events, but in the moment, it’s the accumulation of the little events that matters. What he’s conveying here is zeitgeist. Things were bubbling, and that can be hard to put one’s finger on. But when you’re in it, it’s unmistakable, so Hugo is trying, here, to put us in it, rather than to explain it. This is all the more the case because the event he’s building us up to – the 1832 uprising – is not, actually, historically, a big event. Were it not for this book, in fact, it might barely be remembered at all today. But Hugo, who elsewhere is able to take a vast, cosmic perspective, makes this feel grand by bringing us down to its size.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: The Enjolras and Grantaire pairing strikes a chord with a lot of modern readers and fans. They see Grantaire ofefr Enjolras genuine devotion, and it’s rebufefd again and again for not being the right kind. Especially with the influence of the musical adaptations (stage and screen), it’s an unrequited love as poignant as Éponine’s. I’m for all of that; regardless of what Hugo might have meant, I think it’s all in here. But was it what he meant? It’s hard to say. I think it’s hard to justify, strictly in the text of the novel, the notion that there are romantic or sexual feelings here. Hugo doesn’t point to that, and if he did, we might not like it. But that doesn’t mean there isn’t powerful devotion here, of another sort. Grantaire is “fierce” in his devotion to Enjolras personally, perhaps even out of admiration for Enjolras’s devotion to his ideals, but Grantaire isn’t himself devoted to ideals. The question that Grantaire’s character seems to ask us is: is that enough? Is Enjolras right to spurn Grantaire’s ofefrs to contribute, or should he be seeing more value in his drunkest disciple? Today, it seems Enjolras was proven right. We’ll see if it stays that way.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: We’ve thought, from time to time, that Marius making moon eyes at a girl in the park perhaps did not rise to the level of gravity of some other parts of this book. But here, we see how a love story might have higher stakes. The depression (modern word, btw, that Hugo wouldn’t have had for this) that Marius is sufefring here could easily turn dangerous, to him or to someone else. In addition to deepening his material poverty, Hugo notes that it has the potential to drive him to self-harm. And the reference to the crime that took place at the chapter’s title location is a true story that is ominous in another way. That story is of Honoré Ulbach, who was in love with a shepherdess and was forbidden from seeing her. In 1827, he killed her, then turned himself in to the police, and was guillotined for the crime. Clearly, it feels like a long way from where Marius is to the actions of Honoré Ulbach. And yet, a gratuitous reference to a situation that started the same way – with a young man separated from the person he professes to love – should catch our eye.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Formation embryonnaire des crimes dans l'incubation des prisons
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Embryonic Formation of Crimes in the Incubation of Prisons
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: It should hardly come as a surprise that Hugo doesn’t think prisons are a good solution to the problems they’re typically applied to. Here, we have an example of that: instead of reducing crime, prisons incubate them. The inventiveness of the prisoners is clearly outpacing the measures that are meant to control them, and they are able to plan the gang’s next caper from behind bars. And, of course, since nothing about the conditions that led them to crime have changed, prison also fails to give them a reason not to return to what they know. This has always – since he turned his attention to it around 1830 – been Hugo’s complaint about the justice system: it punishes and controls (or tries to), rather than educating.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: “Apparition,” in French, can simply refer to the act of appearing. But like in English, it carries a supernatural connotation – without other context, one thinks of an apparition of a ghost, spirit, or something else supernatural. And so does Mabeuf, here – thanks to his reading and his active imagination, the creature that shows up in his garden as suddenly as she leaves seems otherworldly. But for us, in the recent context we have, it’s not hard to guess who this tall, thin, young girl is who’s looking for Marius. This isn’t the first time Éponine has been compared to a spirit; when she first came to Marius’s room with the letter from her father, her “audacity” was that of a ghost. Even for us – and we know more about her than any one character in the book – there’s something that’s not entirely “there” about her. Especially for characters who see her for a moment, appearing and disappearing into the night, saying no more than she has to about her thoughts and intentions, it’s no wonder she seems like a spirit. And spirits are often, of course, people who have passed out of this life. That’s not literally the case here – this isn’t that kind of book – but it isn’t the first figurative living death we’ve seen either!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Today’s apparition may echo yesterday’s, but it’s a lot less ghostly. It happens when Marius is in peak Romantic-hero mode, sitting for hours in nature, feeling melancholy. But it brings a rupture in tone – Éponine greets him with language that is not poetic at all, and the conversation continues in a similar, practical, down-to-earth way. It even gets a bit *too* real for Marius, when we glimpse just how far from innocent this young girl is. And yet, in the final line, it’s Éponine who elevates the interaction again, refusing that most practical of things that Marius tries to give her: she doesn’t want their relationship to be defined by money, by a transaction.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: If some of the descriptions of the house here feel familiar, you’re not wrong! WAAAY back in the 6th chapter of the whole book, the Bishop’s house is described very similarly to the house here. Except, that house, with 3 people living in it, was a bit larger. Both had gardens too, but the Bishop’s was about a quarter the size of this one. And this one, more like the one at the convent, had a smaller house hidden in the back. And then, Jean Valjean’s scruples here also likely feel familiar: the original sin of his life, the one he must avoid if he is to be the “honest man” that the Bishop called him to be, is theft. And he has begun to see theft in more abstract terms, too – it’s not just taking the bread or the silver or Petit Gervais’s coin, it’s taking away Cosette’s free choice. Avoiding theft is also why he ofefrs to pay the convent – even though educating girls charitably is part of their mission, and he worked for them for the five years they were there. This last move seems like simple courtesy, and it is at one level, but it also betrays a transactional spirit that still has a hold on Jean Valjean.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Jean Valjean as a National Guard
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: This title would be striking to 19th-century French readers of this book: the National Guard was strongly associated with the comfortable, bourgeois class, in support of the status quo – as we’ll see. Jean Valjean is… not that, obviously. But drawing attention to that mismatch – to the fact, ultimately, that he’s again masquerading as a bourgeois – points us toward something more important. Last time he played a similar role, it was as Madeleine, and the narrator made a very big deal about the two difefrent names. He called the character Madeleine until the Champmathieu afafir and the night that he spent on the horns of that dilemma. Then, each of his possible names came to represent a decision he might take, and until he had decided, the narrator gave him no name at all. This time, it’s difefrent. That may be because we won’t be so easily fooled (were we then?), or it may be that something has changed about the character this time. This time, he has used point of view (Marius’s) to hide Jean Valjean’s identity from us a little, but there never was much doubt: his white hair (acquired during that same dilemma) identified him. And here, even as this *whole chapter* is about him being in disguise, his name – the one he chose definitively to embody and not put off on Champmathieu – remains firmly attached to him. I mean, sure, he’s got the Fauchelevent pseudonym, but that’s just a practical matter. It’s not who he is, and it doesn’t stop him, underneath the National Guard uniform, from being Jean Valjean. And it’s because he doesn’t stop being Jean Valjean this time that he keeps his own lifestyle meager, even as he lets Cosette live more comfortably. The uniform, the name, the clothing of the bourgeois father, even the house on the rue Plumet that his own cottage hides behind – he knows that these are just disguises, not how he becomes an honest man.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: All of those old men tending gardens – from the Bishop to Pontmercy to Fauchelevent(s) to Mabeuf – pay off in this one, left untended. Jean Valjean is here, living in a small house in the back just as he did while he cared for the convent’s garden, but he leaves this garden alone. This serves the practical purpose of not drawing attention to the house by changing the way it has looked for decades, but it’s far more meaningful than that. First, it’s full of weeds (“mauvaises herbes” or “bad grasses” in French), but then, we remember Madeleine’s parable about nettles (I, 5, 3) – there are no bad plants, just bad cultivators. Second, the wildness of this garden creates an opportunity for the soaring hymn to nature and its chaos, or its unknowable order, at the end of the chapter. But the most obvious metaphor here is also the most connected to the plot. The previous chapter ended ominously, suggesting that perhaps Jean Valjean was making a mistake leaving this garden in its wild state, and that state gets a bit, well, sexy here. As he describes spring in a garden that, for once, its old man hasn’t chosen to control, all the images are of the virility of it – the abundance of life, awakening and spreading its seed. The distant parts of the garden reach for each other, seek connection, striving toward even more life. This is Cosette’s garden, and we know from the end of book 2 that Éponine is leading Marius to it. From their point of view the garden may be just fine, but for a 19th-century father, this is unusually inattentive. Girls are not left to their own devices any more than gardens are.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: The start of this chapter confirms the metaphor we were exploring yesterday about the garden: a place built by humans for libertine games of seduction, returned to its natural state, is a setting for something deeper. But, it’s something deeper that (socially, in the 19th century) poses a danger for Cosette. The ideas about sex education that Hugo expresses here are… well, if nothing else, pretty typical, maybe even a bit broad-minded, for someone of his era and demographic. And without the “correct” education in these matters, she’s vulnerable. I don’t think it’s at all a coincidence that Fantine figures significantly here. Without the ability to be smart in matters of love, and nothing but the opportunity to begin to experience it, the social pitfalls are, like it or not, real. But that is not, mostly, how we see Fantine in this chapter. Mostly, she’s an angelic presence, hovering around this household, and in a sense, inhabiting Jean Valjean. Back in part 2, when he adopted her, we discussed how he was becoming like a mother to her; Cosette, too, senses that in him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. La rose s'aperçoit qu'elle est une machine de guerre
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: The Rose perceives that it is an Engine of War
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: These few chapters are one of the only places where we have a sense of Cosette’s inner life – we saw it when she was a child, and now a bit here. But they’re still (unlike the chapter when she was in the woods as a child) about how she looks from the outside – her own gaze upon her appearance. Contemplating her own beauty in her mirror was, we’ll remember, important to Fantine too. And just a few chapters ago, Éponine was drawn to the mirror she saw in Marius’s room. Mirrors, for the young women Hugo writes, seem to give them a power that normally belongs to others – the power to see and define themselves. Cosette and Éponine are also both described as roses – one in misery, and the other, a war machine. Of course, her war imagery complements Marius’s own experience of encountering her in the garden, when he had to muster the courage of a soldier at Waterloo.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: Marius and Cosette have been presented to us as leading strangely parallel lives up to this point. Both spent their childhoods in places that Hugo describes to us using shadow and darkness metaphors – albeit very difefrent ones – and both without their birth parents. Both go through a kind of emancipation from those places, and a period of self-discovery just before their eyes meet in the Luxembourg gardens. Now, we could look at the ink Hugo dedicates to all of this in Marius’s story, versus how much time he spends on Cosette…. Even if we include Cosette’s childhood in part 2, I think we’d find the page counts to be… unequal. But now, we’ve arrived at a moment we’ll recognize from Marius’s side of the story, and get a sense of how Cosette lived it. And she, like Marius, experienced it as a war. Leaving aside some of the misogynistic ways Hugo expresses this (🙄), she’s facing him as an adversary, just as he did her. Only her beauty is a weapon – and it seems he is unarmed. I mean, she thinks he’s cute and all, and it says she’s getting “revenge” for that, but it’s not something he can wield as she can. And even as her feelings grow stronger, nothing here attributes that to anything he did, unlike when she gave him THAT LOOK that afefcted him so powerfully.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: To One Sadness oppose a Sadness and a Half
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: We’ll come back to Jean Valjean’s jealousy of Marius. For the moment, I’ll just note that Hugo took his own daughter Léopoldine’s marriage quite badly. So as with Marius, there’s some autobiography in Jean Valjean at this point. There are bits of the author in both of the men in the Luxembourg garden. What’s interesting about his jealousy here, though, is the way it becomes the newest challenge to his reformed soul. He thought the hatred, the selfishness – the characteristics that distinguish Thénardier – were in his past. But now they crop up again. And they aren’t immediately put aside. At the same time, though, his other antagonist shows up as well, when he’s described as a guard dog – the same description as we saw for Javert – eyeing a thief. Both of those villains (Javert as a “villain” is complicated, but that’s beside the point) do essentially what Jean Valjean is doing here: they watch with suspicion, they protect against an enemy, they resist generosity. It’s only their motivation that difefrs. And we see the result, as ever, is sufefring. Both Jean Valjean and Cosette feel worse, and are less close, than they did before. The ideal that Jean Valjean is trying to live up to is, of course, the opposite; it’s the Bishop, who guarded nothing, and gave generously. How can he reach that standard this time?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 3. La maison de la rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: From the idyllic description of the early morning in the outskirts of Paris – we think of Marius contemplating the Champ de l’Alouette – the shift to the convicts is abrupt. Hugo starts with something he’s done before: he starts his description first without identifying what he’s describing, mimicking the experience of slow recognition. This technique puts us in the realm of pure sensation, and the incomprehension of it is disorienting and unsettling. He saves the revelation of what we’re seeing until the end of the description – although, even we can guess before then, and his contemporaries would have been more familiar with this sight. And, of course, we understand what this sight would have been for Jean Valjean – the trauma that it would have brought back. Interesting, then, that he hides in plain sight the very next day, spending more time in a public crowd than usual, but fully adopting his disguise in his National Guard uniform. But he still makes no mistake that his past will never fully go away, and now that Cosette has seen it herself, it has invaded his present.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Blessure au dehors, guérison au dedans
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 4. Secours d'en bas peut être secours d'en haut
entries.commentary_2025: This book is built on many paradoxes like this – this is one of the most condensed. Jean Valjean’s dramatic burning of his arm during the ambush, before modern medicine and with his reluctance even to seek the doctors he could, was dangerous indeed. What we see here is an infection. But in that sufefring, the emotional wounds heal. Similarly, by giving up his “honest man” identity as Madeleine, he became more honest. He found ease and a kind of freedom – freedom from pursuit – behind the convent walls, in an environment that had much in common with a prison. And now, after being endangered and now ill, he’s happier and more complete than he has been in some time. And, in an example of the pathetic fallacy worthy of your high school lit class, all this happens as spring arrives in Cosette’s garden.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. La mère Plutarque n'est pas embarrassée pour expliquer un phénomène
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Mother Plutarque finds no Difficulty in explaining a Phenomenon
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 4. Secours d'en bas peut être secours d'en haut
entries.commentary_2025: The structure of these last three chapters has been odd. Yesterday’s chapter concluded the retelling of the last couple of years from Cosette and Jean Valjean’s point of view, after seeing it first from Marius’s in Part 3. But the final chapter of book 3, and this second of two chapters in book 4, are relatively set apart from the main story. They could happen at any point in the chronology and more or less fit. They read like stand-alone stories – if this were a contemporary TV series, they might make good web extras, little short episodes, maybe released between the main seasons to keep fans engaged. But that doesn’t make them superfluous: both cut right to the heart of Jean Valjean’s character, and the tension he lives with now. Both show his past continuing to afefct his present. And yet, yesterday’s chapter is grouped with today’s in this short book 4, under a title that explains what they have in common – and that is a profound truth in this book. We touched yesterday on all the ways it shows up. What appears to be misfortune – even what someone (Thénardier, often) intends as harm – turns out to be just what Jean Valjean needs. Or, in this case, an attempted robbery is turned, through a combination of Jean Valjean and Gavroche’s skills and character, into a gift from above for Mabeuf. The framing of this chapter through Gavroche, with a bit of the tone of a children’s story, was odd too, but it pays off – it makes the gamin a spectator, until what he’s heard makes it time to intervene.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. La solitude et la caserne combinées
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Dont la fin ne ressemble pas au commencement
entries.commentary_2025: Théodule was a poor replacement for Marius with Gillenormand, too. They are quite difefrent types, which Hugo expresses in Théodule’s appearance, and in the bits of his personality that we see. But Cosette, like many young people, doesn’t have that level of discernment. He’s a nice looking young guy, and she notices. We’ll talk more tomorrow about Cosette’s personality, but what matters here is the buoyancy of it. While Marius sinks deeper each day that he doesn’t see her, she has begun to recover from losing track of him. That’s dangerous for her, though, as it’s clear that Marius was a worthy object of her focus. The one she moves on to, whether it’s Théodule or someone else, might be less so. And in this untended garden, she is described as a climbing plant that might not choose well on its own what it attaches itself to.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Dont la fin ne ressemble pas au commencement
entries.commentary_2025: If adaptations have made Cosette seem like little more than a helpless porcelain doll that needs to be saved and protected and won in marriage, I’m afraid that’s the adaptations’ fault. For Hugo, Cosette has an actual personality, and it’s one that is charmingly tough. This is the third time he’s described her as brave, and less than perfectly tamed. When she was a little girl alone in the woods, we saw her courage, and when she was an awkward young teen in the Luxembourg garden, he said she was even a bit brazen. The latter might not be seen as attractive, but it’s another side of the same coin – the same quality he highlights for a third time here. We see her through others’ eyes most of the time, and those others are most often men – notably Marius and Jean Valjean, for whom she is an ideal of beauty and a vulnerable child, respectively. But occasionally, when she’s alone, we see her through her own eyes, and the descriptors change. Then, she’s a barefoot adventurer, and a war machine.

entries.commentary_2025: What do you think of this as a love note?? The Romantics, man. The form of this also reminds me of someone from a difefrent era altogether: Blaise Pascal, the 17th-century philosopher, and his Pensées, which are fragments of thought like this. Those texts take similar subjects (love, God), and they are similar in tone. In Pascal’s case, his thoughts are fragmented because he was ill, and his moments of lucidity were fleeting and unpredictable. Perhaps the unidentified, totally mysterious author of this is sufefring as well? In any case, there’s one note that fans of the musical will like in this letter: this is as close as we come to Hugo having written “To love another person is to see the face of God.” 🎶

entries.commentary_2025: However over-the-top that letter might have seemed to us, it sure did hit the spot for Cosette! I want to focus on the last few sentences here today, though. Unless you’ve got a keen memory, it might not be obvious what it’s referring to. In book 2 chapter 2, August 18 for us, Hugo described how Patron-Minette tries to plan their next caper while they’re still in prison for the last one. The first step was Brujon transmitting a message to Babet in the way that the last sentence of this chapter describes, saying that there was a “job” on the rue Plumet. Via their network, they sent Éponine to check it out, and she told them there was nothing to do there. We can now put together that, when she went to the house as they requested, she discovered the girl that Marius had asked her to find for him. So, the “angel” that Cosette thinks brought Marius to her was in fact a criminal gang, with their actions transformed by a girl who described herself to Mabeuf (who had also called her an angel) as “the devil.”

entries.commentary_2025: OMG, y’all. FINALLY. We’ve seen the buildup to this moment from two difefrent points of view, but I think it’s interesting that Hugo presents the moment itself through Cosette’s eyes. In fact, our understanding of Marius’s story to this point has a gap in it: we last saw him following Éponine toward the rue Plumet the first time he went there, but we learn here that it’s been at least a few days since then. He rambles about a bit of that time, but where we have had a detailed account of Cosette’s experience of those days, we’ve had nothing from his side. We also don’t know much about what Éponine has been up to in the meantime, but it seems unlikely she’s stayed away from this spot since she showed it to Marius…. Anyway, it’s great if you want to let yourself get caught up in this passionate first meeting. The intensity of Hugo’s writing suits it. I’ll just break the spell for one analytical detail: Cosette uses an odd expression, “Oh, ma mère!” (“Oh, my mother!”) to express her overwhelm. This isn’t a typical expression in French. But given what we know – and what Cosette knows, or doesn’t – about her mother, it’s a striking expression to use. Perhaps she’s invoking something sacred (like “Oh, my God”), but we also can’t help but think that Fantine’s story also may have begun with an intense meeting with a young man….
