entries.commentary_2025: As is so often the case, the chapter title deliberately buries the lede. The wind is NOT the main villain here. It is, as it so often is, the Thénardiers. They rented out two of their children that they didn’t love, AND cooked up the crime that got the adults responsible for their care arrested. And Mme Thénardier comes out of this particularly badly, as a mother who doesn’t love all of her children. Now, coming from a male author of Hugo’s era, we have to take a beat to think about the sexist tropes this participates in: that motherhood is “natural” for women, and its failure is part of what makes her monstrous. And the opposite – powerful, sacrificial maternal love – was invoked just yesterday as sacred. But this book is also making the case that good parenting is a practical, social good as well, and that its opposite is harmful. Not that the other adults here are innocent: Magnon thought of children chiefly in terms of their ability to bring in money, so for her, they were interchangeable. A number of themes that have frequently been associated with villainy in this book appear here: commodification of human beings, separation of children from parents, and withholding parental love.

entries.commentary_2025: Crime stories were wildly popular in the 19th century. Les Misérables has already included an ambush and a cat-and-mouse police chase, so why not a prison break? The details of how they escaped allow Hugo to show just how inefefctive prisons are at making life safer. But the real story here is Thénardier. Not least because of the resemblance I’ve often pointed out between him and another high-profile bad guy of our acquaintance, I didn’t hate seeing him dangle a while in the cold rain. Gavroche, though, is a better person than I am, and even after he recognized that it was his father up there, he proceeded to help him anyway. It’s heart-wrenching how, even though he knows (as he told the boys yesterday) that with some parents, it’s better not to be around them, he waited for Thénardier to acknowledge him. But he didn’t, so Gavroche left to go be a better parent than he ever had for himself.

entries.commentary_2025: This book 7 is yet another mini-digression, on argot, or slang. Translations will vary, but if you’re reading in French, a LOT of the dialogue in yesterday’s chapter was not understandable without Hugo’s footnotes. This wouldn’t have been entirely unfamiliar to Hugo’s 1862 readers, and not just because Hugo himself had had a character speak argot before, as he tells us here. In 1836, Eugène-François Vidoq, criminal turned police informant turned police officer, had published an argot dictionary, which piqued public interest in this way of speaking. But Hugo doesn’t just gape at it here. He sees it as emblematic of, and a metaphor for, the social problems that this book is about. And, as language is itself a social phenomenon, and points to a social reality, he argues that the thinking that guides us for the rest of the issues here should guide us for argot as well. It aligns with both his social mission and his poetic aesthetic, then, to encourage us to consider and try to understand argot.

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo may say that argot is ugly, or hideous, or horrifci, but what he actually seems to think about it is more complex than that. It represents things that are hideous: social exclusion, poverty, desperation, and the resulting willingness to do harm. But, especially when he writes some of the full sentences of argot that we see in this chapter and others, he also seems to revel in its grotesque musicality. Remember, the grotesque has been a central part of Hugo’s aesthetic since his earliest theoretical writings. While the sound that argot creates here might not be classically beautiful, it’s essential in other ways. It has a strange sort of beauty of its own. Also, in this extensive discussion of where it comes from and how it evolves linguistically, it’s clear that it is no less a language than standard French is. Modern linguists continue to fight this battle, against distinctions of legitimacy between languages or dialects. Those distinctions aren’t inherent in the languages themselves; they’re the products of politics and power. Argot may be, by definition, the language of people without power, but it is every bit as complex and expressive as the most sophisticated French you can find. Maybe, sometimes, more so.

entries.french_title: 3. Argot qui pleure et argot qui rit
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: Slang which weeps and Slang which laughs
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is only barely about argot. It’s actually about the world described in the “Mines and Miners” section, and that this book is all about. In that section he described a thing that he echoes here: that the forces that work against the wealthy and powerful are of two types: productive and destructive. He adds here that those destructive forces are the successors of the excluded and the sufefring, and that succession is when tears turn to laughter. Laughter, in Hugo, is often not a signifier of joy, but rather, of defiance, of revolution. The Joker was inspired by a Hugo character, and is an example of this kind of disconcerting laughter, borne of rage (although the character he was based on wasn’t). It’s rooted in the same social failings that create argot, that are at the heart of this book.

entries.french_title: 4. Les deux devoirs: veiller et espérer
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: The Two Duties: To Watch and to Hope
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: It would take more time than I can dedicate to this daily post to unpack this chapter, and the *many* things it might have to say to us today. Maybe just: reading this chapter in 2025 is good for the soul. Hugo has been using the fact that some of his characters speak in a slang belonging to criminals as a jumping-off place to encapsulate what this book is driving at, before heading into the plot’s climax. And while he doesn’t have policy proposals for us – this book really ofefrs just one specific policy idea, and it’s yet to come – his political postures relative to these issues are pretty clear. First of all, let’s not mince words: he’s talking about socialism, and thinking about wealth collectively first. Not eliminating individual wealth, just not prioritizing it over the basic needs of the poorest. And, he’s talking about something analogous outside the financial realm, too. Not only making sure everyone’s fed, but making sure they’re educated and enabled to thrive in other ways too. It sounds so simple and obvious when he puts it like this, and that may be why he SO firmly believed it was at hand. Even though, in Second Empire France, the evidence wasn’t exactly pointing that way. But he was so sure of what Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. would later call the long arc of the moral universe.

entries.commentary_2025: Chastity, purity, and goodness are conflated a lot in this book. Which is a little surprising, because Hugo, to put it bluntly, liked sex. A LOT. But there’s some indication that he felt kinda bad about it… that’s a WHOLE can of worms. Plus, this isn’t Victorian England, and France will always be France, but he was writing in that same period, after all. All of which is to say, people wanting to have sex, then having it, enjoying it, and neither of them being punished for it, isn’t something we see much of in Les Misérables. Many of the morally upright characters – the Bishop (when we know him), Jean Valjean, Mabeuf, the nuns in the convent, obviously – even Javert, who, while an antagonist to Jean Valjean, isn’t BAD, exactly – are entirely chaste. And where there is sex, it’s often not seen as a good thing: Fantine’s “error” leads to her “descent,” the Thénardiers have bunches of children they don’t love, and their daughters (seem to) be coerced into it. And now, Marius and Cosette, hopelessly in love, are too pure to even *consider* carnal possibilities. They are bundles of feelings, but the package those feelings are wrapped in isn’t part of the conversation.

entries.commentary_2025: The cholera outbreak that was (irl) going on in Paris at this time doesn’t appear by chance at the start of this chapter about being hopelessly, blindly, madly, in love. The spring and summer of 1832 was a bad time to be in Paris – it was when the cholera pandemic that spread around the world in the late 1820s and 1830s came to town. About 100,000 people died in France before it subsided, over 18,000 of those in Paris. There were sections of Paris where 5-7% of the population died within 6 months. So if Marius and Cosette’s sweet nothings can drown out all that, it can certainly drown out other small challenges that their love afafir might face. Memories of whatever happened in the Thénardiers’ room a few months ago? Cosette’s father’s disapproval? Marius’s poverty, and his friends’ increasing political agitation? Irrelevant! But just because they’re ignoring all of that, doesn’t mean it’s gone. Thénardier has escaped. Jean Valjean doesn’t know what Cosette is up to, and would NOT be ok with it. And cholera will soon claim the life of a certain General Lamarque, which will, let’s say, start some stuff….

entries.commentary_2025: The title of this chapter leads us to expect something more ominous than what it is, which is a collection of descriptions of what people around Marius and Cosette are seeing as they’re lost in ecstasy. But, each of these interactions carries a danger: the loss of secrecy would complicate all of this considerably. Jean Valjean could forbid them from seeing each other, Éponine could lead Patron-Minette to them, and Marius’s friends aren’t exactly discreet…. In short, as much as they might try to imagine otherwise, there *is* a world outside their little garden, and they may eventually have to reckon with it. Until they do, though, the charming list of the little pleasures of love that we read here are all theirs.

entries.commentary_2025: I know I say this a lot, but I LOVE this chapter. My Les Misérables-themed tattoo is a quote from this chapter. If you know this scene from the musical especially, it’s important to try to read it with fresh eyes here, because it’s quite difefrent. Specifically: in the musical, Éponine screams. Here, she doesn’t have to. Instead, she simply intimidates them, even as she is outnumbered and out-armed, and out-sized, and she’s interrupted by a dry cough that any 19th-century reader would recognize as ominous. I suppose there are natural explanations for this: confidence is key, maybe, or perhaps they really think she’ll scream, and/or maybe they’re not up to their big talk about killing her. But it does seem a little bit magical. She seems to summon a power here that is hard to explain – weirdly, in the same way Javert did at the end of the ambush scene. Those two characters don’t have much in common overall. But here, like Javert, she’s a guard dog guarding a barrier that also excludes her, and using an almost supernatural power to do it.

entries.commentary_2025: Éponine has been portrayed to this point as a devil, a specter, a ghoul. She’s had “apparitions,” like a spirit, or like a vision of a religious figure. This book isn’t (officially) the kind of book that deals in the supernatural. But when it comes to Éponine, and to some moments with other characters (like we said yesterday), it seems like it might be. And the one thing that is more terrifying than six (totally real, human) armed men, with very real weapons, is a ghost, something they don’t understand, but can sense. The animal and material worlds might be wild and dangerous to humans, but the spiritual wins out over the material. Poverty and sufefring have made characters animalistic – Jean Valjean and Fantine, at their lowest points, were described in beastly terms. But for Éponine, it has another efefct entirely. One final word about this chapter: if you are remotely able to deal with a page or so in French, this is the one to try. This chapter, in the original, is a prose poem.

entries.french_title: 6. Marius redevient réel au point de donner son adresse à Cosette
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: Marius becomes Practical once more to the Extent of Giving Cosette his Address
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les enchantements et les désolations
entries.commentary_2025: The phrasing in the title here (at least in the original) is great. Marius, for all this romance, hasn’t been real. But, one might say, sh*t’s getting real. First, let’s be precise about how he hasn’t been “real.” The first way is obvious, maybe – these two have been described as souls, as spiritual beings, not corporeal ones. The other, maybe related, is how fused he has been with Cosette, which is described here. He hasn’t been a separate, autonomous, coherent self. And neither a disembodied soul nor a part of Cosette has an address to give her! But the prospect of all of the reality outside separating them brings him back down to earth, and all of his corporeality and individuality come back. He promises to die without her, which, while dramatic, is also a fundamentally physical threat. And, whatever his plan is at the end, it’s his own. He will take action to solve this problem, and do it autonomously.

entries.french_title: 7. Le vieux cœur et le jeune cœur en présence
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: The Old Heart and the Young Heart in the Presence of Each Other
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.french_book: Livre 8. Les enchantements et les désolations
entries.commentary_2025: Conflicts within our characters are nothing new. Jean Valjean, Marius, and others have faced dilemmas where difefrent parts of themselves were pulled in difefrent directions. They have done things that they were not yet capable of, or things that they were already no longer capable of. But Gillenormand’s division of himself is between his outside and his inside. Inside, he loves his grandson desperately, and any anger has its root in that love. Outside, though, he’s all bitterness. And Marius depends on him utterly: at the time, young men needed their parents’ permission to get married if they were younger than 25. But the fundamental incompatibility of their characters still stands in the way, even if politics are (for the moment) set aside. Gillenormand can’t take Cosette seriously, and Marius can't take his love lightly. Now, both characters face despair again: Marius because he has no way of staying with Cosette if Jean Valjean moves to England, and Gillenormand because he has, again, lost his beloved grandson. And despair is deadly: Marius has already considered death for this despair, and Gillenormand, in the final lines of this chapter, appears worryingly death-like as well.

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Fun fact: this is the second section (chapter, book or part) titled “Jean Valjean.” The first was way back in Part 1, book 2, January 20 for us, when we learned his backstory, and this will also be the title of Part 5. Here, though, it’s the first part of a 3-part answer to the question in the title of book 9 – where are they going? (For fans of the musical, it’s easy to see how they got from this part of the book to the number that ends Act I. Everyone is on the move at this moment.) The chapter doesn’t answer the question for Jean Valjean – we don’t know where he’s going, but it’s clear that he will now be spooked enough to have to go. Having all of our characters active means having people who will recognize him (Thénardier, and the police, which means Javert) around and attentive. It will be far more difficult to stay hidden.

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: This is the second chapter in a row to end with a young, maybe adolescent man running of fafter delivering a message, and the mystery around who it might be is not especially deep. But that person has now sunk Marius into despair by encouraging Jean Valjean and Cosette’s departure and then pointed Marius toward the barricade. It’s interesting, by the way, that the barricades of the June 1832 uprising – the historical event that many of Hugo’s original readers would have seen coming for a while now – have gone up in the background. Like the July Revolution of 1830, the start of this event initially went by without much interest from our narrator. Marius – who is, according to his grandfather, a revolutionary – was too preoccupied to care. His friends invited him to Lamarque’s funeral, which is a signal to the reader that this is that day, but that is not what the story is about right now. Instead, it’s about heartbreak, and it’s increasingly hinting at becoming a tragedy, even as Hugo tells us quite directly that he is avoiding the tropes of the theater. The mention of the pistols, Marius’s despair such that he sees only darkness after what he assumes will be his last meeting with Cosette… There are many reasons for us to be very worried about what he’ll do next.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Early in this chapter, we’re told that Mabeuf continues to “descend” – your translation may vary, but in the original, this is a word closely related to Fantine’s “descent” that titled Part I book 5. And the two descents resemble each other, as Mabeuf, too, loses what he loves, what makes up who he is, bit by bit. It’s not his physical body, as it was for Fantine, but it’s a similar progression, from his means of making an honest living, to beautiful things that he loves, to a final, desperate sacrifcie in response to an illness. And his final action in this chapter is weighty too: remember that he moved house once because he didn’t like hearing the sounds from a firing range. Now, this gentle old man who just wants politics to leave him alone, heads toward the sound of gunshots.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Two things, both EXTREMELY hugolian, happen in this chapter. First, a riot (that’s the English word I’m going to use for the French “émeute” – vocabulary will become important) becomes a phenomenon of spirit, bigger than, and beyond, the people involved in it. The people matter, and we feel what they feel in the first part of this chapter, but they don’t create the riot. The riot comes over them. And second, quite difefrently but just as characteristically, Hugo rejects the notion that we should start with financial cost to measure the impact of a riot. Money is simply not an appropriate unit of measure in this book. Not for people, not for their time or labor, and not for the cost/benefit of something like a popular uprising. Because it’s spiritual, like human beings, it needs to be judged in other ways. And what those are will be the subject of what comes next.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: The good news in chapters like this, in Hugo, is that you don’t have to understand all the references to get the gist. Each one adds nuance, but you only need to get a couple of them to grasp the main idea. And, in the broadest sense here, the main idea is this: insurrection, good; riot, bad. Of course, the devil’s in the details, and the details here are how we’re defining “good” and “bad.” And he does that in a few difefrent ways. He defines an insurrection as having right on its side, whether that takes the form of the will of the majority, or the ideals of progress. A riot doesn’t represent the majority, and it’s just a reaction to discontent. It doesn’t espouse ideals of any sort. But of course (gestures wildly at the USA) sometimes the will of the majority and the ideals of progress are not the same thing. That’s where things get murky, and where Hugo seems to side against democracy just a bit. All of this is very informed by Hugo’s own political views of course, which, by this time, tend toward democracy. Mostly. But you may remember back in the first part of the book, when we spent a bunch of time thinking about Napoleon and Waterloo…. His views on particular sorts of tyrants were complicated. Napoleon’s antidemocratic tendencies, for Hugo, accomplished something for a while. The “genius despot” that he discusses for a while here might get a temporary pass. But in the end, a despot has to be fought, and that might go so far as being an insurrection. Hugo is now ready to reframe what readers his age would have remembered as a bloody street skirmish as a grand historical event that has been gravely misunderstood.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: A Burial; an Occasion to be born again
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo’s description of how this uprising started is stylized, and there are details that are likely poetic license, but the broad strokes are right. The insurgents took control of Lamarque’s funeral cortege, and by day’s end, occupied sections of the center of Paris. The intent was to start a new revolution and install Lafayette (yes, that one – he was an old man by this time) as president of a republic. Hugo was in Paris at this time, but was not present for the events he’s describing here. He was writing in the Tuileries gardens when he heard gunshots, and, sensibly, went toward them. Briefly, on June 5, he was in a narrow street, pressed up against a building between two columns while bullets whizzed by in each direction. That’s as close as he came – quite close enough! – to the action he’s describing.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: The insurgents’ positions in Paris on June 5 are documented, and this is, I think, largely right. With one exception, which he alludes to a bit here: the characters that we’ll be following are fictional. But he’s already discussed here that the center of things, the middle of the city around Les Halles, will be what matters. That is where we’ll spend our time too. Our characters will resemble some of the last insurgents to be defeated, but they, and the location of their barricade, will be slightly difefrent. For readers who would have remembered this historical event, though, much of what Hugo says here would have been familiar, and placed them in a real time and place.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.commentary_2025: Whether or not June 5, 1832 was actually difefrent from other uprisings in the ways Hugo describes here is unclear. Even if it was, it’s likely Hugo is exaggerating this difefrence in any case. And partly, that’s hard to say because 1) some people are probably nervous in these ways anytime there’s violence in a civilian space and 2) historical memory of this event has, since 1862, been deeply afefcted by this book. But what’s important here, I think, is what Hugo says about Paris, and about this uprising. Paris’s usual nonchalance about political street violence is portrayed as largely commercial. Most of the activity that he shows continuing unafefcted, even things like theaters and billiard rooms, are businesses. That is, what makes 19th-century Paris truly unflappable, what brings out their inner courage in the face of violence, is the drive to continue making money. If we think about the rest of the context of this book – the kinds of roles that commerce, buying, selling, and commodified relationships have had – this might not be an entirely complimentary observation. And then, saying that something about June 1832 overcame even that commercial impulse gives the events we’re about to read about a unique, even spiritual power.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Quelques éclaircissements sur les origines de la poésie de Gavroche. Influence d'un académicien sur cette poésie
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: Some Explanations with Regard to the Origin of Gavroche's Poetry. The Influence of an Academician on this Poetry
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: When Hugo refers to Gavroche as an “atom,” he’s figuring him as the smallest unit of something (Paris) that is still identifiably that thing. This is now the second time he’s done this in the title of a book: first in Part 3 Book 1, and now in Part 4 Book 11. But since Paris has changed, so has Gavroche. Now, Paris has heated up (to continue the chemistry analogy), and as it becomes revolutionary, Gavroche does too. And for the same reasons: Gavroche is hungry, poor, and alone, and when the spirit of revolution moves, he moves with it. As for the poetry mentioned in the chapter title: it is actually Hugo’s, and Hugo pours more of his own poetic energy into Gavroche’s songs than most other characters in the book!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: This book is full of practical, mostly apolitical old women who keep things functioning. These four are no exception. They join the ranks of women like Mme Magloire, mame Bougon, and Toussaint – working class women whom we find alongside our main characters, cooking their meals and holding their material world together. But these women are also a group of four, which has generally been a bad omen in this book. Notably, Hugo made a big deal of Fantine’s group, when she was with Tholomyès, being two groups of four. While they’re apolitical, Gavroche has become a little fount of revolutionary discourse, even when it contrasts with his actions, like helping the National Guardsman’s horse get back up. He reminds us a LOT here of the gamin in Delacroix’s “Liberty Leading the People.”
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: Of course, we know the answer to the question at the end of this chapter: he refused to help two little children in need, and scolded them for letting the heat out of his shop when they came in to ask for help. As we’ve seen Gavroche take on the ideas of the revolutionaries, and become a revolutionary as the city he represents does, he also applies these ideas concretely to his world. The uprising is, according to him, in the interest of the poor women we saw in the last chapter, and its destruction is directed at people who have made the sufefring of the poor worse. Well, Gavroche happens to know someone like that – he hasn’t forgotten. He’s uniquely able to see how that one failure to be merciful is connected to the big ideas of the revolutionary cause. But these men can’t – a “hero” and an admirer of Napoleon’s wars, violent as they were, can’t understand why a gamin would be so destructive as to throw a pebble through their window.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: The Child is amazed at the Old Man
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: And Gavroche has finally caught up with the people we knew would be here, the Friends of the ABC. Enjolras and Bahorel’s disagreement is interesting here, and takes us back to when we first met them. It’s a matter of temperament, of course, but it also shows two difefrent sides of the spirit of the revolution – with Bahorel being much more Gavroche’s style! But the lightheartedness they bring to the moment doesn’t just contrast with Enjolras, it contrasts with the chilling sight of Mabeuf. We’ll see more about that tomorrow. For today, one last note: the May 1968 protesters in Paris picked up a line from Bahorel in this chapter for a poster:

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: We had already compared Mabeuf’s descent to Fantine’s, and now here he is at the very bottom. Like her, he’s lost everything that made up his character, right down to personality traits. For her, it was modesty that defined her, and then was ripped away. For him, it’s his apolitical peacefulness. The things he calls “good” here – political action, violence, gunshots – are things we’ve seen him actively avoid before. And like her, he’s a sleepwalker, no longer present in his body, like the living dead, or an empty shell. That vacancy may be what allows the revolutionaries who don’t know him to imagine that he was involved in the events of 1793, and take from his presence the OG Revolution’s blessing on their cause.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep43 - IV,11,i-vi - How to Become a Revolutionary
entries.commentary_2025: Courfeyrac’s grim announcement that he won’t be returning apparently didn’t discourage the young person who was waiting for him in his building concierge’s office. This is now the third time we’ve seen a person matching this description. First, when Jean Valjean got the note telling him to move, then when Marius was encouraged toward the barricade. And now, the person is looking for Marius again and, unable to find him, follows the crowd despite the obvious danger. You may have identified this particular recruit already. But there was another one, in the first lines of the chapter – don’t gloss over that one either. We’ll be seeing both of them again.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Histoire de Corinthe depuis sa fondation
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: History of Corinthe from its Foundation
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: To be perfectly clear: Hugo says the barricade we’ll be focusing on has just been forgotten in favor of the famous one nearby – it is in fact his invention. The geography of the streets was real at the time, though. The area is totally difefrent now, but old maps show the streets he describes. And describing it initially in the way that he described Waterloo is not a coincidence either. Keep that analogy in mind…. Meanwhile, the Corinthe bar being steeped in wordplay beyond the possible intention of anyone involved is a sign that it’s destined to be a part of the events to come, with Gavroche and the Friends of the ABC, who engage in the same. (If you’re reading in translation, I hope it allows you to follow the twists and turns of that wordplay!) There is also a fair bit of nostalgia in this description for the old Paris, which by 1862 was well on its way to being destroyed and built over by Haussmann’s renovations. The fact that everything about Corinthe and this section of Paris is run-down and dilapidated is, paradoxically, part of its charm. It has the musty smell of the history that was being lost.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: We’ve now seen all – well, almost all – of our characters through the morning of June 5, and we know how they wound up at the rue de la Chanvrerie. For these three, not for lack of commitment to the cause, what initially brought them here was the oysters and wine. (Which – and I say this as a fairly adventurous eater – oysters and wine at 9 am?!?) They know about the planned uprising, and they’re game, but they figure they don’t need to miss this good time to stand in the rain at the funeral that precedes the action. Even Grantaire, whose priority is often wine, expresses disappointment at Enjolras’s lack of faith in him. He’s as willing to be in this as anyone, and wishes Enjolras could see that. But it’s not that he’s NOT drinking either. And when people drink in this book, they RAMBLE. I find these rambling passages interesting, because they seem to do two things at once. They show that the person is in their own world, talking without much regard for their audience’s (lack of) interest, and, given that, they seem to channel Hugo to a surprising degree. These two things don’t seem to go together – why would Hugo put his own musings in the mouth of a drunk? To me, it seems like having a drunk character to work with loosens Hugo’s own inhibitions as much as the character’s. He lets it be time to indulge in verbal play.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. La nuit commence à se faire sur Grantaire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: Night begins to descend upon Grantaire
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: Pulling up paving stones and appropriating random objects to build barricades are classic moves in Paris, and the former, especially, has become a symbolic one. Also in May 1968, in addition to the quote they borrowed from Bahorel a few chapters back, the protest movements used the phrase “Sous les pavés, la plage” (“Under the paving stones, the beach”). It’s disputed whether or not the phrase originated with May 68, but it’s definitely associated with it, and it speaks to our guys too: the disruption of pulling up the stones gives hope of rest and reward on the other side. Meanwhile, as most of our friends build the barricade, Grantaire gets drunker, but that doesn’t mean he doesn’t want to be part of things at the barricade. And yet, Enjolras can’t see the value of his loyalty. We might – gasp – compare Enjolras’s strictness on this point to Javert’s strict adherence to the law. Even in his drunken state, even as he literally passes out, Grantaire knows Enjolras is wrong to count him out. And he’s sure that Enjolras will come to understand too.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Essai de consolation sur la veuve Hucheloup
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: An Attempt to console the Widow Hucheloup
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: Much of this chapter is about building energy and anticipation for the coming battle. We see them busy themselves with preparations, while Gavroche rallies the troops verbally. The way it’s written builds energy and excitement too, as we jump from one area to another, and one activity to another. But there’s a subtle critique of all of this embedded in the part of the chapter highlighted by its title: Mme Hucheloup, owner of Corinthe, is not on board with any of this, and isn’t convinced by Courfeyrac. And why would she be? She’s just trying to keep her business running, and even if this uprising succeeds, it’s not at all clear that this won’t do more harm than good to her personally. Having a better government is a fine idea, but she frankly doesn’t have the luxury of being concerned with it. And yet, because of an accident of Parisian geography and the revolutionaries’ caprice, she finds herself as much at the center of this as them. Shouldn’t she have had a choice?
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: What was a buzz of excitement yesterday gets a bit more real today. Putting the whimsy of youth into building a barricade in front of your favorite bar is one thing. Fun times. But here, they’re thinking about real tactics, balancing defense with preserving a line of retreat. And they’re distributing ammunition that they might really have to use. It’s not that anything about their plans has changed, but the tone sure has. Government forces will come – the alarm that’s calling them (probably bells) provides the background soundscape, and the gravity of both the sound and what it means sets the tone of their waiting.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: This is one of a handful of chapters that got some phrases inserted directly into the original lyrics for the musical. (You can hear them starting at about 1:07 here: https://youtu.be/glN 0K cgw8?si=f8Um-YNQBb0OV9rJ ) It’s the song that would become “Drink with _ _ Me” in the English version. (That clip is from the original French concept album, which is an interesting listen if you know the show today!) The reasons why they didn’t need to change much may be obvious – this is already a lyrical moment of nostalgia, of appreciating the pleasures of life before facing its horrors. The theatricality of Hugo’s writing, in the way he manages the rhythm and emotional folw of the action, makes this kind of thing more likely, and is probably why this book makes a good musical in the first place. But this is one of the moments that comes through most powerfully on the stage – down to the red flag with the light shining on it on top of the barricade.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: The Man recruited in the Rue des Billettes
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep44 - IV,12,i-viii - What Barricades are Made Of
entries.commentary_2025: Told you we’d see this guy again. Did you know who he was last week when we first saw him join the insurrection? Of course, by now we’re used to the kind of coincidence that would have *this* police officer show up in the middle of the action. Of all the barricades in all the insurrections in all the world….. That’s something we have to just let go of about this novel, if we intend to enjoy it. The world of its characters is small, and they keep running into each other. But Javert is also a bit difefrent – he’s almost allegorical, more than any other character; he’s the embodiment of the law. When he shows up, we have to think of it on a symbolic level as well. Here, behind the barricade, Javert is immediately bound, and Enjolras declares himself a judge, not an assassin. The laws of the state that Javert supports(/represents) are not in force here, and a new system of crimes and punishments has taken over. Gavroche sums this up succinctly, drawing on an image that terrified the little boys during their night in his elephant, of a cat being overcome by animals that are normally its prey.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: Many Interrogation Points with Regard to a Certain Le Cabuc, whose Name may not have been Le Cabuc

Javert lost his trail then, but we saw him outside the rue Plumet gate. There was speculation after the ambush that he was a police informant, and that he was released as a reward – without Javert’s knowledge of course, because he would never tolerate such a thing! entries.french_title: 1. De la rue Plumet au quartier Saint-Denis
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: From the Rue Plumet to the Quartier Saint-Denis
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: What a very strange way to get from one part of this Part IV (titled “L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis”) to the other. In a sense, it’s a pretty typical narrative device – we’re following a character as he moves physically, and psychologically, between these spaces. And the itinerary we follow is realistic – it’s possible to more or less trace this route on period maps. But the way Hugo executes it here is striking in its embrace of the other-worldly feeling of Paris during an uprising. We’ve been seeing the uprising so far from the inside, watching the barricade go up, and following the characters who are, for now at least, in the driver’s seat. But that’s not Marius. Contrary to the idea created by many an adaptation, he is very much an outsider to this uprising. So this hallucinatory experience, the strangeness of Paris in revolt and of the people who populate it, is an outsider’s impression.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: This chapter title is a direct reference to Hugo’s famous novel from 30 years earlier, Notre-Dame de _ Paris , which included a chapter titled “Paris à vol d’oiseau.” There, the “bird’s-eye view” provided the _ social geography of Paris in 1491, with commerce north of the Seine, the university south of it, and the cathedral on the island in the middle. This “owl’s-eye view” shows us the social geography of Paris on the night of June 5, 1832, in concentric circles, with the uprising around Les Halles and the government forces surrounding them. We also, in a sense, reverse in this chapter the irreversible journey that Marius made in the last one, into a dark abyss that he does not expect, or hope, to leave alive. Perhaps thanks to the owl’s ability to take flight, this chapter starts in that abyss and moves back outward, but only to show us the deadly standoff that is underway.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: So this is the question isn’t it? Who is the enemy? Who is “us” and who is “them?” When is taking up arms the right thing to do? Hugo has covered this, in a way, in defining an insurrection, and in another way, at Waterloo. But now, it’s human-sized: Marius has two small pistols in his pocket, and he has to decide whether or not to use them, tonight. And, since the human in question is Marius, he starts from a point that’s a bit myopic, thinking about it through essentially two other humans: his father, and Napoleon. Hugo can’t keep it human-sized, though, so we get another of the vast and dizzying scenes of introspection that make moments of dilemma and decision in this book so intense. Part of that (always) is a visionary moment of clarity, a flash of understanding, that brings him to what feels, at least, like an answer. But it hasn’t translated to action yet, as Hugo says it must. We’re left with Marius’s gaze on a man whose death was far less well-thought-out than this.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: Another massive reality check, as our characters see the first violence of the type they came here expecting. It’s a real army that’s come to face them. But at the same time, there’s something unreal about it, a strangeness that wouldn’t be there in daylight. The flashes of reflection of the bayonets and rifle barrels in the otherwise crushing darkness, the efefcts of the sound seeming to come from nothing. Much as he did as we followed Marius across Paris toward the barricade, Hugo achieves this by focusing on the moment-to-moment sensation, without interpreting it – a fairly postmodern move! And afterward, there’s the fallen flag. Climbing back up to the top of the barricade, into the line of fire, to replace it, is a mission from which the volunteer shouldn’t expect to return.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: After he lost everything he had, and gazing into utter desperation, it’s hard not to think that this has always been the reason why Mabeuf came to the barricade. The Mabeuf we see here bears little resemblance to the Mabeuf we met in Part III. Like others, the depths of poverty mean he couldn’t even afofrd to be who he was. Where that Mabeuf avoided politics, he espouses a radical position; where that Mabeuf fled gunfire, he goes toward it. The result, though, can serve a new purpose: he can become a symbol for the revolutionaries. For them, he’s a connection to the original French Revolution. It is entirely imagined, of course, that he was a Conventionist, that he voted for the death of Louis XVI. But that fiction is now more important than the reality that Courfeyrac shares with Enjolras.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. Gavroche aurait mieux fait d'accepter la carabine d'Enjolras
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: Gavroche would have done better to accept Enjolras' Carbine
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: I’ve read this book a bunch of times, and something was REALLY difefrent for me today. Previously, I’ve always felt that the government forces were cartoonishly evil, not really characters, and that was a weakness in the believability of this section. In 2025, I somehow don’t feel that way anymore. 🤷‍♀️ Part-time soldiers from the ‘burbs coming at a child like this seems…. oddly more believable for some reason…. Aaanyway, it looks like Marius decided to use those pistols! And thank goodness. Gavroche was in a tight spot because Javert hadn’t been carrying a loaded weapon – reasonable, as he didn’t intend to fight. But let’s not forget that it WAS Javert’s weapons that saved the day in this scene: the two loaded pistols that he gave Marius months ago to fire as a signal during the ambush. Despite his intention, Javert contributed to the insurrectionists’ cause.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: In which our heroes are also having a No Kings protest! This is a scene that I was SO PLEASED to see reincorporated in the 2012 film version of the musical – and it’s easy to see here why it’s more efefctive on film than it might be on stage. Marius’s arrival was just in time for Courfeyrac and Gavroche, and now, it turns out, for the barricade as a whole. Like Mabeuf, he came here out of despair, seeking death, and like Mabeuf, that gives him a kind of power that self-preservation would make impossible. Marius, though, uses it to intimidate the government soldiers. If he’s less afraid to die, he’s more dangerous and more powerful, even if – especially if – they have the numbers. Also like Mabeuf, true belief in the cause is secondary at best – for Mabeuf, it was more distant than that. Marius did think through the morality of participating in this and conclude it was a battle worth fighting. But mostly, this is about saving his friends, and using what he has – his desperation itself – to do it.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Fin des vers de Jean Prouvaire
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: End of the Verses of Jean Prouvaire
entries.french_volume: Partie 4. L'idylle rue Plumet et l'épopée rue Saint-Denis
entries.companion_episode: Ep45 - IV,13,i - IV,14,v - The Will to Die
entries.commentary_2025: I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the first victims of this insurrection are mostly the ones who pose the least actual danger to the people in power. (Exception: Bahorel). Jean Prouvaire was the artist and dreamer of the group, the gentlest possible version of a revolutionary. He was still one of them – he wasn’t like Mabeuf, who didn’t really have a commitment to the political cause – but Jean Prouvaire got here via feeling and sensitivity. There was a lot of Hugo in this character too: a thinker, a writer. But then, that’s true of a lot of these characters! Marius, of course, remains at the top of that list. Hugo didn’t ever play the role in an insurrection that Marius does here, but if he did, it’s not hard to imagine him sharing this deep ambivalence.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: The Agony of Death after the Agony of Life

entries.commentary_2025: 😭 Éponine said she wasn’t afraid to die, when she was facing down Patron-Minette at the rue Plumet gate, and she also described the “agony” of her life that this chapter title refers to. Because of that – because she was brave, and (sort of) made her own choices, even this one – it’s not necessarily the end of her life that feels so tragic here. Although, of course it is. The specific thing that feels tragic is the unrequited love, and the contradictory and deadly choices it drives her to, beyond what even she understands. (We’ll look more at that lack of understanding tomorrow.) I say she “sort of” made her own choices because, while she wasn’t doing anyone else’s bidding, and she stood up to her father, she wasn’t able to make entirely coherent and rational plans either. And the result is that she both drives Marius into danger and dies trying to rescue him from it. All she wants, in the end, is for her death to matter to him, even if it matters to no one else, including herself.

entries.commentary_2025: The explanation of Éponine’s actions now, after her death, reflects the obscurity that she lived under, which was too deep to make her even this coherent while she was alive. She did have a plan, in defiance of her father and of Marius, in response to her own wishes. That’s more agency and independence than any other woman in this book! But her feelings and wishes are confused. Defying her father means protecting the couple she wants to separate, and while she loves Marius, she tempts him into this death trap at the barricade, but then dies saving him. Another character – notably, Jean Valjean or Marius (both male) – might observe these contradictions and work through them philosophically in a sweeping tempest in a skull of introspection. But for Éponine, all these impulses can exist together, and they don’t need resolution. When she told the bandits at the gate that she was “everyone,” she wasn’t kidding! For us as readers and for the characters who meet her – especially, but not exclusively, in these last few days – she is mysterious. The way she speaks, as well as her actions, only provide glimpses of what’s inside, but we assume there’s more, that the riddles have an answer. This, from beyond the grave, is as clear it will be.

entries.commentary_2025: The first thing that’s interesting here is the handwriting in the mirror and the optical illusion. Reversed writing that is readable in a mirror is an old trick – DaVinci famously used it – and Hugo was fascinated by optical illusions and things that aren’t as they appear. In this scene, though, it creates a very postmodern situation, where the devastating reality of Cosette being in love seems both real and not real. Then, there’s a second big idea: Jean Valjean’s reaction. Everything we see about Jean Valjean watching Cosette grow up and get married is influenced by Hugo’s own life. (Almost everything: Hugo was FAR less lonely and did have other loves in his life, so the uncomfortable double-speak around the ways Jean Valjean loves Cosette may be more distant from Hugo’s experience.) Hugo’s daughter Léopoldine hid her romance with the man who would become her husband from her father at first, and other members of the family helped her. Then, after he was finally asked for his permission and, at length, gave it, the young couple drowned together in a boating accident a few months after the wedding in 1843. The anguish of all of that – not just the feelings of betrayal from his family’s secrecy, but also the profound grief that would follow – influences what we will start to see here. He wasn’t enthusiastic about his daughter growing up and getting married as it was happening, but two decades later, as he was writing this into Jean Valjean’s story, we can feel the anticipated grief. And the crushing despair that it causes, followed by him asking where the fighting is, just as Mabeuf did, is chilling. He hasn’t left for the barricade yet, though. This new tempest in a skull rages on.

entries.commentary_2025: As far as the gamin Gavroche is concerned, the regime has changed, the new revolution would like the lamps OUT, and nothing is going to change his mind! This is not the frist time that Jean Valjean, in the first efefcts of a shock to the way he sees the world, has met a young boy. The last time was Petit-Gervais, back in I, 2, 13, our January 27. Then, he didn’t give the boy money – he stole from him. But a lot has changed since then: he’s learned the lessons of the Bishop, and Montreuil-sur-mer, Fantine, and Champmathieu, and the nuns of Petit-Picpus. Even now, in crisis, he responds to a hungry child with compassion – so how will he respond to the crisis?

entries.commentary_2025: Yesterday, we recognized an echo of Petit-Gervais in Jean Valjean’s encounter with Gavroche, but said it was reversed – instead of stealing from him, he gave him 5 francs. Now, we see it might not have been as reversed as we thought – Jean Valjean recognizes theft in the way he misled Gavroche to get the letter from him. It would have been quite normal at this time for a father to read letters addressed to his teenaged daughter. But he lied, and took something that he might not have been given otherwise. And then, when he learns from the letter that Marius expects to die at the barricade, we hear another echo: the Champmathieu afafir. Back then – I, 7, 3, our Feb. 26 – he realized he only needed to let things be, and his empty place in prison would be filled, and he’d be free. Here, he deploys the same logic: he only needs to let things be, and the man who is about to take Cosette away will be gone, and he’ll have what he wants. Does he hear that echo, as he puts on his National Guard uniform and heads for the barricade?

entries.commentary_2025: The soldiers in this chapter are such bufofons. And similar to what I said a few days ago, their overreaction to a child making a racket in the street used to seem exaggerated to me. It doesn’t anymore. What Hugo sees and shows, in several of these scenes where police or other government forces are interacting with the least threatening revolutionary imaginable, is the soldiers’ fear. They’re terrified, not of Gavroche himself, but of what he represents: the spirit of revolution, the willingness to defy their authority. They’re used to being in charge, and don’t know what to do otherwise. Meanwhile, we have another of Gavroche’s songs here – singing about women in a way that he can’t possibly understand, and about revolution in a way that he very much seems to. The racket he makes may be disruptive, and it may leave the bourgeois shaking in their beds, but it’s not explicitly threatening – it’s joyful.

entries.french_title: 1. La Charybde du faubourg Saint-Antoine et la Scylla du faubourg du Temple
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Charybdis of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and the Scylla of the Faubourg du Temple
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: Before we jump into this chapter: welcome to Part V, the third section (chapter, book, or part) of the novel titled “Jean Valjean!” This is the home stretch! Now on to a bit of background about the history he’s talking about here, the June 1848 uprising in Paris. The July Monarchy (the government that had been in place since 1830) was overthrown in February 1848, and the Second Republic had been established. Then, in June 1848, the National Assembly voted to abolish the “ateliers nationaux,” by which the government provided work for unemployed laborers. Laborers, of course, were displeased, and there was an uprising that looked a lot like the one we’re following in this novel – barricades, etc. Hugo, who at the time was an elected member of the National Assembly, was in the fray – on the government side. So, you can see why he might want us to see that incident as difefrent from this one! But the distinction he makes also aligns with the distinction he made between riot and insurrection a few weeks ago. In 1848, they were rising up against a republic, but in 1832, it was against a king. Otherwise, the two barricades described here are best read, I think, as metaphors for the extremes that revolution should avoid like Charybdis and Scylla. On one hand, the Saint-Antoine barricade was all feeling, and it was chaos. On the other, the Temple barricade was all precision, and it was murderous.

entries.french_title: 2. Que faire dans l'abîme à moins que l'on ne cause?
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: What Is to Be Done in the Abyss if One Does Not Converse
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: The characters haven’t yet given up hope, but the narrator has sort of given up on their behalf: the mention of the final hours of the Saint-Merry barricade, the use of the word “abyss” in the chapter title. Of course, Hugo and his readers know how this uprising is going to end, whereas the characters don’t. For now, they wait. And as they wait, they work, and prepare, and think, and chat. They reflect on political violence, justice, and, well, cats. / But that’s not random either. Remember what Gavroche said to Javert after he exposed him and the revolutionaries had tied him up? “The mouse has caught the cat,” he said. Javert had been a predator, pursuing people to arrest like a cat pursues a mouse, but then the roles reversed. The rats in Gavroche’s elephant ofefred one way that could end: those rats ate the cat that Gavroche had brought in to control them. But now, without realizing the metaphor he’s participating in, Joly flips the script back. Cats hunt mice. In the end, that’s the way it’s most likely to go.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: Now, a more honest assessment of their chances takes hold among the insurgents – they are coming to understand what has been obvious all along for us, with the benefit of hindsight. And, Hugo makes sure that hindsight is top of mind for us: twice more, he refers to that other barricade, at Saint-Merry, “Jeanne’s” barricade. / Plus, Hugo said pointedly a few chapters back (IV, 11, 6) that our group passed up Saint-Merry before ending up at the rue de la Chanvrerie. This barricade has always been a sort of fictional double of that one, so perhaps it’s worth a moment to understand what Hugo’s original readers would have known about this Jeanne. Charles Jeanne was the leader of the last barricade to be overtaken in the June 1832 uprising, on the rue Saint-Martin, in the Saint-Merry (or Merri) neighborhood. He had also participated in the 1830 Revolution, and probably imagined, as many did, that this action would complete what was left unfinished then, and establish a republic. He had about 100 men defending that barricade. Most of them died, but Jeanne himself did not; he was given a high-profile trial, imprisoned and died in prison a few years later. If our fictional barricade is following a path that parallels that one, then maybe there is a glimmer of hope – not that they’ll succeed, but that some of them will survive. But they don’t seem to think so anymore, and are willing to defy until death, just as Jeanne had been.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Cinq de moins, un de plus
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: A few days ago (in IV, 15, 3), we wondered if Jean Valjean understood the morality of “letting things be” as he put on his National Guard uniform and headed for the barricade. Now we see: of COURSE he did. At some level, didn’t we know that? He certainly wasn’t going to join the ranks of the National Guard. Combeferre puts it best: he’s a man who saves others. He was never going to do anything else. I always find that moment a bit funny, actually – not on the first read-through, but once you know it’s going to end up here. It’s like Hugo was pointing out that this COULD have been another long tempest in a skull, with a moral dilemma to pick apart, but we’ve done that – kind of a lot. “See above,” he seemed to be saying. Meanwhile, Combeferre is using a similar logic here to a part of what we saw in that original tempest in a skull, during the Champmathieu afafir. Self-sacrifcie, paradoxically, can be selfish. The images that Combeferre evokes are images we recognize from the rest of the novel: women and children with no means of support, surviving as they can, or dying from hunger. When that was Fantine, her means of support was taken from her by a more obvious kind of selfsihness: Tholomyès prioritizing his respectable middle-class future. These men are pursuing a difefrent kind of glory, and it’s one that is covered in ideas of heroism, but the result for people who depend on them is the same. And so, five men are identified to leave, and Jean Valjean arrives just in time to make sure all 5 get out. We still don’t know what that will mean for Marius, but Jean Valjean’s fate is now tied to the barricade too.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Quel horizon on voit du haut de la barricade
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: The Horizon Which One Beholds from the Summit of a Barricade
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: By the time he wrote Les Misérables (but not so much in 1832, or even 1848), the ideas you see Enjolras express here were Hugo’s own. He was a 19th-century guy, and the 19th century believed in progress. Technological, political, and social life would continue to get better. The sky was the limit. So he was (here and elsewhere) just a LIIIITLE off, in terms of what the 20th century would actually bring. Didn’t account for our ability to ignore good political and social ideas, or use technology to destroy each other. 🤷‍♀️But for Enjolras, in this moment, none of that is the point, because he and his friends don’t expect to see the next day, never mind the next century. For him, this is all a question of what their sacrifice is for. They came here hoping to overthrow their current government and establish a republic, and it now seems they’ve failed. But if they’re actually here, as Enjolras puts it, to pay a toll – if even their death helps move the world toward the future he envisions – then they’ve already won. In that case, what they’re doing isn’t a military act, it’s a mystical one.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: Talk about awkward moments with your girlfriend’s father! Marius doesn’t even know if “M. Fauchelevent” recognizes him, or if he knows about the time spent with Cosette in her garden…. And now they might have to die together. And, Marius has vouched for him, so he can’t pretend he doesn’t know him. Like, what does one SAY in this situation? 😳 Javert, meanwhile, isn’t saying much, but we have enough here to know that he’s still the same ol’ Javert. (And that will be important later!) He knows they plan to kill him, but he’s also utterly certain that he’s in the right. He gives them orders with clarity and certainty, in the imperative, just as if he were still acting as a police officer. EXCEPT: he uses the respectful “vous” forms with Enjolras, which he would never do as an officer speaking to someone he considered a criminal. (This change was conspicuous when Madeleine became Jean Valjean.) Enjolras responds with the “tu” forms. The revolutionaries use “tu” amongst themselves out of friendship and familiarity, but with Javert, it creates a hierarchy. Jean Valjean, also an unknown, was called “vous” when he arrived at the barricade, which is normal to show respect for a stranger. Javert is now being treated as the criminal. But he still lives in the rigid, black & white world he has always lived in. His finding it “simple” that Jean Valjean would be in this place speaks volumes on that point. It’s also “simple” that he would be in the position he’s in here, in a place where rioters and criminals are in charge. In a world with only two neatly-divided sides, this is how it goes when you’re on the wrong one. Not only does he not doubt himself because of it: for him, being a criminal in this place, even if he dies for it, is only further proof of his righteousness in the world that matters. So, he’s calm and certain, awaiting what must come.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: We started Part V by examining two barricades from 1848, mostly as metaphors. One was a big chaotic pile of junk, built of the people’s feeling. The other was built of paving stones, so straight and square it was as if a stonemason had built it, and it was precise and deadly. This barricade resembles both of them, one in front of the other. The inside, toward the insurgents, is a wall of paving stones, but they’ve stacked a jumble of softer stuff (mostly wooden) in front of it. It’s this hybrid construction that makes it hold up so well against cannonfire: the pile of wooden objects absorbs the energy and deadens the ball, and the stone wall keeps broken splinters from reaching the people inside. Hybridity is a hallmark of good in this book. Jean Valjean learned this early on, and has exemplifeid it since.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 8. Les artilleurs se font prendre au sérieux
entries.english_hapgood_title: 8: The Artillery-men Compel People to Take Them Seriously
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: The government forces didn’t take long to find a way around the advantage that the barricade’s construction gave it yesterday. It’s clever, and deadly, and the countermeasure that Enjolras takes is not to be taken lightly. This isn’t the first time they’ve fired at the attacking enemy, and it’s not like they didn’t come here expecting to do violence. Previously, their tactic was to fire a volley, all at once, into the enemy line. If they hit anyone (and the first time, they didn’t) they wouldn’t know who had killed whom. It was impersonal. By contrast, the conversation that Enjolras and Combeferre have here shows us the difefrence between that tactic and this one. Enjolras has time to examine this young man closely as he aims and fires and chooses to end his life. That is a WHOLE difefrent thing. It’s more like the action he took in executing Le Cabuc, and Enjolras seems similarly troubled by it, even as he, also similarly, sees it as his duty. But there’s another layer here, and that’s this young man’s similarity to Enjolras. They even look alike. That, plus the fact that the gun captain is also (unlike Le Cabuc) doing what he sees as his duty, makes this moment especially poignant.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: We’ve noted many an occasion in this book when Hugo is strikingly ahead of his time, and seems to exhibit types of thinking that would not be theorized for decades after him. The way he discusses Cosette here is not one of those. He spends a page telling you all the things he mustn’t tell you, and that a man (which he is) mustn’t even see or know, about the interior of a young girl’s bedroom and morning routine. 🙄 And he imagines Cosette – who has been through some things, and whom he’s described as intrepid and seeing her beauty as a weapon – afraid of her own unclothed reflection in the mirror because of her extreme virginity. 🙄🙄But leaving aside all of that, we do see some of her buoyant spirit here: her bouts of sadness don’t last, and she maintains hope that she will see Marius again. Her relationship to recent events is compared more or less explicitly to both Jean Valjean’s and Marius’s, and she, arguably, handles them the best. Where Marius fell into despair at their separation, she sees it as temporary – it MUST be, they love each other so. Where Jean Valjean was troubled by his mind’s resistance to seeing reality via the blotter reflected in the mirror, Cosette takes her hope as a certainty. Now, we could talk about how she’s pushing away a whole bunch of evidence. But from another point of view, we could say that she’s filling in her information gaps with optimism. We’ll see how these difefrent responses serve each character. But in this moment, there’s something to be said for her resilience.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 11. Le coup de fusil qui ne manque rien et qui ne tue personne
entries.english_hapgood_title: 11: The Shot Which Misses Nothing and Kills No One
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: Jean Valjean really is kinda like a superhero. Impossibly accurate aim with two difefrent unfamiliar 19th-century firearms is only one of his superpowers. He’s also remarkably strong, has an astounding tolerance for pain, is a social chameleon, has the ingenuity of MacGyver, and is generally super smart. And, he uses his powers heroically. A few chapters ago, he was called “a man who saves others,” and that continues here, even as he defends the barricade. Unlike Le Cabuc, who took the insurrection as a chance to kill with impunity (or so he thought), Jean Valjean refrains from killing, even when it might have been excused, at least by Enjolras. He helps save the lives of the men behind the barricade, at least for a bit longer, but he also saves the enemy’s rooftop spies – from what anyone else would likely have done.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: The first part of this short chapter is a bit like a mini digression, here in the middle of the action. The topic is MUCH larger than the length of the passage would suggest: the dominant culture in France in this period. One of the biggest changes that the 19th century brought to France, which might go unnoticed to us today as it’s the water we’re swimming in, was an individualistic, capitalistic culture where power came from money, not noble birth. Early in his life, Hugo critiqued this as a pale reflection of the noble values of the past, but by the time he wrote Les Misérables, he was more inclined to critique it as unworthy of the future that Enjolras described a few days ago. This least worthy of cultures, then, where armies fight to defend piles of money rather than either the king or the people, is the one attacking the barricade. And, predictably, it’s not a very competent attack. Individualism is no good in a military situation like this, and Fannicot shows us why. But Hugo doesn’t let us take courage from this on behalf of our insurgents: they’re vastly outnumbered and outarmed. Fannicot and his men will be easily replaced.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: What insurrectionists hope for in an uprising like this is that more and more people will join them, and they’ll gradually come to occupy enough of the city to be able to make demands. That’s why they build barricades: to hold a position until more people join their cause. But the pressures on a barricaded section of the city are those we’ve already seen: assault from a vastly larger force outside, and limited resources inside. It’s a game of timing: will their food and ammunition hold out long enough for enough of the people to rise up to face the army? So they look for any sign that they have support beyond the walls of the barricade, even though by now, hope is slim.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 14. Où on lira le nom de la maîtresse d'Enjolras
entries.english_hapgood_title: 14: Wherein Will Appear the Name of Enjolras' Mistress
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: Maybe this is the other reason why a love story belonged in Les Misérables: because alongside sufefring and politics, love drives our characters to this point. Which is why Bossuet is surprised at Enjolras’s revolutionary fervor, since there’s no woman in his life to motivate him. Like many of this novel’s Good Guys, notably Jean Valjean – as well as its “Good” Guy, Javert – Enjolras seems to transcend romance and sexuality. In fact, we’ve compared him to Javert before, in his single-minded focus on his ideals. And here, that’s the name of the mistress he mutters: Patria, the root word of “patriotic.” As Javert is the law incarnate, lover of order and hierarchy, Enjolras is the revolution incarnate, lover of what he dreams his country can be. And neither is human enough for sex.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: 😭😭😭 It’s hard to say why this event is here in this way. It goes for the pain emotionally, certainly. And it gives Gavroche a moment where he can show us that he has agency in joining the barricade in its fate. It also makes the National Guard soldiers look especially cruel, as Hugo specifies that they can see the child through the smoke as they fire on him. And, of course, it’s a theatrical moment, written by an experienced playwright. Gavroche, like many of his other memorable characters, gets a curtain call. And that moment isn’t just for Gavroche: to the extent that he’s been the hopeful spirit of this uprising, it’s the curtain call for that spirit too. As he does all this, Gavroche remains very much the gamin, frolicking and singing in spite of grave danger, and thumbing his nose at the army. And, at the same time, there’s a reminder of his origins, as he collects items of value from the bodies of fallen soldiers, just as his father did at Waterloo. But Gavroche makes this action his own, and turns it to good.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 16. Comment de frère on devient père
entries.english_hapgood_title: 16: How from a Brother One Becomes a Father
entries.french_book: Livre 1. La Guerre entre quatre murs
entries.commentary_2025: We cut away from the barricade a few chapters ago to check in on Cosette, who was in a beautiful, peaceful setting, in contrast to the violence of the insurrection. Now, a few hours later in the story’s chronology, we’re appreciating this lovely early-June morning from a difefrent perspective, while being reminded not to forget human sufefring. And we can’t, because Hugo reminds us not only that Gavroche’s little boys are hungry, but that they’re the only hungry beings in this garden. Thanks to that beautiful spring morning, all the other creatures are well fed. The children going hungry in this way is what’s unnatural here. It’s an odd take on the Biblical instruction not to worry about what you’ll eat, and to consider how God feeds the birds of the air, etc. Consider the birds of the air, Hugo seems to say, but then consider these little boys. Who will feed them? Not this bourgeois dad, that’s for sure. Hugo says he “might” be the guy Marius overheard a year ago (III, 6, 4, our July 10), telling his son to avoid both despotism and anarchy. As a good moderate, he didn’t join the force that just killed Gavroche, but he dressed his son up as one of them for more empty hypocrisy: be content with little, but you don’t have to be hungry to eat cake! (Just ask Marie Antoinette!) The hungry little boys, meanwhile, are “the beginning” of “anarchy.” In a sense, he’s not wrong: letting kids starve does make them more likely to be displeased with the status quo. Can you blame them? And the older brother’s final line here is more revolutionary than it sounds; I hope your translation did it justice. Literally, it’s “stick this in your rifle.” He does what Gavroche was just doing – finding something for his companion to stick in his “rifle” – while repeating the phrase Gavroche said to him when he fed him his first meal as a gamin. He not only imitates this gamin father figure, but he also takes on the spirit of revolution that Gavroche represented.
