entries.commentary_2025: In the unreal reality of the barricade, Enjolras has recognized that the end is coming, and he’s making preparations for them to hold out inside Corinthe for as long as they can. Part of that is ensuring that Javert can’t get out alive if they can’t – his end has come too, and he’s characteristically stoic about it. Even when Jean Valjean asks for the privilege of executing him – and uses a fairly graphic phrase to do so – Javert still seems as calm as he has all along, as if all is in order. To him, the world of chaos behind the barricade is exactly the sort of place where someone like Jean Valjean would execute someone like him. All is, paradoxically, still in order this way. As he’s escorted to the place where he expects to die, he is reassured that he’s right – that even if he got caught on the wrong side of it, the order that holds the world together is as he has always believed.

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is so interesting. But let’s start with the easy part, which is Marius ALWAYS misunderstanding EVERYTHING. This is a particularly significant case: everyone behind the barricade assumes they’re going to die, and Javert is being held prisoner by Marius’s side in this fight, but he wants to intervene to save him? And he’s seen Jean Valjean avoid killing already here. So now he assumes that Jean Valjean is someone Javert needs to be rescued from? Aaaanyway… The really interesting part is, clearly, the conversation between Jean Valjean and Javert. Jean Valjean’s act of mercy is maybe not surprising by this point, but it is a stroke of brilliance. Death, right now, is something that Javert can face with his dignity, his sense of superiority, and his identity intact. What Jean Valjean does here is the one thing that’s worse. We’ll see a lot more about why. But the most interesting, most telling moment, is when Javert tries to refuse his mercy, and asks Jean Valjean to kill him instead. Jean Valjean has already given Javert the info he needs to arrest him, to set the world back in order. As he crosses back over the barricade into the world he knows, he can resume his duty, and pursue this criminal. But something has changed. We see it first when he switches to the formal “vous” form of address with Jean Valjean, which he would never use with a criminal, without realizing he’s done it. Whatever the change is that this moment has made in Javert, he would rather die than face it.

entries.commentary_2025: What’s the point of this uprising if it’s so completely doomed to failure? That is certainly the point of view of most of the residents of Paris, who have not decided to join the cause. And I think Hugo is sincere when he says he understands how people would choose not to sacrifice themselves on the barricade. After all, he never did. And if they won’t, it’s because they have something to lose. What makes (and has made, for those who have already made their sacrifice) our characters so powerful/dangerous is that they have nothing to lose. Éponine, Marius, Mabeuf, to some extent Gavroche – all have come here in part because it’s the one thing they have left. This is what they think their life is for. And Hugo sets that fact in the grandest possible perspectives: the law of the universe is progress, and this is what it takes. Participating in this sort of uprising, even if it’s the losing side, is responding to a universal law, to the general thrust of humanity. It’s also the law of this book, he declares, despite evidence to the contrary, much of which is coming in the next few chapters. He uses an eclipse as a metaphor: it might get apocalyptically dark, but the sun is still there. Progress IS, no matter how a particular story ends. And, for those of us who feel like we’re living in a dark world right now, let’s remember that Hugo wrote these optimistic words in exile, from an authoritarian regime. He was living in one of these eclipses, as are we, and he thought the “grave in exile” that he mentions could easily be his. It wasn’t. He was buried in the Third French Republic.

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo was a lot more aware of the traditions of epic literature than most of us are today. He referred to them in his theoretical work, and drew on it for some of his own long-form poetry.He understood that the modern novel was something difefrent, and we’ve seen many places where he capitalizes on the (then fairly new) conventions of that genre. But at Waterloo, and now again here, we see him dip into the epic – after all, battle is where that genre excelled. The difefrence here is that the usual external trappings of epic glory are replaced by the glory of our heroes’ ideals. It’s their cause and their courage, not the splendor of their deeds or their armor or their weapons, that we admire. The deaths of some characters that we have come to know personally – Courfeyrac in particular for me – are painful, but Hugo doesn’t go for the pain with them as he has with others. Instead, he embeds them in a narrative mode that has a long tradition of making death valiant, glorious, and valuable in its own right, and all that rests on the cause they’re dying for.

entries.commentary_2025: If you’ve been wondering since March why we spent all that time on Waterloo, this is partly why. What’s happening in this chapter bears a striking resemblance to Hugo’s description of what happened at Hougomont, where a small group also defended a position in a building. And, the overall combination of glory and horror, the admiration of bravery without denying the hell that violence created, is much the same. Both battles are, in the short term, victories for the wrong side, for monarchy. But, of course, we’ve seen in both cases that Hugo thinks it’s more complicated than that. Waterloo cleared the way for progress that could never happen under Napoleon, and now the barricade pays a toll for entry into the future with its blood. Hugo believes persistently in the vision that Enjolras saw from atop the barricade. He won’t give up on that, even from exile, even from Paris under siege in 1870. Defeat is just one chapter in a very long story.

entries.commentary_2025: After all we’ve seen about this battle and the insurgents’ defeat, it’s not difficult to understand the value of what Grantaire does here. He may not have contributed much to their actual fight when they were hoping to win, to set the spark that would start the new revolution. But here, he contributes to the larger efofrt, to the blood sacrifice that pays the toll to the future. It’s not contradictory that, as he wakes up and understands what’s happening, the first thing he says is “Long live the republic” (“Vive la république”), before ofefring to die alongside its current best hope. In the cosmic landscape that Enjolras and Hugo have shown us, for the idea of republic to live on, its martyrs must die for it. And, of course, this gesture is also a personal one, of afefction and loyalty. His ofefr and Enjolras’s acceptance, resolve a tension that has been with us for as long as we’ve known these two. Just before Grantaire passed out drunk (IV, 12, 3), Enjolras included dying on the list of things that Grantaire was incapable of doing for the republic, to which he responded, “You’ll see.” Believing was also on the list, and Grantaire is certainly our skeptical nihilist, but he believes in Enjolras, and he always has. Nothing has changed for him in the 24 hours he’s been passed out. But Enjolras has come to understand that, at least in this revolution, the sacrifice is the point.

entries.commentary_2025: Several previous sections of this book come together brilliantly here. A couple of them are fairly obvious. One, the chapter mentions itself: Jean Valjean escaping with Cosette into the convent, which this replays sort of in reverse. Another is implied pretty clearly in the chapter title: Marius has been “taken prisoner” before – by Cosette, when she chose to walk by his bench in the Luxembourg garden, after realizing she was a war machine. Jean Valjean’s past is also here, not only in the superpowers of escaping it gave him, but also in the bagne itself, which is an “underground” space, like the metaphorical mines that represent the criminal world. We’ll spend the next week talking about underground tunnels, so I’ll wait to elaborate on that, and instead point out that the bagne was also compared to the convent while Jean Valjean was there. And, finally, much of Jean Valjean’s character to this point is in evidence: he’s here, silent, more skilled than anyone, and only interested in saving lives and helping the wounded. “A man who saves others,” he was called when he arrived. And the way he kept his eye on Marius, we can assume his goal was always to save him, which is also an act of self-sacrifice that we’ve only begun to understand..
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. La terre appauvrie par la mer
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Land Impoverished by the Sea
entries.commentary_2025: Of all the digressions in this novel, Waterloo gets attention because of its length, but this one stands out for the surface-level absurdity of its subject, especially at this point in the story. Not that it’s not clear why we’d talk about the sewers right now – Jean Valjean just disappeared into them – but is all of this *strictly* necessary? It might not surprise you by now that I’m going to say…. Yeah, probably. Or, if not necessary (what would that even mean in literature?), then important and enriching – like, say, fertilizer. For one thing, this is Hugo’s only real, practical proposal for a solution to the problems this book points out: better fertilizer means more food, and fewer hungry people. He also takes a new angle on an important theme of the novel: wasted potential. Something of value is lost, because people find it disgusting and fear the harm it might cause. That could be waste in the sewer, or it could be people, like the characters we’ve just seen take refuge there. Not that he doesn’t take the potential harm seriously: the 1832 uprising took place during a cholera outbreak, and, on the metaphorical level, this book includes Thénardier too. But like Jean Valjean’s nettles back in Part I, to discard something entirely because it has downsides is mostly a reflection on the person doing the discarding. The sewer is an underground space, like the mines in the Mines and Miners section. And remember, those mines were complex. Some miners worked for good, others worked selfishly. And the quintessential animal of the sewer is the rat – maybe like the ones that ate Gavroche’s cat, in that image that we came to see as revolutionary.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: The contents of the sewer may tell the truth, but this chapter title doesn’t – this isn’t actually much of a history of the sewer. It’s something much more interesting. Hugo starts, early in the chapter, by doing something we pointed to yesterday: he says that the sewer has housed people, of a particular sort – or, rather two. You may recognize them. It’s been a home to crime as well as social protest. Freedom of conscience, and theft. Principled rebels and unprincipled ones. These were the two categories in the “mines” back in part 3, united by the fact that they lived outside society. So the sewers, first of all, are those “mines,” incarnate in this real structure in Paris. But they’re something else too: “conscience” on a societal level. This book has been interested in deep dives into its characters’ consciences – Jean Valjean’s “Tempest in a Skull” comes to mind, but there are other examples, including some still to come. Delving into this physical space is like delving into those consciences – in fact, if it weren’t decades too early, I’d liken his description here to the Freudian unconscious. What’s in there is unseemly and chaotic, it’s what society wants to forget and be rid of, but it’s TRUE.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Hugo is probably exaggerating somewhat here about how little was known about the sewers under Parisians’ own feet before the 19th century. In some places, in fact, they weren’t under Parisians’ feet at all – they were open to above, either like gutters in the streets or repurposed natural small waterways. However, he’s right that they hadn’t been a rational, one-time city planning project, but rather a network of various drainage solutions that all wound up in the Seine. They also – and you’d NEVER know this based on this section, especially chapter 1 – contained far less 💩than you’re probably imagining. It was wastewater and the stuff that got washed away with it. Gross, sure, but less so. This is because, through the end of the 18th century, people were largely doing exactly what Hugo advocates for in ch. 1. But by 1862, it was falling into disfavor, and a modern system was taking over. In any event, his description of the old sewer here is doing two things: 1) contrasting with the sewer that was being built in Paris as he was writing this from exile, the one you can visit in Paris today… and 2) serving, once again, as a metaphor for the city’s conscience, or, as he puts it in this chapter, its remorse. This image of massive sewer backups is ofefred as a metaphor on two levels – remorse, which is individual, and anger, which brings to mind civil unrest, especially given where the story has just been. Now, it’s not just that what’s in there is true and unacknowledged, it’s also bound to come back, and insist on being dealt with, especially if the cause of the backup isn’t understood – and so, per Hugo, enter Bruneseau.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This is a lot more like a history of the sewer than chapter 2 was! Through Bruneseau’s eyes, Hugo takes us into this mysterious system that seemed to have grown there on its own. Bruneseau’s work is described as a “voyage of discovery,” and I think the analogy that implies is entirely intentional, if we take it on Hugo’s (19th-century) terms. Bruneseau’s project is to discover this chaotic, untamed thing, record it, and tame it. And like those other voyages of discovery, his object of study is less unknown than he makes it out to be. After all, people did build this sewer, and all those outcast types that he listed in chapter 2 have been hiding in there all along. It’s just that the guys in charge don’t understand it. The colonial analogy makes Bruneseau seem like less of a hero to us than Hugo meant it to. But we can think of his work through another analogy too – it’s a bit like what Hugo is doing in this book. He’s taking us, and especially his contemporary readers, into a world that is unfamiliar to us, but that they lived alongside every day. Both analogies are fairly limited – the sewer was a good hiding place, but it didn’t contain whole civilizations for the explorers to exploit. And where Bruneseau cleans up the sewer a bit but largely leaves it as it is, Hugo (along with many of his characters who just met their end) dreams of a world where most of what he describes in this book is just a bad memory.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Between when Hugo went into exile in the early 1850s and when he completed Les Misérables in 1862, his home city had been transformed. Napoleon III – of whom Hugo was a vocal opponent, hence the exile – ordered a massive modernization of Paris, both above and below ground. On balance, there was a lot of benefit from this for the health of the population. But Hugo, who couldn’t be sure he’d see Paris again at all, now knew for sure he’d never see the Paris where he spent his youth, as much of it had been built over. The same nuance applied to the sewer: the city was healthier for having better water and sewer systems. In fact, part of the immediate context of the 1832 uprising was a cholera outbreak, which modern infrastructures generally prevent. But Hugo still laments the loss of the history, the character, the authenticity of the old city, and its old sewer. The improvements don’t come without a sacrifice. And, of course, this all continues to operate as a metaphor too. Napoleon III’s Paris might be “respectable,” but the less respectable parts that it tries to hide – the things, and people, that have always hidden in the sewer – aren’t gone. As long as there is an underground – of crime, of revolution, and of people being tossed away and their value ignored – the more-respectable-looking city is just hypocrisy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: So why have we been reading about the sewers for a week? (Apart from, obviously, the setting for what’s coming next…) Hugo comes back now to the literal connection to the subject matter, and to its clearest metaphorical importance: washing away all this valuable stuff is wasted potential. But it’s also an image of what’s underground, what’s hiding beneath the respectable parts of the city – the things, and people, that MUST hide for the city to be respectable. It’s an image of the “mines and miners” who not only hide beneath the city’s surface, but work against what’s going on above, for selfsih ends or for revolutionary ones. It also reflects society itself, the history of the city and the legacy of its past. So it’s people whose lives are discarded like Fantine’s, who must hide in the dark like or Éponine, who undermine society like Thénardier or who work to remake it like Enjolras or Gavroche. And now Jean Valjean and Marius are in there too, and we will see which of these they become. So, yeah, the sewers kinda matter. 🤷‍♀️
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: Jean Valjean has disappeared into the sewer, and now, Hugo adds a metaphor: the sea, like the one that the man overboard fell into WAAAY back at the beginning of the novel, also to illustrate Jean Valjean’s situation. But the meaning of this dive into oblivion is radically difefrent – now, he’s escaping death, rather than waiting for it in a state of suspended animation. Where the man overboard, and Jean Valjean initially falling into the carceral system, meant slipping from life into living death, escaping society at this moment is more like taking refuge. Refuge from death, but not danger. He’s navigating unfamiliar tunnels in the dark, carrying a grown man on his back on slippery wet stone – and that’s when there are no floods or clogs or sinkholes, which we know there are! And, of course, the police. It is mentioned early in the chapter that they are likely to pursue insurgents into the sewers….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: Jean Valjean is skilled, but he also has moments when he gets pretty lucky – sometimes in the novel’s many implausible coincidences, and sometimes, in moments like this. Think of him escaping from Javert by climbing over the wall into the VERY convent where he had placed Fauchelevent years earlier. Or, think of the fact that, when Thénardier ambushed him, someone who knew him by sight and also wanted to protect Cosette was watching through the peephole. Hugo would – and in other places, does – chalk this up to Providence, not luck – a force that doesn’t seem interested in making things pleasant or easy, but does seem to look out for him in other ways. As difficult as Jean Valjean’s life has been, Hugo wants us to believe something higher is seeing him through to the end of his mission.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: A sneaky looking little guy trying to evade a cop, both people we “might” recognize? Who oh who could they be?? And if this police officer is who we think he is, he HATES losing track of a suspect like this. Hates when they disappear inexplicably into sewers just as much as into convents. Only this time, he’s worked out pretty quickly how it happened: the suspect’s got a key that should only be in the hands of an official. And that’s got to grate this officer’s cheese too. Hugo also connects the work of this mysterious officer with the whole apparatus of the state more directly here than he does elsewhere, in the wordplay about the clothing. Can’t help but feel like that is related to the violent exertion of state control we’ve just witnessed in the uprising. That is of a piece with small acts of policing like this one. Given who we suspect he was following, it’s hard to condemn him for trying to nab him. But the critique is of the system more broadly. The same system that did this is the same one that brought down the barricade, is the same one that arrested Fantine, is the same one that put Jean Valjean away for 19 years over a loaf of bread.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: The geographical detail of this trip may seem – let’s call it excessive – at times, but it pays of fin the middle of this chapter. Surely you noticed that the place where Jean Valjean stops to regroup is called Madeleine. Back when he first headed to the barricade, we noted that his temptation to act selfishly came in the form of wanting to “let things be,” just as it had in the Champmathieu afafir. Except then, his decision about what to do required a 20 page chapter detailing hours of internal struggle about whether to remain Madeleine or reinhabit the name Jean Valjean. This time, the solution was obvious. That was the last time we saw Madeleine – because from then on, what it meant to be Jean Valjen changed. Sure, he has false names that he uses to avoid arrest, but he has never alienated his true identity from himself again. Instead, that incident transformed Jean Valjean from a “hideous convict” into “a man who saves others.” As he continues to do here, in spite of his own feelings and wishes, carrying the instrument of his sacrifcie. We’ll see how well he understands that transformation. But we sure see it, to the point where, by now, we would never expect anything else from him. The surprise, in fact, is the hatred he has for Marius, not the tender care he takes of him, or the extraordinary efofrt he makes to save his life.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

That chapter, like this one, emphasized the specifci horror of being alive, but utterly without hope, waiting for an end that is slow to arrive. There, the man fell abruptly from a ship into the sea, and continued treading water; here he sinks slowly but certainly into quicksand. The man overboard was left behind by the ship he fell from, but the man sinking into the quicksand, especially in

entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: I insist all the time that Les Misérables – despite resemblances to authors like Balzac or Flaubert, who were contemporaries of Hugo – is not realism, and it’s a bit late and a bit gritty to be romanticism. Then what is it? Understanding a scene like this one is a way to approach answering that question (although the answer probably still won’t fit neatly into a 19th-century movement). So what just happened here? Is Jean Valjean just endowed with super-human strength, and knew how to use it in this situation that was set up to be unsurvivable? Maybe this is a superhero story. Was this just another lucky, dramatic, narrow escape? Maybe it’s a crime thriller. Did something magical or spiritual just happen? Is this a fantasy story with actual magic? Is it a religious story, in which divine providence intervenes directly? Was this experience – where Jean Valjean was, after all, alone in the dark – even real? Are we meant to read it all metaphorically, in spite of the technical detail? And if so, is it a social metaphor, the way we read it yesterday, where Jean Valjean’s triumphant story defies a vast, broken system? Is it a spiritual metaphor, with a strange hideous baptism followed by a “clarity in his soul,” or an image of a man collapsed under the “cross” he carries on his own via dolorosa? Or maybe it’s not so sophisticated as a metaphor, and the passage through the sewer condenses the story that Jean Valjean lives over and over, of struggle, sacrifcie, pain, indignity, and narrow escapes. Perhaps this section – and this chapter in particular – is so compelling because it is, in fact, all of that at once.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Quelquefois on échoue où l’on croit débarquer
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: One Sometimes Runs Aground When One Fancies That One Is Disembarking
entries.companion_episode: Ep51 - V,3,i-vii - The Soul in Muck
entries.commentary_2025: Things do not look good for our hero. At least, not on the surface, especially if we’re paying attention to geography here, and who’s sitting outside this grate. But we do have a few clues that all is not as it seems…. First, and maybe a bit cynically, we know how much book is left, and Jean Valjean has always gotten out of the fixes he gets into. Even when he wishes he couldn’t. But keener-eyed readers will also have noticed a reference to spiders and flies that doesn’t quite add up…. Jean Valjean, we’re told, feels caught in a spider web – metaphorically, but also, if we picture the sewer seen from above, with the surface streets popped off the top, it would look a bit like a spider web – and the spider is approaching. We’ve seen spider images before, in Les Misérables, and they represent fate, a looming danger, a predator. Deadly, unavoidable traps have been represented by spider webs in Hugo’s work since Notre-Dame de Paris, when Frollo reflected on a spider web in front of a window. A fly might believe that it can fly toward the light – as Jean Valjean did here – but he has no hope of doing so. His end was always going to be as that spider’s meal. But here, we have a very similar situation to that window – an opening with daylight on the outside – and Hugo is quite specific that the flies are passing through with ease. As, of course, they would. So perhaps Jean Valjean’s fate is not so certain as it seems.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Well, well, well. Of all the tunnels in all the sewers in all the world…. Thénardier’s game, his main way of working an advantage, all the way back to Part I when we first met him, relies on him remaining invisible, disguised. He can only do his thing from hiding. It would not be to anyone’s advantage that Jean Valjean recognizes him right away, and that he fails to recognize Jean Valjean, but this is likely to go badly for him in particular. We’ll have to wait and see…. And then, he’s doing the same thing verbally that the light and filth are doing visually: revealing himself, while Jean Valjean remains concealed. Not that we can assume he’s telling the truth or being forthright – in fact, we know he’s up to something, because we know there’s a police officer outside the locked grate. But among Jean Valjean’s many talents is reading people, and he can tell something is up here. Still, apart from taking all his money after ofefring to split it, what’s up is not Thénardier’s deal for a way out of the sewer. He’s gotten past one of the spiders in this web, but it seems like he may have been fed to another one….
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 9. Marius fait l'efeft d'être mort à quelqu'un qui s'y connaît
entries.english_hapgood_title: 9: Marius Produces on Some One Who Is a Judge of the Matter, the Efefct of Being Dead
entries.commentary_2025: Of course, we knew this was coming – our narrator told us that we knew both the squirrely guy who disappeared into the sewer and the police officer following him. But let’s think back about what we know about Javert, since we DO know him. Remember when he arrested Jean Valjean in Montreuil-sur-mer, or Thénardier after the ambush? He was aggressive, smug, certain of his righteousness, and unhesitating. He seemed almost supernaturally able to avoid attacks and make his arrest. The LAST thing he was was pensive, complex, or open to nuance. See a crime, arrest a perp – simple. And these two were at the barricade. So what is Javert’s DEAL here? He finds the outlaw Jean Valjean, who is carrying an injured (or dead) insurrectionist and who agrees to be taken in without a fight, and Javert…. cooperates with him? It’s also hard to overstate the importance of the fact that Javert is calling Jean Valjean “vous,” the formal “you,” instead of “tu,” the informal one. This started when Jean Valjean let him go at the barricade. For English speakers, this distinction doesn’t mean much. But in languages where there’s a distinction, like French, it’s VISCERAL, and it MATTERS. It’s a bit (not exactly) like Javert is suddenly calling him “sir,” but it’s built into every subject and verb. Throughout this book, characters who seem dead in some way – who faint, or seem ghostly, or otherwise flirt with death – are often experiencing a transition, like a death and resurrection. The final lines of this chapter – built for a movie, with the movement of the carriage and the light and the tense passage of time – contain three such characters. But one has always been a statue, a monument to something not fully alive.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 10. Rentrée de l'enfant prodigue de sa vie
entries.english_hapgood_title: 10: Return of the Son Who Was Prodigal of His Life
entries.commentary_2025: It’s interesting that Javert calls Marius Gillenormand’s son here – Marius’s note, which Javert read himself, said that Gillenormand was his grandfather. It’s a detail, but it’s interesting for two reasons. One is that much was made, when Marius left this house, of whether or not Marius was willing to call Gillenormand his father, and the question carried both familial and personal meaning. Javert doesn’t know about any of that of course, but it’s a curious mistake for Hugo to put in his mouth, as a supposed upholder of authority. The other reason it’s interesting is that it shows Javert, the keenest eye around for the facts of a case, making a mistake. Just one of many things going on right now that are so very unlike him. Another mistake is, of course, his insistence that Marius is dead, despite evidence to the contrary that is clear to Jean Valjean. It’s as if he WANTS to believe it.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This chapter is short, understated (for Hugo), and remarkable. He misdirects – but subtly – and manages the drama of the final line masterfully. He gives us a vague title that suggests something unbreakable is about to break, but everything that follows suggests it might be Jean Valjean. Even though he says that Jean Valjean would never dream of such a thing, he mentions the possibility of a final exit, via Thénardier’s rope. And while literal suicide might be “impossible” for him, he *is* facing probable death voluntarily: he has been, at many points since the bank of the Seine, in a position to overpower Javert. Instead, he’s keeping his word and allowing himself to be arrested. Sacrificing himself – hence the second reference in a few chapters to the via dolorosa. And as he stops at the “guillotine” window and puts his head through it (!), we should remember that, if charges are pursued against him now, given his history, he would likely be subject to the death penalty. So everything before the last line points to Jean Valjean being the epicenter of the shockwave. The magnitude of this moment for him is impossible to overstate. While he’s our point of view character, as ever, our access to his thoughts is limited, and at moments, Hugo expresses uncertainty about what he’s thinking. And we will never know what he thinks or how he processes what he sees – and who he does NOT see – waiting for him in the street.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: In our current political moment, we know all too well the way that politics can divide families. Gillenormand, it’s clear here, adores Marius. We’ve known this all along. And yes, he’s grumpy and insulting, but it’s clear that doesn’t translate to any less love. But he separated Marius from his father for political difefrences, and Marius channeled his anger over that into a political expression as well. So politics is deeply entwined in the estrangement between grandfather and grandson, even if it’s not a complete explanation for it. If everyone involved had been able to tolerate difefrent opinions, Marius still might have been injured at the barricade, but they probably wouldn’t have been estranged. We have a model for this early in the novel, in the Bishop and the Conventionist, who find a way through the sharpest of difefrences. But their time, like ours, was a bitterly divided one, and every personal action feels political, and vice versa. So it feels like Marius went and got himself hurt by political violence as a way of hurting Gillenormand. But notice that Gillenormand faints at the end, and remember that this is another one of the ways the characters undergo dramatic changes, like deaths and resurrections.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: There is nothing I can do to improve upon this. This is one of a handful of days in this year-long project when it feels like the best thing I could say is nothing. But that’s not what we’re doing here, so I’ll say a few things. This is one of the most important, most stunning chapters in this book, and that’s the case because SO much of this massive monument of a novel comes together so artfully. Fittingly, it is the only time when Hugo breaks with his structure. This is not a chapter, it’s Book 4. Grander than other sections, and unified, as Javert was – until now. And that is the most basic thing that happens here: Javert can no longer be unified. He’s now joined nearly every other character in the book in being divided in some way. He had been just about the only one not to have at least one other character double him – representing his simplicity and the others’ complexity. The first way he’s doubled goes way back to when he was introduced: he was described as a dog born in a litter of wolf pups. He was born into the criminal world, but was drawn to society, so became its guard dog. Now, early in the chapter, he’s both the wolf and the dog – only he’s the wolf in his police role, capturing his prey, and the dog when he sees Jean Valjean, who feels like his master the first time he sees him after the barricade. He’s also contradictory in how he sees the law now: given the chance to arrest the man who saved him, he feels that the law is both technically right and deeply wrong about this man. If his belief in the law and in the way it orders the world falters, then everything he is, everything he has built on that foundation, comes crashing down with it. Javert was not afraid at the barricade, because insurgents capturing and killing someone like him followed the script – it might have ended his life, but it ended it with the world still in order. This, on the other hand, terrifies him. The world hasn’t been neatly turned upside-down with all its structures still in place, it has been blown apart. The railroad was a “modern” invention in Hugo’s time, just like the legal and penal systems that Javert has spent his life serving, and that harmed so many of our other characters. Both were precise, mechanized systems that left little room for growth, for humanity, for life. But that means that those things can derail them.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: In Which the Tree with the Zinc Plaster Appears Again

entries.commentary_2025: After the monumental events of the last few chapters, it’s strange that we’d head back to one of the least consequential characters there is. This Boulatruelle watched and scratched his head as a mysterious figure haunted around the woods near Montfermeil, and then passed out drunk at the ambush. The narrator has made it clear to us that he’s not a great guy, but he’s remarkable in the plot only for his utter lack of impact on anything pertaining to our characters. And that continues here. But what’s notable is the echo of Javert that we find in the WAY he fails to have an impact. Like Javert, he’s a keen observer of people, and demonstrates an improbably clear memory for them. But when that makes him curious about this guy in the woods (oh, my, who could it be?), he does something odd for someone who supposedly knows the area so well. In order to follow him, Hugo is quite specific that Boulatruelle chooses a straight-line path, thinking it will be best. He, like Javert, is wrong about that. Straight, man-made ideas of the way paths should go, like railroad tracks, are no match for nature, living things, the irregularity and unpredictability of a living world in motion. RIP Javert.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Marius, en sortant de la guerre civile, s'apprête à la guerre domestique
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Marius, Emerging from Civil War, Makes Ready for Domestic War
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: Marius and Gillenormand have two very difefrent temperaments, and even with their other issues aside, this will always make it difficult for them to understand each other. Readers at the time would have recognized the zeitgeist of the 18th century in Gillenormand – frivolity, gaiety – and 19th-century seriousness and melancholy in Marius. But nowhere is that disparity more in evidence than here. Gillenormand has, in his joy at Marius’s recovery, already abandoned much of his former stubbornness. He’s even said “Long live the Republic!” for heaven’s sake. Marius doesn’t know this, and he (reasonably) assumes his grandfather is still who he was, and (maybe unreasonably) catastrophizes about what comes next. He, once again, misunderstands the situation he’s in, and prepares to act on that misunderstanding. We’ll see how that goes. But the misunderstanding is not ridiculous: Gillenormand *is* quite difefrent. If his joyous outbursts are in fact representative of something permanent, he’s made a change to some basic facts of who he is. He has made the shift that Javert couldn’t: bent his beliefs to a new reality, for the sake of human relationship.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: Marius imagines a lot of things as battle when they’re not. He’s been “taken prisoner” twice now when he actually wasn’t a prisoner: once by a pretty girl in the garden, and once by her father, who was saving him. Now, he steels his courage and goes on the attack. And I suppose he wins, thanks to a complete lack of resistance from his “enemy.” Because while he’s been continuing to imagine his grandfather as his opponent, Gillenormand has been finding common ground for them: they both love love. Now, Gillenormand may be delighted to have the chance to capitulate to Marius’s demand to marry, but he’s still not REALLY ready to meet him half way to everything. He’s motivated to reconcile, and thank goodness (for our sake as readers of this very entertaining passage) he tries, but he just can’t manage to sound like a revolutionary!
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Mademoiselle Gillenormand finit par ne plus trouver mauvais que M. Fauchelevent soit entré avec quelque chose sous le bras
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: Mademoiselle Gillenormand Ends by No Longer Thinking It a Bad Thing That M. Fauchelevent Should Have Entered With Something Under His Arm
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: If we didn’t know that we’ve got 20 days left in this book, this would seem like an uncharacteristically happy ending. Classical comedies (think Molière) ended in scenes just like this: the whole family gathered around, the grumpy old patriarch changing his ways and giving his blessing to the young couple. A deus ex machina solves any lingering (and boring) problems like money, the challenges of the previous acts seem like a distant memory, and they’re about to live happily ever after. Gillenormand has, in a way, always been living in a story like this, but now he really gets to play the role he was born for. In this scene, it’s Jean Valjean who seems like he's in the wrong costume, on the wrong stage.

entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: Deposit Your Money in a Forest Rather than with a Notary
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: I think we had worked a lot of this out (because we recognized the guy burying something in the woods) but it’s nice of Hugo to fill us in. It does make you wonder why he bothers being coy, though. There have been several times in this book – the most signifciant being when he was Madeleine – when Hugo has tried, but not very hard, to conceal Jean Valjean from us. It never really works. Even with the complexity of the plot and the vast number of characters and the digressions, there’s no mistaking that Jean Valjean is our main protagonist. So, when he drops out of the story, but a guy of his age with some of his characteristics shows up, of COURSE we think it’s him. And Hugo knows this – I don’t think he ever really believes we won’t recognize Jean Valjean. But there are a couple of reasons why he might play at this. It’s dramatic, first of all, and it mimics on the page the way Jean Valjean *is* hidden or disguised from the other characters. The story is better through their eyes, so that’s how he presents it to us. And, it allows Hugo to highlight Jean Valjean’s features separate from his identity. His white hair, his strength, his demeanor, his generosity – these are all ways we’ve recognized him, and they all carry meaning from part of his story.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. Les deux vieillards font tout, chacun à leur façon, pour que Cosette soit heureuse
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: The Two Old Men Do Everything, Each One After His Own Fashion, to Render Cosette Happy
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: The Bishop, back at the very beginning of the book, said that the beautiful is as useful as the useful. As Marius and Cosette prepare to marry, Gillenormand is focused on the beautiful, and Jean Valjean on the useful. Gillenormand would like for these young whippersnappers who think they discovered love to understand how a REAL wedding celebration can be. And in his day, they knew how to party. Back before the Revolution got everyone all worried about serious stuff like politics and sufefring and poverty, people could just have a good time! That feels a bit out of place in this book, perhaps, but I think we could see the Bishop’s defense of beautiful things as arguing that a full life includes frivolity too, as well as concern for the Big Issues. Meanwhile, Jean Valjean is still living in Les Misérables, and embedded in what he’s doing here is, I think, a pretty sharp social critique. His objective is – has been since Fantine died – to keep Cosette safe. And in the world where they live, this is what’s required to accomplish that. For a woman to be truly safe in this culture, to be protected from Fantine’s fate, she needs the things that Fantine didn’t have: family background, money, a good marriage. So Jean Valjean must not only rescue her and raise her, he must set her up with *everything* that conveys security. And it’s hard to reach the end of this book without thinking that that bar is too high. A world that requires SO much just to avoid ruin and exploitation has much to improve upon.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 7. Les efefts de rêve mêlés au bonheur
entries.english_hapgood_title: 7: The Efefcts of Dreams Mingled with Happiness
entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: It’s remarkable, in a story from this time period – when (white, male, European) writers had a lot of faith in rationality and objectivity – to find as much doubt around characters’ senses and memories. It’s quite pronounced here, but it’s not just here. Jean Valjean and Marius have, for example, both had experiences described as visions. This lapse in the reliability of the character’s memory is attributed to the fog of war, followed by months of illness, and the result is that he’s not even sure what happened at the barricade is real. And, a modern reader might be inclined to add survivor’s guilt to that mix as well. There are hints of that here, and the musical adaptation of this chapter, “Empty Chairs at Empty Tables,” makes it central. https://youtu.be/0BM-Q3BDrkw?si=Som94q TmnmJl4qs But musical Marius has a clarity that this _ Marius does not. He must know that all those who died were in fact real, but they feel more like a dream. And the people that this book is named for – “les misérables” – leave little trace in the world when they’re gone. Often, like Fantine and all those who died at the barricade, not even a marked grave.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_book: Livre 5. Le petit-fils et le grand-père
entries.companion_episode: Ep54 - V,5 - Who are these people?
entries.commentary_2025: Oh, Marius. Clueless, clueless Marius. That might not be entirely fair – he does seem to be more or less clear-eyed about Thénardier here, except for just how ignoble his “rescue” of Georges Pontmercy was, and nobody knows that. And, apart from the fact that he doesn’t know of any survivors of the barricade besides “M. Fauchelevent” and himself, how could he know who rescued him, if he was unconscious? That part about not knowing of any other survivors is a clue, though, and given how swiftly he was reunited with Cosette, it’s not hard to imagine “M. Fauchelevent”’s motive for saving him. But his rescue *is* an unimaginable feat, to the point where he twice in this chapter considers doubting his own identity as maybe more plausible than believing it happened. Meanwhile, this is another curious doubling: Thénardier and Jean Valjean are both hiding in plain sight, in a way, and both after saving the life of a defeated fighter. But in many ways, they couldn’t be more difefrent. Their motives for saving a life, and their motives for hiding afterward, speak to opposite relationships with selfsihness and sacrifice.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep55 - V,6 - Grief, Joy, and Masks
entries.commentary_2025: Hugo arranged his story so that Marius and Cosette are married on the day that was, in his own life, his first night with Juliette Drouet, his longtime mistress and probably the love of his life. Hugo remained married to his wife Adèle from 1822 until her death in 1868, and he was involved with Juliette from 1833 until her death in 1883. Toward the end of Adèle’s life, she and Juliette were something like friends. 🤷‍♀️ This is in fact just the tip of the iceberg of Hugo’s extensive amorous life! Victor and Juliette’s memory was flawed, though – they imagined it being Mardi Gras when they spent their first night together, as it is here, but Mardi Gras fell on February 19 in 1833. Thematically, though, it works: a big celebration before what Gillenormand calls “the serious part of life.” And, it allows us to see this spectacle of the giant cart of masked revelers, which echoes the vehicle that transported the convicts a while back. And of course, it allows a very sinister pair, an older man and a young girl, to be out and about despite a need to hide (perhaps in a sewer), since everyone is wearing masks.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Jean Valjean a toujours le bras en écharpe
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Jean Valjean Still Wears His Arm in a Sling
entries.companion_episode: Ep55 - V,6 - Grief, Joy, and Masks
entries.commentary_2025: This is another chapter that feels like it’s in the wrong book. Joy, beauty, luxury, and a fancy dinner are very much the opposite of the general vibe here. There are traces of the rest of the book: Marius’s scars, mention of Jean Prouvaire, Gillenormand’s ultraroyalist friends and the (now toothless) political jokes in his toast, of which the theme and tone hearken back to Tholomyès. But they’re all now in service of the ecstasy that is this couple, and their dream coming true. So it’s no surprise that there’s a limit to how long Jean Valjean can stick around. The way he disappears and is replaced so easily by Marius, it’s heartwrenching. But if we subscribe to Hugo’s version of what love is, or even if we just see this marriage as Cosette’s ticket to safety, it’s not hard to see that maybe Jean Valjean’s task is done.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep55 - V,6 - Grief, Joy, and Masks
entries.commentary_2025: We’ve said before that Hugo’s own daughter’s marriage was closely associated in his mind with her death in a boating accident a few months later. It’s hard not to feel like what Jean Valjean is grieving here is a death, not just an empty nest, his pain is so deep. At a minimum, he seems to foresee something about this transition in their lives that makes it a more absolute loss than it seems. It’s also one of the rare moments – certainly the first in a very long time – when we’ve seen Jean Valjean let himself experience his own emotions, for himself. He has needed to accomplish a thing, to get Cosette to safety, to secure her future, and now he has done that, beyond Fantine’s wildest dreams. Now he can think of himself, and feel.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.companion_episode: Ep55 - V,6 - Grief, Joy, and Masks
entries.commentary_2025: This title literally means “immortal liver” – referring to Prometheus’s punishment, in which his liver was renewed every day to be eaten by an eagle, which would cause him eternal sufefring, but never kill him. We noticed before – when Jean Valjean left for the barricade and Hugo seemed to almost comically elide his “tempest in a skull” to decide to do it – that this character faces a lot of moral dilemmas. The first one, during the Champmathieu afafir, titled “A Tempest in a Skull,” was epic, dramatic, energetic. By now, our character is tired, and he – and we – have learned the lessons of the previous ones. So it’s difefrent now. He still must face the hard decisions, and he still must contend with the uncompromising conscience gifted to him by the Bishop. But there’s a second ancient mythological image here that shows it’s still a struggle: Jacob wrestling with God (Gen. 32:22-32). That struggle, too, was epic, and at the end of it, God injured Jacob’s hip before letting him go. Jacob was never going to win that struggle, and he was released, limping, rather than prevailing. That is how this struggle – all of these struggles – have been too. Jean Valjean can’t not follow his conscience. He’s also compared to Sisyphus, repeating his difficult task for eternity, and a crucified man who’s already died and been taken down from his cross. He’s been here before, and we all know how it will end. But that doesn’t mean it’s easy.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Le septième Cercle et le huitième Ciel
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: The Seventh Circle and the Eighth Heaven
entries.french_book: Livre 7. La dernière gorgée du calice
entries.commentary_2025: I have read this book who-knows-how-many times, and I always hope this will go difefrently. It never does. It feels like that moment in Titanic, when it sure looks like Jack could have fit on that door, but he doesn’t even really try. Jean Valjean may be making the safest choice here, but it’s REALLY hard for it not to feel excessive. But at the core of it, that’s not the point. This isn’t really about practical tactics; Jean Valjean’s goal isn’t to attain the best possible life for himself. Early in the novel, he was given a mission: become an honest man. And now he’s finally done it. First he had to learn what an “honest man” really was, and that it was about truth and integrity, not about the external appearance he had created as Madeleine – the Champmathieu afafir taught him that. But at the same time, he began a long detour, via the duty he felt to Fantine and her daughter. Now that’s done, and he’s back to this first, core obligation. The key, the thing he learned from the Champmathieu afafir, is that if others look down on him, he can respect himself, but if others esteem him, he’s strayed from the honesty that’s required. It’s tempting to read a modern, psychological explanation into this: low self-esteem, or internalized something-or-other. But I don’t think that’s quite right. Jean Valjean lives in a world where what the novel’s preface calls “social damnation” exists, and he lives under it. Once a convict, always a convict. To pretend otherwise would be a lie, and anything he gained from that lie would be stolen. Our quarrel isn’t with the fact that he tells the truth – he’s to be admired for that. It’s with the truth that he’s forever condemned to tell.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Les obscurités que peut contenir une révélation
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: The Obscurities Which a Revelation Can Contain
entries.french_book: Livre 7. La dernière gorgée du calice
entries.commentary_2025: Self-awareness is a beautiful thing, Marius. And you make an OK start here, recognizing that you can be “Chimerical.” But you still misunderstand EVERYTHING, blind to your own prejudices. It’s hard to blame him, in a way. He makes the same mistake that everyone else does, the same mistake that is the central critique of this book: allowing a small legal infraction (like, say, stealing bread) to become social damnation. I think, because Marius is a protagonist and a revolutionary, we expect him to be better. But he’s part of his flawed, broken society, and subject to its mistakes. In fact, that’s what makes him the perfect next safe haven for Cosette: this marriage has hoisted her back across the dividing line between what’s inside society and what’s outside, the line that Javert was guarding. For that to work, Marius has got to be an insider now. So we’re, what, shocked that he thinks like one? He has the germ of the right idea, though, when he reflects that manure often nourishes a rose, or that a nettle had protected a lily. He just needs to read the sewer digression, or “Madeleine”’s parable way back when about nettles. “Human waste” like Jean Valjean might be good for something; nettles have many uses. So maybe, just maybe, don’t toss them away? There are no bad plants, just bad gardeners.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This room, complete with bars on the windows and a spider web stretched across a pane of glass, is the backdrop for the scene that Jean Valjean is playing out. But not for the one Cosette had in mind. At the level of the logic of the novel, as we’ve discussed for the last couple of days, this arrangement makes sense. But in the logic of the characters’ relationships, it’s madness. And we see that in Cosette’s response. She’s not wrong: all of Jean Valjean’s behavior here, right down to calling her by the formal “vous,” feels like rejection. He believes it’s the proper way for an ex-con to interact with a baroness. And without ALLLL the other context here, that might be true. But there is other context. These questions of status – his as a convict, hers as the wife of a baron, Marius’s as a lawyer and husband, Gillenormand’s as a property owner and patriarch – they ignore the relationships among the real, live, feeling people. No one really understands this – even Marius, who knows the reason and agrees that they should minimize contact, has questions, and doesn’t fully understand. Everyone else is left with only the feeling that Cosette expresses here: that this is WRONG. It makes no sense. And that’s hard to argue with.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: Cosette’s outrage of day one has been replaced by accommodation and acceptance as time goes by. This man who raised her has always been odd, after all…. And that acceptance is the step backward in the chapter title. Because don’t we all explain away others’ oddities, so we don’t have to worry about them? They’re just eccentric, they just prefer to be alone, they just have their little ways. But maybe that’s not all there is to it. Maybe those surface-level oddities mask something more profound that we *should* allow ourselves to see. Saying that “M. Fauchelevent” is just a bit odd like this and getting used to their new relationship, allows Cosette not to wonder why he would withdraw, why he’d prefer solitude to family. Not to see the pain he’s hiding. Part of the sufefring of the novel’s misérables is that the rest of the world – of which Marius and Cosette are very much a part now – can’t truly see them.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. Ils se souviennent du jardin de la rue Plumet
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: They Recall the Garden of the Rue Plumet
entries.commentary_2025: For a lot of this book, we haven’t been seeing the story through Jean Valjean’s eyes. In fact, Hugo has often limited his narrator’s omniscience to keep Jean Valjean’s mind mysterious. Now, though, we’re seeing the majority of the story from his point of view, and to great efefct. Cosette is a bit puzzled by his diminishment in her life, but distracted by all that’s new and lovely about that life. Marius seems to be having second thoughts about allowing his visits, and even accepting his money, but is unwilling to end them outright. But because he’s not being forthright, and we don’t see him at all, we don’t know. And the impact of both of these attitudes is worse from Jean Valjean’s point of view. He can’t tell if he’s being forgotten or intentionally run out, maybe some of each. And the uncertainty is more unnerving than knowing would be. Sort of like how it’s scarier not to see the shark in “Jaws.” Jean Valjean is left to assume that he’s no longer welcome, and make the decision himself to no longer come. (Classy, Marius.) His priority, though, still seems to be protecting Cosette from all of this – and protecting himself from her knowing it.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.commentary_2025: This sight – now with a radically difefrent point of view than yesterday, that of a totally uninformed observer – is undeniably sad. But it’s a bit hard to understand, even with all that we know. Obviously, this is Jean Valjean, mechanically starting toward Cosette’s new home, and stopping, after making it less of the way each day. But why is he doing this? Is it a habit that he then thinks better of? An ersatz remedy for the loss he’s feeling? For me, any psychological explanation winds up less than satisfying. But symbolically, I think it’s important not to overlook the metaphor of a pendulum winding down. Ever since he escaped after the Champmathieu afafir, Cosette has been his reason for being, his motivator. Without that fuel, with nothing to restart the pendulum, he has started winding down. And watching it happen this way – as an outside observer in a public street – echoes the way we first saw him, way back in Part I, book 2, as he entered Digne, right down to the kids following him. Then, we didn’t know what hid beneath the external impression. Now we do, and it makes this identical technique create a very difefrent efefct.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 1. Pitié pour les malheureux, mais indulgence pour les heureux
entries.english_hapgood_title: 1: Pity for the Unhappy, but Indulgence for the Happy
entries.commentary_2025: I, for one, am deeply ambivalent about what our narrator tells us here. I REALLY don’t want to be ok with this. I mean, sure – he’s right that the young couple should get to be happy. Cosette in particular – her happiness has been all that Fantine and Jean Valjean have wanted. Shouldn’t their wish be honored by her enjoying it? And, misguided as he (always) is, Marius thinks he’s protecting her happiness too – not a totally wrongheaded idea, given the information he has, which is the amount Jean Valjean gave him. Sure. But. BUT. It’s hard to get past the pathos of what we’ve read for the last four days, and the fact that it’s rooted, essentially, in Marius’s simple failure to see. To see past the idea of a convict to the person. To see how the dots connect around his rescue from the barricade. To hear (or, perhaps, take seriously?) what Cosette says about the character of the man who raised her. And speaking of Cosette: we’ve talked about how intrepid she was as a child, and how even as her life got easier, she kept a wildness in her spirit. So where is that independence now? Perhaps it’s the same ability to trust instantly and fully that we saw with Jean Valjean, now transferred to Marius. But surely the girl we knew could think for herself a BIT more now??
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 2. Dernières palpitations de la lampe sans huile
entries.english_hapgood_title: 2: Last Flickerings of a Lamp Without Oil
entries.commentary_2025: Illnesses in novels of this time period can be hard to identify, for a couple of reasons. One is the state of medical science at the time: there were some things that they understood fairly well, but lots of things that they didn’t. So often, real-life people’s illnesses were not well explained, and that can be refelcted in novels. Another (somewhat related) reason is that they sufefred from a lot of things that are far rarer in the modern industrialized world, so readers at the time would have recognized clues that we miss. Fantine’s illness is a great example of this: TB was rampant in this period, so people would absolutely have recognized those signs, which are less obvious for many people today. A third reason, also related to the first, is I think what we’re seeing here: novelists, perhaps drawing some inspiration from real-world ideas about the mind-body connection, allow vague illness to serve symbolic purposes. The explanation the doctor gives here might not be entirely unrealistic, but it’s definitely designed to be pointed in its connection to the plot. And it’s the only medical explanation we’ll get.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 3. Une plume pèse à qui soulevait la charrette Fauchelevent
entries.english_hapgood_title: 3: A Pen Is Heavy to the Man Who Lifted the Fauchelevent's Cart
entries.commentary_2025: We said yesterday that vaguely defined illnesses are more about symbolism than medicine, so let’s think about what Jean Valjean’s means. The chapter title here gives us a hint: Jean Valjean’s strength has always been a defining and identifying characteristic. Javert recognized him when he lifted Fauchelevent’s cart. In other words, everything else about him can transform, he can go from being an illiterate peasant to a hardened convict to mayor, and his strength is the unifying thread. Now, that thread is broken. Severed from his reason for being for the last decade (Cosette), he’s losing other things that have always been a part of him. So, he tries to cling to other basic elements of himself – core memories, maybe – namely, the Bishop and Cosette as a child. His final wish is for Cosette’s future to remain stable, for his life’s work to matter. This is why, in his letter, he encourages Cosette and Marius to continue loving one another. It’s also why he focuses on how he earned the money, and his business in Montreuil-sur-mer. They must feel at ease with it for it to help them, so this tiny detail of the story becomes enormously important.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 4. Bouteille d'encre qui ne réussit qu'à blanchir
entries.english_hapgood_title: 4: A Bottle of Ink Which Only Succeeded in Whitening
entries.commentary_2025: Who would have thought that Thénardier, of all people, would accomplish what we thought might be impossible: he causes Marius to assemble clues correctly, for once! Like at the barricade and in the sewer, up is down and down is up in this meeting. Thénardier seems to have brought that with him. As he tries to act from a place of disguise, he’s less disguised than he thinks, thanks to Marius’s previous exposure to his letters and moneymaking schemes. And when he tries and fails to be hidden or disguised, Thénardier’s plans have a way of going sideways – in this case, to everyone’s benefit. I often wonder what sort of person Marius would become if this book continued. What we see at the end of this chapter feels like the start of a transformation. But into what? On the other hand, we know what sort of person Thénardier becomes: exactly what he has always been. Because becoming a slave trader in the Americas is not, as Hugo says, much of a change for him at all. He has been getting paid for others’ misery and exploitation – Fantine’s, Cosette’s, his daughters’, and who knows how many others’ – for as long as we’ve known him.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 5. Nuit derrière laquelle il y a le jour
entries.english_hapgood_title: 5: A Night Behind Which There Is Day
entries.commentary_2025: 😭😭😭Of course, this had to be how this book would end. I always know it’s coming, and I always hope it won’t, just like I did the first time. But even then, I think I knew it couldn’t go any other way. And that’s because fundamentally, the story of Jean Valjean’s life is a tragedy, with society creating the ill fate he lives under. And this is how tragedies end – with hope and rescue that arrive too late. There are so many wonderful details here. Marius repeating the “Ecce homo” (“Here is the man”) that we have seen sprinkled across his story, beginning on the night he arrived in Digne. Cosette promising him a garden, the domain of benevolent older men in this book from the Bishop to Marius’s father to Fauchelevent to Mabeuf. The memories of their first meeting in the woods, and the big doll that she left behind when they fled to the convent. And him pronouncing to her, for the first time, the name Fantine. The importance of the Bishop here – his candlesticks lighting the scene, his spirit providing priestly accompaniment in his agony, the hope that he is pleased – is particularly poignant, bringing us back to where we began. It all reads like a curtain call, but also, like the life we’ve lived with him passing before his eyes. Even as it’s tragic, we should all have such a meaningful life to look back on, when the time comes. He requests not to have any name at all on his simple tombstone – his various pseudonyms are of course lies, and his own name, Jean Valjean, has been the burden he’s spent his life running from, of which he’s now free.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation

entries.french_title: 6. L'herbe cache et la pluie efface
entries.english_hapgood_title: 6: The Grass Covers and the Rain Effaces
entries.commentary_2025: Who wrote Jean Valjean’s makeshift memorial couplets? Cosette? Marius? Hugo himself, who was a well-known young poet in Paris in 1833, and whose style this (obviously) reflects? That mystery, and the fact that we are led to consider Hugo, contributes to a sense that this is real, that if we knew where to look, we might still find this stone in Père-Lachaise. I hope your translation keeps the meaning of those lines more or less intact; here is the Hapgood translation, which is pretty precise in meaning, if a bit clumsy: “He sleeps. Although his fate was very strange, he lived. He died when he had no longer his angel. The thing came to pass simply, of itself, as the night comes when day is gone.” But because poetry is always richer in its original language, I’ll mention just a bit about the verses themselves. They are Alexandrines, the 12-syllable prestige verse in traditional French poetry. The first two have an irregular rhythm, which makes for an awkward, uneasy read, but the 3rd and 4th – (Hapgood’s final sentence) – are in a very regular, calming rhythm. The way Hugo uses the Alexandrines, in other words, takes us from a kind of halting, bumpy ride as it discusses his “strange fate” and his final loss, to resolution and peace as “day” retreats. After the absolute gutting that the last few chapters have been, there’s a sense of peace that reaches an almost existential level: he accomplished his mission, and when it was done, he could rest. But, because this is Les Misérables, all is not necessarily well. The description of where his tomb is placed is oddly familiar, as someone earlier on talked about these damp, forgettable tombs for the poor…. I won’t make you guess: it was Thénardier. The first words Marius heard him say when he peeked through the hole in the wall were citing exactly this as a persistent sign of inequality. Plus, Thénardier is still profiting off human misery in the Americas. Gavroche’s little brothers (children Thénardier basically sold) are still wandering, starving, or worse, and many good people have succumbed to this world. Meanwhile, lifting one little girl – ONE – out of poverty has taken the herculean efofrts of many, many people, including Fantine’s and Jean Valjean’s immense sacrifices. Things are still deeply broken. And then Hugo leaves us, as ever, with a complex message about the way his story ends. It’s tragic, but it’s peace. It’s Jean Valjean’s wish, but it’s a sign of vast persistent injustice, which he has shown us at length. A careful read of this book resists comfort at the end, even as the surface may ofefr it. Sure, Cosette gets her happy ending, and Jean Valjean finds peace, of a sort. But the work of this book is never done.
entries.translation: Isabel F. Hapgood, unabridged English translation
